**`HttpCx`** is `Clone + Send + Sync`: an `ExecutionRef`, an `Arc<RequestHead>`, the matched route, path parameters, the client address, a take-once body slot, an interior-mutable response-head writer, and the app's `Timer`. Its methods include `head()`, `method()`, `uri()`, `headers()`, `route()`, `mount_prefix()` (§3.8), `exec()`, `ext::<T>()`, `take_body()`, `response_headers()`, `client_addr()` and `timer()`, the app's `Timer` as an `&Arc<dyn Timer>`, which anything timed inside a response reads.

**Extractors** [17] are `Path<T>`, `Query<T>`, `Json<T>`, `Form<T>`, `Bytes`, `BodyStream`, `Multipart`, `Header<H>` (typed, from the `headers` crate), `HeaderMap`, `LastEventId`, `HttpCx`, and every container type. `Json`, `Form`, `Bytes`, `BodyStream` and `Multipart` consume the body. The body limit is a server setting (`.body_limit(2 * MB)`) that `#[meta(BodyLimit(..))]` can override per route. Bodies over the limit fail with 413 before deserialization. A `multer::Error` a handler returns with `?` is mapped to an `ExtractError`: `TooLarge` (413) when the body stream ended at the limit, `Malformed` (400) naming `body` otherwise.

**Responses** [18] are any `T: IntoReply<Http>`:

- `Json<T>`, `Bytes`, `String`, `()` (204), `Created<T>`, `NoContent`, and `(StatusCode, T)`.
- `WithHeaders<T>`, and `Response::builder()` for any status, headers and body.
- `Body::stream(s)` for a streaming body.
- `Sse<S>` with `Event::default().data(..).id(EventId).event(EventName).retry(..)`. Data is split into `data:` lines at CR, LF and CRLF alike, since a reader ends a line at any of the three. `EventId` and `EventName` are built fallibly (`EventId::new(..)?`) and refuse line terminators, and the id refuses U+0000, which a reader ignores, so a bad value fails where it is built and never mid-stream. Keep-alive comments are written as `: keepalive`, per the SSE spec, when the period passes with nothing written. The period is timed by the app's `Timer`, which `HttpCx::timer()` reads; `fw-http` picks no runtime, and a body with `keep_alive` is polled wherever the app runs. `Timer` offers `sleep(d)` and no resettable sleep, and the body requests one sleep of the period at the first poll that finds the stream waiting after a write; a write drops the running sleep, and events written back to back request none. The guarantee is a comment after at least the period of idleness, sometimes a little later, never sooner. A period comfortably below the shortest proxy idle timeout in the deployment is the one to set. `keep_alive(Duration::ZERO)` turns the keep-alive off, as leaving it uncalled does, and a later zero turns off an earlier period: a zero period taken literally would write a comment every time the stream is found waiting. An error after the stream has started (§2.3) is written as an event named `error` carrying the problem document, and the stream ends. The content type is `text/event-stream; charset=utf-8`, with `Cache-Control: no-cache`.

### 3.2 Routing [15]

`fw-http` owns the router, so every backend routes identically:

- Patterns use `{name}` segments plus an optional trailing `{*rest}`. A name is identifier-like, Unicode included; an empty segment (`/a//b`) is refused. The attribute macro and the router check one grammar with the same reason texts, so a literal refused at compile time and a prefix-joined pattern refused at `prepare` read alike.
- A trailing slash is insignificant: both the pattern and the request path drop it, except for `/`.
- Each request segment is percent-decoded as a path: `+` stays `+`, `%2F` decodes to `/` inside its segment without splitting it, and a `{*rest}` value is the raw remainder decoded the same way. A static segment matches the request segment as sent or once decoded, so `/caf%C3%A9` matches `/café`. A decoded sequence that is not UTF-8 is captured with U+FFFD per invalid sequence, since the path does name a route; a typed `Path<T>` over it then fails as `Malformed` naming the field. A parameter or rest never captures an empty segment: `/u//x` does not match `/u/{id}/x`.
- Precedence is decided once, in `prepare`, by a key compared segment by segment, static before parameter before rest, so `/users/me` answers before `/users/{id}` whatever the declaration order. The first matching pattern decides the method check: its handler, else `GET` for `HEAD`, else 204 for `OPTIONS`, else 405. A less specific pattern is not consulted for the method: with `GET /users/me` and `DELETE /users/{id}` declared, `DELETE /users/me` answers 405, because the URI names the resource and 405 says that resource lacks the method (RFC 9110).
- Routes are built in `prepare`. Two routes with the same method and the same normalized pattern, or two patterns that differ only in parameter names at one position (`/u/{id}` and `/u/{name}`) whatever their methods, are a `Configure` error naming both handlers as `Controller::method`; `HttpCx::param` would otherwise answer differently by method.
- `prepare` also checks every `Path<T>` against its route, by running `T`'s `Deserialize` impl against a deserializer that records what it asks for, so a mismatch is caught at startup rather than by the first request. A struct is checked by its field names, serde renames included; a tuple by its count; a scalar or newtype requires exactly one parameter. A map, a `#[serde(flatten)]` struct and a hand-written impl calling `deserialize_any` ask for no names and are not checked, which the documentation says.
- A path that matches nothing answers 404. The global error handlers receive it as `CallError::new(NotFound, ..)` whose source is `fw_http::NoRoute`, a public marker, so `source_as::<NoRoute>()` tells a miss from a handler's own `NotFound`; unclaimed, it renders by kind.
- A matching path with the wrong method answers 405 with an `Allow` header, which RFC 9110 requires. The error handlers receive it as a `CallError` of kind `BadRequest` whose source is `fw_http::MethodNotAllowed`, a public type with `method()`, the request's, and `allow()`, the header value as the router computed it; `err.downcast_ref::<CallError>()?.source_as::<MethodNotAllowed>()` reaches it, the pattern `NoRoute` uses. It is wrapped rather than offered bare because `from_boxed` answers `Internal` for a type it does not recognise, and an app reshaping every error would then send a 500 for a 405. No `ErrorKind` is 405: every kind maps on all four transports and 405 is HTTP's alone. `BadRequest` is the generic client-error kind, and 413 and 415 already ride on it with the exact status applied at rendering: an unclaimed 405 renders as problem details with status 405 and `Allow` while the kind is `BadRequest`, and one reshaped to another kind renders by that kind. `Allow` is the pattern's methods in declaration order, then `HEAD` after `GET` when only `GET` is declared, then `OPTIONS` when no handler declares it, computed once in `prepare`.
- `HEAD` is answered from the `GET` handler with the body omitted, unless a `HEAD` handler exists (RFC 9110 requires general-purpose servers to support `HEAD`). The body is dropped unread, a body of unknown length reporting its end as `Completed`, a `HEAD` answer owing the client no body (§2.6); when the response carries no `Content-Length` and the dropped body's size hint is exact, that size is set, except on 1xx, 204 and 304. A `HEAD` handler's own stream is left in the response for the backend to discard and reports `Completed` the same way.
- `OPTIONS` without a handler answers 204 with `Allow` directly, offered to no error handler. CORS preflight never reaches routing (§3.4).

### 3.3 Pre-dispatch [19]

Middleware is HTTP-specific, so it isn't a core role. Middleware types are still ordinary container bindings, and the metadata that declares them reports its dependencies (`Meta::dependencies`), so wiring checks them.

```rust
pub trait Middleware: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn handle(&self, req: Request, next: fw_http::middleware::Next<'_>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Response, BoxError>> + Send;
}
```

A middleware's `Err` is a pre-dispatch failure like a layer's: an authentication middleware returns `Err(CallError::unauthorized(..).into())` and the app's error handlers shape it; no middleware renders its own errors. The `Err` is caught at the entry's own boundary, where its panic is caught, and offered from there. `Next::run(req)` answers the same `Result<Response, BoxError>`, and what it answers is `Ok`: a failure further in has already reached the error handlers and been answered or rendered at its own entry, and that response is what the outer middleware receives, so an outer CORS entry adds its headers to the 401 an inner authentication middleware's `Err` became, which a browser needs to read the 401. Propagating the inner `Err` outward would skip every outer entry's response handling on a failure and move a scoped entry's failure to the unscoped side, where only the global handlers apply. The `Result` keeps `next.run(req).await` a middleware's answer as it stands, and `?` on it compiles. `fw_http::middleware::Next` holds the middleware chain and the request; the core's `Next<'a, T>` holds the interceptor chain. A module importing both qualifies one or writes `use .. as ..`, as std's `fmt::Result` and `io::Error` are imported by module. No alias ships, and the two differ in signature, so a wrong import fails at the type.

There is one middleware stage, **pre-dispatch**, declared in module metadata:

```rust
m.meta::<fw_http::PreDispatch>()
    .apply_value(Cors::new().allow_origin("https://app.example").allow_credentials(true))
    .apply::<RequestId>()                                           // unscoped: every request, misses included
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())                              // tower, unscoped (§3.4)
    .layer(HostAuthLayer::new()).supplies::<CurrentUser>()          // the layer inserts `CurrentUser` (§3.8)
    .layer_for(["/files/*"], RequestBodyLimitLayer::new(50 * MB))   // tower, scoped by route pattern
    .apply_for::<ApiKeyAuth>(["/admin/*"]).exclude(["/admin/health"])
    .adopt::<CurrentUser>();                                        // into the execution, as `Ext<CurrentUser>`
```

`.adopt::<T>()` is a further entry, unscoped, which copies `T` from the request's `http::Extensions` into the execution's at its place in declaration order (§3.8). `.supplies::<T>()` is a declaration about the entry written before it: that entry puts `T` in the request's `http::Extensions`, as a tower layer authenticating the request does. The declaration runs nothing, on a backend or embedded, and only an embedding whose adapter declares `host_extensions: false` reads it, where the entry runs (§3.8). `prepare` refuses a `supplies` with no entry before it, on a backend as well, as it refuses a stray `exclude`: "`supplies` at src/main.rs:196:33 follows no pre-dispatch entry; it declares what the entry before it inserts, and a value the host keeps is copied in by the embedding with `Embedded::forward`". A `supplies` written after an `adopt` entry is refused the same way, on a backend and on every embedding and whatever the two types, with "`adopt` copies a value out of the request and inserts none; declare the `supplies` after the entry that inserts it", and the declaration is kept off the entry, so the embedding's check counts only entries that insert.

The stage runs in two sub-steps, because a path rewrite has to happen before route matching while scoping by route pattern needs the match. Unscoped entries run first: they can rewrite the path with `req.set_path(..)`, they see misses, and they can answer without calling `next`, which is how a CORS preflight is answered; an authentication middleware refuses by returning `Err`, which reaches the error handlers. Then the route is matched and `route_to` (X8) switches the execution to the controller's module. Then the entries whose pattern matches the route run. Then `dispatch` (guards, interceptors, handler, error handlers). To the user it is one stage in one order: the order written, with modules in collection order (DESIGN §3.2) where several declare entries. Both sub-steps run inside the error chain: an entry's `Err` reaches the error handlers as a `BoxError` and its panic as `PanicRecovered`, and on a miss only the global error handlers apply, since no handler matched. A request that arrives with no execution to open, during the drain, never reaches the stage (§10).

A scope is a route pattern whose last segment may be `*` or `{*name}`, matching one or more segments: `/admin/*` covers `/admin/users` and `/admin/{id}/notes`, not `/admin`, and a scope's parameter covers a route's parameter or static segment whatever the names. `exclude` applies to the entry written before it; `apply_for` or `layer_for` with an empty pattern list is refused at `prepare`. Each scope of a scoped entry must cover a route the entry does not exclude, on HTTP and on gRPC alike: `prepare` refuses a scope that covers none, so `["/admin/*", "/typo"]` is refused for `/typo` and an entry whose covered routes are all excluded is refused for each scope. `ulo_http::stage::Stage::unreached` runs the check once for both transports and answers one `Failure` per refused scope, carrying the declaring `location`, the `subject` `"pre-dispatch entry"` and the scope in `scopes`, which `PrepareError::entries()` hands to a test as data.

The request has two heads. The `RequestHead` input is seeded at `Execution::open` with the head as the client sent it, and the `HttpCx` that `dispatch` receives is built from the request as the stage leaves it, so a rewritten path or a header an entry set reaches the extractors: `HttpCx::head()` reads the stage's head, `Dep<RequestHead>` the client's. An entry's failure is offered with a context built from the head as its sub-step received it, no body and no upgrade; in the scoped sub-step the matched handler's tiers run before the global ones, in the unscoped sub-step only the global ones run, even when a route matches later.

Each entry is resolved through the module that declared it, inside the request's execution: `Mounted::module_meta::<T>()` (X9) yields `(ModuleRef, Arc<T>)` in collection order, and `ModuleRef::with_execution(&ExecutionRef)` gives a resolver with that module's visibility, so a per-execution middleware is built once per request and a binding only its own module sees resolves as `wire()` checked it.

There is no per-module middleware. Auth for a group of routes is a pattern-scoped pre-dispatch entry, which runs before guards and can set `CurrentUser`; logging, metrics or transforming a module's responses is an interceptor; rejecting a request is a guard. What the stage cannot express is "every controller in this module" by naming the module: `.at(prefix)` (§2.5) with a pattern-scoped entry covers it. If a case needs the module named, the enhancer stack gains a module tier (global, module, controller, method), inside the error chain and with the existing tiers' semantics; middleware does not return for it.

### 3.4 CORS and tower [20]

`fw_http::Cors` follows the Fetch specification's CORS protocol. It answers preflights (`OPTIONS` with `Access-Control-Request-Method`) with 204 and the `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers, adds `Vary: Origin`, and never echoes `*` together with credentials. That last combination is forbidden by the spec, so it's refused in `prepare`.

`.layer(L)` accepts any `tower::Layer` over `fw_http::Service`, which is `Service<http::Request<HttpBody>, Response = http::Response<HttpBody>>`, and `.layer_for(patterns, L)` scopes one by route pattern. Layers are composed once, in `prepare`, never per request. An unscoped layer wraps the whole stage before matching, so it can rewrite and it sees misses. For scoped layers, `prepare` builds each route's own stack from the layers whose pattern matches it, in declaration order, and routes with the same set of layers share one stack; a matched request runs its route's prebuilt stack. Layers run inside the pre-dispatch stage, so they behave the same on the backend and under every embedding host (§3.8), the native ones that are not tower-based included, and they sit inside the error chain: a layer's `Err` reaches the error handlers as a `BoxError` and its panic as `PanicRecovered`. A response a layer builds itself, tower-http's auth answering 401 for example, is a response and not an error, so error handlers don't see it; that is inherent to tower, and the documentation says so. The continuation (the rest of the chain, the connection info and the upgrade future, which an `http::Request` cannot carry) rides the request's extensions in a take-once slot every clone shares, and the chain is one-shot: a layer that calls its inner service twice for one request, a retry layer, or that builds a new request without the original's extensions, gets a bare 500 and an `error` log line. The body has been read and the middleware consumed by then; no slot shape could replay it, and `layer`'s documentation says retries belong in a client. **X23: one stage type for HTTP and gRPC.** `PreDispatch<T: HttpCarried = Http>` is one type and one set of scope rules: `fw_http::PreDispatch` is HTTP's instance and `PreDispatch<Grpc>` gRPC's, each a distinct metadata key read by its own server (§6.2), so an entry declared for one never runs on the other. `HttpCarried` is `Transport + __private::Carried`, `Carried` a public, doc-hidden trait that `fw-http` implements for `Http` and `fw-grpc` for `Grpc`, the two transports whose requests are `http::Request`s, so `m.meta::<PreDispatch<Ws>>()` is E0277. The seal holds by the `__private` convention, the workspace's boundary for sibling and generated code, and not by the compiler: a `pub(crate)` seal would keep `fw-grpc` out, and moving `Grpc`'s impl into `fw-http` behind a feature would couple the two crates. `fw_http::stage::{Stage<T>, ScopedStage<T>, StageHost, Rest}` are public so that `fw-grpc` runs its `PreDispatch<Grpc>` entries through the one stage rather than a copy of it. WebSocket and RPC have no pre-dispatch stage: guards and interceptors cover them.

### 3.5 WebSocket upgrades [21]

When a gateway's path matches a request carrying `Upgrade: websocket`, the router hands the request to `fw-ws` through the upgrade future the backend (§3.7) or the embedding adapter (§3.8) took from the connection; an adapter declaring `upgrades: false` has no gateway on its port, refused in `prepare`. `fw-ws` decides the RFC 6455 handshake from the request's head and runs the connection on the upgraded I/O, an `Upgraded` it reads through `futures-io`'s traits as they stand, with no conversion (§3.7). The hand-off is `fw_http::UpgradeHandler`, registered through the `Upgrades` module metadata by `fw_ws::WsModule` (§4.1), and the server reads it before route matching on any request carrying `Upgrade`.

**X21: the upgrade handler has the server's lifecycle.** An upgraded connection has left hyper, so the backend's `drain` and `close` never reach it, and the handler holds the connections nothing else sees. `UpgradeHandler` therefore carries, beside `paths(&self, &AppHandle)` and `upgrade(&self, Request)`, four defaulted methods mirroring `Server`: `prepare(&self, app: &AppHandle) -> Result<(), BoxError>`, whose failures join the HTTP `PrepareError` (duplicate gateway paths, a gateway's own zero limits); `bound(&self, app: &AppHandle)`, called after `bind`, where `AfterInit` runs; `drain(&self, token: DrainToken) -> BoxFuture<'_, ()>`, the 1001 close of idle connections and the stop of reading on busy ones; `close(&self) -> BoxFuture<'_, ()>`; and `release(&self)`, synchronous, which drops what the handler's `prepare` built that holds the app. Each HTTP server calls `release` once for each `prepare`, whatever `prepare` answered, and a handler two HTTP servers share keeps what it built until the release matching its last `prepare`: the hand-off counts its holders under the lock that holds its table. `Server<B>::drain` and `close` call every registered handler's beside the backend's, concurrently, and `Embedded<A>` does the same, since a host with `upgrades: true` has the same connections. `Server<B>`'s `Drop` and `Embedded<A>`'s call `release` on every handler they prepared (157). The handler finds its gateways through `AppHandle::mounted::<Ws>()` and `::<WsConnect>()` (X20, §4.1) and builds a `GatewayTable` from them in its `prepare`, under `WsModule`'s defaults (X32, §4.1), the broadcast adapter's `prepare` running beside them and its refusal joining the same report (§4.3); its `bound` is the table's `start`, its `drain` and `close` the table's, and its `release` takes the table out of the hand-off and drops it, the table holding the app's `AppHandle` from inside the app's graph, where the hand-off sits as `Upgrades` metadata (157). Its `upgrade` answers 404 off the table's paths and 400 for a request its host hands over with no upgrade future before the table's handshake runs, so a request that cannot be upgraded never reaches the connection phase; on a 101 it hands the host's `OnUpgrade` to `Switch::serve` and returns the response. On the HTTP port, the HTTP server's drain and load shedding answer first: a gateway there is the HTTP server's guest, and an upgrade request arriving once `Execution::open` is refused, or over the server's `max_inflight`, gets the HTTP server's own 503 `application/problem+json` document (§3.6) before routing hands it to the hand-off, so the table's own drain refusal, the handshake's `text/plain` 503, is written by a standalone server alone (F368, §4.1). The alternative, handing an upgrade request to its taker before the execution opens, would take new WebSocket connections out of the server's load shedding, and each is long-lived, so under overload they are what should be shed first; the client gets a 503 either way, and a browser reads no refused handshake's body. The hand-off's module doc, `WsModule`'s and `GatewayTable::handshake`'s state the rule, and the suite's drain scenario asserts the status alone on that port with a comment naming it. A gateway on the HTTP server's port and one on its own port are otherwise identical in what runs for them and when: both servers serve through the one table type.

For a separate port, `fw_ws_hyper::ServerOn::<L>::new(endpoint)` is an HTTP/1.1 server over `fw-server-hyper` (§3.7) on listener `L`, in a crate of its own as `fw-http-hyper` is to `fw-http`: `fw-ws` knows the protocol and owns no socket, the server crate knows the loop, and the listener crate the sockets. `fw_ws_hyper::Server` names it on `fw_listener_tokio::TokioListener` behind the crate's default `tokio` feature, so `Server::new("0.0.0.0:9001")` is the tokio spelling and `ServerOn::<fw_listener_smol::SmolListener>::new(..)` smol's, the feature off compiling no tokio runtime crate. It carries hyper's `http1::Builder` with upgrades enabled, its timer `RuntimeTimer` over the app's clock, the same `header_timeout` and `handshake_timeout` settings as the HTTP server with the same zero refusals, `fw_net::Tls` for `wss` with ALPN `http/1.1`, and the six gateway settings and the server-wide `server_max_inflight` as one `GatewayDefaults`. Its `prepare` pushes its two timeout refusals, then calls `GatewayTable::own_port` under its own name, whose refusals follow in the order it pushes them, the server's gateway defaults, its gateways, the absence of any `port = own` gateway and the broadcast adapter's `prepare` (§4.3), then resolves its endpoints and loads TLS, every failure in one `Configure` report and in that order on every run, since `Failures` keeps the order pushed and the table walks the mounted handlers as listed; `Server`'s doc states the order and `tests/prepare.rs` pins it; `bind` binds every endpoint, all-or-nothing, builds `Serve::<L>` on the app's runtime from `Mounted::runtime()` and calls `GatewayTable::start`; each request is `GatewayTable::handshake` on the head, its response written as hyper's, and on a 101 `Switch::serve` over hyper's upgrade wrapped as `Upgraded::from_futures(FuturesIo::new(io))`, which is the one place the server touches an I/O type and reads the same on every listener; `drain` and `close` run the accept loop's beside the table's. The accept loop, TLS and the HTTP/1.1 exchange up to the 101 run on the listener's sockets, every task of theirs on the app's runtime through `fw-server-hyper`, and from the 101 the connection runs on it through `fw-ws`'s driver, as one on the HTTP server's port does; the two runtime-count tests, `fw-ws`'s and `fw-ws-hyper`'s `tests/runtime.rs`, count the server's own tasks beside the hub's, three once the server serves, broadcast delivery, `AfterInit` and the accept loop, five after a connection's 101, its HTTP/1.1 task and its WebSocket task, six after one message. A request off the gateway paths is answered 404. The upgrade is HTTP/1.1's: the HTTP/2 builder does not advertise extended CONNECT (RFC 8441, `SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL`), and WebSocket over HTTP/2 is `fw-ws`'s to decide. A server on another HTTP stack or runtime is the same calls around its own sockets (X32, §4.1); `fw-ws`'s `tests/table.rs` writes one over an in-memory pipe with no hyper and no socket, and its `tests/conformance_pipe.rs` writes one as a `Host` of the conformance suite on smol, which the suite holds to every scenario (§4.1).

### 3.6 Wire behavior, limits, shutdown

- **Success:** the answer's status, headers and body. Streaming bodies use chunked encoding on HTTP/1.1 and data frames on HTTP/2.
- **Failure:** RFC 9457 problem details (§2.4). Extraction failures are 400, 413, 415 or 422 depending on the `ExtractError` variant, with field violations in `details`; the renderer reads the variant off the `CallError`'s source and applies the exact status while the kind is still `BadRequest`, and a 415 carries `Accept` naming the media type the extractor expected. An error reshaped to another kind renders by that kind.
- **Load shedding:** over the server's in-flight limit, 1,024 requests unset (§2.8), a request gets 503 with `Retry-After` set to `.shed_retry_after(..)`, one second unset, and `Routing::Unrouted`. The admission is the service's first step, before an execution opens and before routing, so a shed request runs no pre-dispatch entry and opens no execution. On HTTP/2, `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` bounds each connection, and excess streams are refused with `RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM)` per RFC 9113.
- **Cancellation:** the peer closing the connection or resetting the stream before the response has ended fires `Disconnected`. The service wraps every response body without an exact length in `Tracked`, just inside `ExecBody`, the body that holds the execution and the in-flight permit, whoever built the response (§2.6); `ExecBody`'s drop runs first, so a peer leaving cancels the execution with `Disconnected` before the `Tracked` inside reads the reason. A body the backend never writes, on a `HEAD` answer or a 1xx, 204 or 304, is not wrapped: it reports `Completed` as the service answers (§2.6), and `ExecBody` holds it as ended, so the backend dropping it unread fires no `Disconnected`. A route timeout (`#[meta(Timeout::after(..))]`, below) is armed after routing, on the app's `Timer`, around the scoped sub-step and `dispatch`; the unscoped entries run before it. When it passes first, the pipeline is dropped at its current await, the execution is cancelled with `Deadline`, and the error handlers run with a `Timeout` `CallError`, the matched handler's tiers then the global ones, under `timeout_grace`: a `Bound` on the server (`Server::timeout_grace(..)`), one second at `Default`, `Unbounded` waiting for the handlers, timed by the same `Timer`. They see `cancel_reason() == Some(Deadline)` and the matched handler, and read a context built from the head as the scoped sub-step received it, with the matched route, no body and no upgrade. Their answer is the response once its body has completed within the grace. The body is read under what the handlers left of the grace, the two sharing one sleep; a body that ends in time, by its end or by its trailers, is rewritten as one data frame and the trailers with an exact `size_hint`, so the backend writes its `Content-Length`, and a body already at its end is passed on as it stands. HTTP has no message boundaries, so a body that completes is HTTP's single reply (§2.4), and a single payload written through `Body::stream` is delivered. A body still open when the grace runs out, an `Sse` among them, was not a single reply produced in time: it is dropped for the canonical 504 without the headers they wrote, logged at `warn` naming the route; a body failing while it is read answers the same 504, logged at `debug`. Under an `Unbounded` grace the body is read until it ends. The read takes at most 32 ready frames per poll and then yields, since a body whose frames are always ready never returns `Pending` on its own and the grace's timer fires only once the task yields; a body that returned `Pending` wakes the task itself when it has a frame, and the read wakes it only after 32 frames that were all ready. A body whose end is reached on its first poll, by `None`, by its trailers or by `is_end_stream`, was produced before the server read it: it is buffered whatever its size, a `Full` of any length among them, and no type is named. Any other body is one the server waits on, and the buffer holding it is capped at 1 MiB, a fixed limit with no setting: the path is rare, and the cap has only to keep an error handler whose body arrives over time from making the server hold an unbounded one while it waits for the end. The bytes of the first poll count toward it, so a body already past the cap when the server first waits is dropped then, and a later frame that would pass it is dropped at that frame; each answers the same 504, logged at `warn` with the route and the limit, as a body larger than the buffer for a reply after the deadline. A body of 33 or more ready frames over 1 MiB is one the server waits on by that rule, the first poll reading at most 32, and answers 504 though every frame was ready. The cap bounds bytes read, not `size_hint`: a body of known length that produces its bytes over time is held to it as a stream is, and exactly 1 MiB is buffered. The buffered copy carries the stream's end to its write: the `on_stream_end` callbacks receive `Completed` once every frame has been handed to the backend, and `CutOff` when the backend drops the copy before that, the client having left, so the outcome means on this path what it means on every other, that the transport finished writing (§2.6). That `CutOff` carries `Deadline`, the route timeout having cancelled the execution first and the first reason staying. This path wraps every body of unknown length in `Tracked` itself before reading it, whoever built it: a body it drops, still open at the grace's end, over the cap or failing, never reaches the service and would otherwise report nothing, and each such stream reports `CutOff(Deadline)`. The copy's report comes first, so the stream it was read from, which read its own end, adds nothing. The service's wrap is applied once this path has answered, to a copy of exact length it leaves as it is. A body of known length is never tracked and reports nothing. An error they return renders as it stands, an unclaimed `Timeout` as 504 and a reshaping to another kind by that kind; §2.4's `Deadline` rule does not apply, since the error offered already says `Timeout`. When the grace passes first, their future is dropped and the canonical 504 renders without the headers they wrote. When the pipeline answers first, the pending deadline moves into the response body, inside the service's `Tracked`; a streaming body observes it through `cancelled()`, and an SSE error written on an execution cancelled with `Deadline` renders as `Timeout`.
- **Route timeouts:** `fw_http::Timeout(pub Bound)` is declared metadata on a handler or a `#[routes]` impl, `#[meta(Timeout::after(Duration::from_secs(5)))]`, with `Timeout::after(d)` for `Timeout(Bound::After(d))` and `Timeout::OFF` for `Timeout(Bound::Unbounded)`, both usable in a `const`. The most specific declaration wins, as for all metadata, so under an impl that declares a timeout a handler's own declaration decides:

  | Handler declares          | Effect                                            |
  | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
  | nothing                   | the impl's timeout                                |
  | `Timeout::after(d)`       | `d`                                               |
  | `Timeout::OFF`            | no timeout                                        |
  | `Timeout(Bound::Default)` | the server's route-timeout default, which is none |

  `Bound::Default` means the server's default here as it does on a hook or a construction, never the impl's timeout; a handler inherits by declaring nothing. The router resolves the declaration each route runs with to an `Option<Duration>` in `prepare`, which is how a handler's `Timeout::OFF` lifts the timeout its impl declares. A zero, `Timeout::after(Duration::ZERO)` under either spelling, is refused in `prepare` once per declaration, listing every route that runs with it in declaration order: ``#[meta(Timeout(..))]` on the `#[routes]` impl of `ZeroFive` would cancel every request on `GET /a`, `POST /b`, `GET /c/{id}`; write `Timeout::OFF` to turn the timeout off``, or "on the handler `Api::slow`" for a handler's own declaration. The text writes `Timeout(..)` whatever the zero's spelling, and the controller is named as the route table's other failures name one. These failures follow the route table's others, each at the position of its declaration's first route, since a declaration's list is complete only once the whole table is walked. A zero that every handler under it replaces reaches no route and is not refused.
- **Server settings:** `fw_http::Server::new(endpoint)` takes text, an `Endpoint` or a `SocketAddr` (§2.7) and carries `tls`, `body_limit` (2 MiB unset; `#[meta(BodyLimit(..))]` overrides per route), `max_inflight`, `shed_retry_after`, `challenge` (the 401 default, §2.4), `h2c`, `timeout_grace`, `max_concurrent_streams`, `header_timeout` and `handshake_timeout`. No setting is an `Option`, because `None` would leave "the default" and "no limit" indistinguishable: a count is `fw_transport::Count { Default, Max(u32), Unlimited }`, and a timeout is the core's `Bound`. Each setting documents what its `Default` is. `Count` lives in `fw-transport`: a WebSocket connection limit and an RPC in-flight bound are the same three-state count, and its count is a `u32`, which no in-flight or stream limit exceeds. Neither type takes a conversion: `.max_concurrent_streams(100)` does not compile, and `Count::Max(100)` is the one spelling, as `Bound::After(d)` is for a timeout. `max_inflight` at `Default` is `Count::DEFAULT_MAX_INFLIGHT`, 1,024 requests (§2.8), `Unlimited` bounds nothing, and `Max(n)` sheds over `n`; `Count::max_inflight()` converts each to `Admission`'s `Option<usize>` at that one boundary. `max_concurrent_streams` at `Default` leaves hyper's own value, which hyper places outside its stability guarantee; the documentation names no number. `Max(n)` advertises `n`, and `Unlimited` sends no `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`. `header_timeout` bounds the arrival of a request head from the moment the backend starts reading it, a clock that also runs while a keep-alive connection waits for its next request, and `handshake_timeout` bounds a TLS handshake; both are 30 seconds at `Default`, and `Unbounded` turns the clock off, under which a peer can hold a connection open until the drain's deadline. The 30 seconds is the server's, not a backend's: `HttpConfig::header_timeout_after()` and `handshake_timeout_after()` resolve each `Bound` to an `Option<Duration>`, `None` for `Unbounded`; every backend applies one value, and `None` means no clock. `header_timeout` is HTTP/1.1 only; an HTTP/2 connection is bounded by the backend's own HTTP/2 limits, hyper's HTTP/2 builder having no head-read clock. A failed or timed-out handshake is logged at `debug` with the peer address and the connection dropped, the accept loop unaffected. `HttpConfig`, which `Backend::bind` receives, is `#[non_exhaustive]` with those fields. The types the builders take from other `fw` crates are re-exported under `fw_http::config`: `Bound`, `Count`, `Tls`, `Endpoint` and `EndpointSpec`, each `#[doc(no_inline)]`: each type has one documentation page, at its defining crate, and an application configuring HTTP imports from one place with no `fw-net` or `fw-transport` dependency of its own. A type an application only matches on (`ListenerName`), only receives in a `prepare` report (`TlsError`, `EndpointError`) or a backend alone names (`BoundListener`, `rustls::ServerConfig`) is not re-exported.
- **Refused in `prepare`:** a setting that would refuse everything it governs as a standing configuration. `Bound::After(Duration::ZERO)` on `header_timeout`, `handshake_timeout` or `timeout_grace` is one `Configure` failure each: ``.header_timeout(Bound::After(Duration::ZERO))` would close every connection before its first request head; write `Bound::Unbounded` to turn the timeout off``, and the same form for `handshake_timeout` ("drop every TLS connection before its handshake") and `timeout_grace` ("send the 504 before any error handler could answer a route timeout"). `Count::Max(0)` on `max_inflight` or `max_concurrent_streams` is refused the same way, ``.max_inflight(Count::Max(0))` would shed every request; write `Count::Unlimited` to remove the limit`` and "would let no HTTP/2 stream open": RFC 9113 §6.5.2 sanctions a zero stream limit for short durations, and a configured zero is not short. A server that must refuse traffic for a while does it with a pre-dispatch entry it can switch. Each hint names its type's spelling of no bound, `Bound::Unbounded`, `Count::Unlimited` or `Timeout::OFF`. The embedding runs the same checks over the settings it has. A `Duration` setting is not refused: `shed_retry_after(Duration::ZERO)` is a valid `Retry-After: 0`, and a zero `Sse::keep_alive` is defined as off (§3.1), being built per response where `prepare` cannot see it. The check covers HTTP's settings; a `Bound::After(Duration::ZERO)` on a hook, a construction or a readiness check is not refused by the core's wiring pass.
- **Shutdown:** at `drain` the backend stops accepting, sends HTTP/2 GOAWAY, closes idle HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, and marks busy ones `Connection: close` on their next response. SSE handlers observe `draining()` and end their streams. A request that still arrives once `Execution::open` is refused, on a keep-alive connection before its `Connection: close` response, is answered directly with 503, `Retry-After` and `Connection: close`: no execution exists, so the pre-dispatch stage does not run for it. `close` closes everything that's left.

### 3.7 Backend SPI [16], written without macros

```rust
pub trait Backend: Send + Sync + 'static {
    const NAME: &'static str;
    fn limits() -> BackendLimits;                    // documented limits, checked in `prepare`

    fn bind(&mut self, listeners: Vec<BoundListener>, tls: Option<Arc<fw_net::rustls::ServerConfig>>, svc: AppService, cfg: &HttpConfig)
        -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), BoxError>> + Send;   // the loaded configuration; the backend's listener builds its acceptor with its runtime's TLS crate
    fn serve(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), BoxError>> + Send;
    fn drain(&self) -> impl Future<Output = ()> + Send;   // GOAWAY, close idle keep-alives
    fn close(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), BoxError>> + Send;
}

/// What a backend calls per request: global middleware, routing, dispatch, rendering.
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct AppService { /* Arc inside */ }
impl AppService {
    pub fn call(&self, req: Request) -> impl Future<Output = Response> + Send;
    pub fn runtime(&self) -> &Arc<dyn Runtime>;      // the app's, from `Mounted::runtime()` in `prepare`: what a backend spawns its connections on
}

pub struct Request {
    pub head: http::request::Parts,
    pub body: HttpBody,                              // stream of Bytes; dropping it unread is not a disconnect (§2.6)
    pub conn: ConnInfo,                              // peer address, TLS info, protocol version
    pub upgrade: Option<OnUpgrade>,                  // resolves to an `Upgraded`; `Some` only for an HTTP/1.1 request asking to upgrade
}

/// An upgraded connection's I/O, whatever the backend's type, as `futures-io`'s traits.
pub struct Upgraded { /* Pin<Box<dyn futures_io::AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Send>> */ }
impl Upgraded {
    pub fn from_futures(io: impl futures_io::AsyncRead + futures_io::AsyncWrite + Send + Unpin + 'static) -> Self;   // smol's I/O, or any on `futures-io`'s traits
    #[cfg(feature = "tokio-io")]
    pub fn from_tokio(io: impl tokio::io::AsyncRead + tokio::io::AsyncWrite + Send + Unpin + 'static) -> Self;      // tokio's; the adapters hand hyper's upgraded I/O over through `TokioIo`; wraps in `Compat` and calls `from_futures`
}
impl futures_io::AsyncRead for Upgraded {}  impl futures_io::AsyncWrite for Upgraded {}
#[cfg(feature = "tokio-io")] impl tokio::io::AsyncRead for Upgraded {}  #[cfg(feature = "tokio-io")] impl tokio::io::AsyncWrite for Upgraded {}
```

`Upgraded` is `futures-io`'s: smol speaks those traits natively, so an outside backend implements what its runtime already uses, and hyper's own traits buy nothing on an upgraded connection. Its two constructors are named for the trait family each takes, `from_futures` and `from_tokio`, so a tokio caller finds its constructor by name rather than by decoding a trait-bound error on a constructor that looks runtime-agnostic. The `tokio-io` feature, off by default, adds `from_tokio` and the two tokio impls, both through `tokio-util`'s `compat` layer, so a backend whose upgraded I/O is tokio's hands it over and an upgrade handler written against tokio reads it, whichever of the two built it; an `Upgraded` built from tokio I/O and read through tokio's traits crosses two `Compat`s, and the tokio-reads-`futures-io` direction initializes the unfilled part of the caller's `ReadBuf` before each read, a cost accepted at this layer. The axum, salvo, poem and rocket adapters enable it, and actix's adapter, which hands over no upgrade, does not. `fw-http-hyper` and `fw-ws-hyper` do not: each builds its upgraded `Upgraded` with `from_futures` over `fw_server_hyper::FuturesIo`, which carries hyper's upgraded I/O out to `futures-io`'s traits on either listener (below); `from_tokio(TokioIo::new(io))` would convert twice and hold the connection on tokio. `fw-ws` reads `Upgraded` through `futures-io` and enables the feature in its tests alone, for the tokio pipe `tests/table.rs` serves over, and `fw-ws-hyper` in its tests alone, for its tokio clients; the conformance suite's echo handler reads its connection through `futures-io`. `fw-http` alone, without the feature, has no tokio in its tree, and `cargo test --workspace` unifies the feature on, so that build is compiled only by a check selecting `fw-http` by itself; the unification also hides a crate whose tests use `from_tokio` without naming the feature, which is why `fw-ws-hyper` names it as a dev-dependency and each crate's tests are run alone, `-p` by `-p`. Neither impl family overrides `poll_write_vectored`.

`fw_http::Server<B: Backend>` implements the core `Server`. `fw-http-hyper` is the one backend, the reference and the default: its type is `fw_http_hyper::HyperOn<L: Listener>` with `NAME` `"hyper"`, `Default` and `read_count()`, it binds the listeners through `L`, runs the accept loop and drives hyper 1.x connections into `AppService`, handing hyper each response as `http::Response<HttpBody>` with no body wrapper, and the `http` crate's types are the common language. The runtime is the listener's: `Hyper` is `HyperOn<fw_listener_tokio::TokioListener>` and `Server` is `fw_http::Server<Hyper>`, both behind the crate's default `tokio` feature, which is what brings `fw-listener-tokio`, and `ServerOn<L>` is `fw_http::Server<HyperOn<L>>` on any listener, so `Server::new("0.0.0.0:8080")` and `Hyper::default()` with `Server::with_backend` are the tokio spellings and `ServerOn::<fw_listener_smol::SmolListener>::new(..)` smol's. A generic type with aliases rather than a defaulted type parameter, because a default does not drive inference in expression position, `Server::new("..")` under `type Server<L = TokioListener>` being E0283, and a builder method choosing the listener after construction would change the type, which is the parameter again.

The accept loop is not the backend's own. `fw-server-hyper` holds it once for the three hyper servers, the HTTP backend, the gRPC server (§6.2) and `fw-ws-hyper`'s standalone WebSocket server (§3.5), over a plug point a runtime crate implements:

```rust
// fw_server_hyper
pub trait Listener: Sized + Send + Sync + 'static {
    type Io: hyper::rt::Read + hyper::rt::Write + Send + Unpin + 'static;
    fn adopt(listener: BoundListener, tls: Option<Arc<rustls::ServerConfig>>) -> io::Result<Self>;   // into the runtime's reactor, with its TLS acceptor; from a server's `bind`
    fn accept(&self) -> impl Future<Output = io::Result<Incoming<Self::Io>>> + Send;
}
pub struct Incoming<T> { /* peer, local, the handshake as a boxed future */ }
impl<T: Send + 'static> Incoming<T> {
    pub fn plain(io: T, peer: SocketAddr, local: Option<SocketAddr>) -> Incoming<T>;
    pub fn handshaking<F>(peer: SocketAddr, local: Option<SocketAddr>, handshake: F) -> Incoming<T>
    where F: Future<Output = io::Result<(T, TlsInfo)>> + Send + 'static;
    pub fn peer(&self) -> SocketAddr;
}
pub fn tls_info(session: &rustls::ServerConnection) -> TlsInfo;   // ALPN and SNI, off either TLS crate's session

pub struct Serve<L: Listener>;
impl<L: Listener> Serve<L> {
    pub fn new(listeners: Vec<BoundListener>, tls: Option<Arc<rustls::ServerConfig>>, config: &ServeConfig, runtime: Arc<dyn Runtime>) -> io::Result<Serve<L>>;
    pub async fn run<F, Fut>(&self, connection: F) -> Result<(), BoxError>
    where F: Fn(Accepted<L>) -> Fut + Send + Sync + 'static, Fut: Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static;
    pub async fn drain(&self);
    pub async fn close(&self);
}
pub struct Accepted<L: Listener> { pub io: Io<L::Io>, pub conn: ConnInfo, pub draining: Draining }
pub struct Io<T>;   // the listener's I/O on hyper's traits, counted at its first read; `get_ref()`
pub struct ServeConfig { pub handshake_timeout: Option<Duration>, pub read_count: ReadCount }

#[derive(Clone)] pub struct RuntimeExecutor;   // `RuntimeExecutor::new(Arc<dyn Runtime>)`; `hyper::rt::Executor<F>` for every `F: Future + Send + 'static`
#[derive(Clone)] pub struct RuntimeTimer;      // `RuntimeTimer::new(Arc<dyn Timer>)`; `hyper::rt::Timer`
pub struct FuturesIo<T>;                       // `new`, `get_ref`, `into_inner`; hyper's `Read`/`Write` over `futures-io`'s traits, and `futures-io`'s over hyper's

// fw_listener_tokio
pub struct TokioListener;   impl Listener for TokioListener { type Io = hyper_util::rt::TokioIo<TokioStream>; }
pub struct TokioStream;     // plain or TLS, tokio's `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`; `is_tls()`
// fw_listener_smol
pub struct SmolListener;    impl Listener for SmolListener { type Io = FuturesIo<SmolStream>; }
pub struct SmolStream;      // plain or TLS, `futures-io`'s `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`; `is_tls()`
```

`Serve::<L>::new(listeners, tls, &ServeConfig, runtime)` takes the `BoundListener`s `fw-net` bound, an optional `Arc<rustls::ServerConfig>`, a `ServeConfig { handshake_timeout: Option<Duration>, read_count: ReadCount }` and the app's runtime, `Arc::clone(mounted.runtime())`, and adopts each listener through `L::adopt`, which hands the configuration to the listener's own TLS crate: `fw-listener-tokio` builds a `tokio_rustls::TlsAcceptor` and adopts the socket through `TcpListener::from_std`, `fw-listener-smol` a `futures_rustls::TlsAcceptor` over an `async-net` `TcpListener`. Adoption can fail and the tokio one needs tokio's reactor current, so a server builds `Serve` in `bind`; `TokioListener::adopt` outside a tokio runtime answers an `io::Error` naming the endpoint and `fw_runtime_tokio::Tokio`, which `bind` reports as `StartupError::Bind`, where `from_std` panicked. Both listeners adopt `fw-net`'s std sockets, so an endpoint, port 0 and a socket inherited through the activation protocol serve alike on each, which `fw-http-hyper`'s `tests/listeners.rs` holds them to, the inherited socket handed to a child process started with `LISTEN_PID` its own. `ServeConfig::default()` carries no handshake clock; a server passes its resolved `handshake_timeout`, which is why the field is an `Option<Duration>` rather than a `Bound`. `accept` answers an `Incoming`: the peer and local addresses and the handshake as a boxed future yielding the I/O and the `TlsInfo` the session settled, read by `tls_info` off rustls's `ServerConnection`, which both TLS crates expose; a plain listener answers it ready through `Incoming::plain`. The handshake travels with the connection rather than through a method on the listener, so the connection's task holds a clone of the acceptor, an `Arc` in both TLS crates, and nothing holds the listener, and so the socket, past the drain; the cost is one boxed future per connection. `Serve` races it on the connection's own task against the handshake timeout, slept on the app's `Timer`, and against the drain, which abandons it, so a slow handshake holds up no accept. `ReadCount` counts the connections the loop has handed to the server that the server has read from: `Io<T>` wraps any listener's I/O on hyper's traits and counts each once, at the first read that yields bytes, after the TLS handshake where there is one, in the task that polls hyper's connection, so the bytes are in hyper's read buffer before a drain signal can reach the same poll; the count never goes down, and every clone reads the same value. hyper's `ReadBufCursor` is moved into the read it is handed and cannot report how far it was filled, so until the first counted read the wrapper reads into a zeroed stack buffer of its own, `min(buf.remaining(), 8 KiB)`, hyper's initial read buffer, through hyper's `ReadBuf::new`, and copies the bytes into the cursor with `put_slice`, one copy of a connection's first bytes, at most 8 KiB, and that buffer zeroed on each poll until the first byte arrives, with no `unsafe`, which `listener.rs` forbids with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` beside the workspace's `deny` (§0); after that the cursor passes straight through. The count sits in the loop rather than in each listener crate, which every listener, a third one included, would otherwise repeat. It counts reads rather than accepts because hyper's graceful shutdown closes a connection it has read nothing from as idle (F377), so a connection sent half a request is shown in progress only once hyper has read some of it. The HTTP backend and `fw-ws-hyper`'s server each keep a clone from their construction and hand it out through `read_count()`, since the server has moved into the app by the time a test reads it; the gRPC server passes the default and exposes nothing. `run(&self, connection)` spawns one accept loop per listener and one task per accepted connection, each in a `TaskSet` on the runtime it was given, so the loops, the connections and, through `RuntimeExecutor`, HTTP/2's stream tasks are the app runtime's tasks and a panic in one is redacted with the app's secrets; the loop selects by polling its own branches, the close, the drain, the accept and a finished connection, in that order. It hands the `connection` closure the consumer supplies an `Accepted { io, conn: ConnInfo, draining: Draining }`: `conn.version` is HTTP/2 where ALPN settled `h2`, and `Draining` carries `wait()` and `is_draining()`, on which the closure starts its hyper connection's `graceful_shutdown`. `run` takes `&self` because a server calls `serve`, `drain` and `close` on one `&self` and holds one `Serve` across the four; a second `run`, or one after `drain` or `close`, returns at once. That closure is where the three differ: the HTTP backend drives hyper's auto builder with upgrades, or `http1` with upgrades where neither TLS nor h2c selects HTTP/2, the gRPC server drives `http2`, and the WebSocket server drives `http1` with upgrades. `Serve::drain()` stops accepting, drops the listeners and resolves every connection's `draining`, then waits for the tasks; `Serve::close()` aborts whatever is left through the set's `abort_all` and `join_all` and marks the loop finished, on which `drain` and `close` wait; the three signals are `fw-transport`'s `Watch`. A `drain` or `close` before `run` releases the listeners. A failed or timed-out handshake is logged at `debug` with the peer address and the accept loop is unaffected.

What hyper needs beyond a connection's I/O comes from the app's runtime too. `RuntimeExecutor` spawns each future hyper hands it on the app's `Runtime` and detaches it, as hyper-util's executors do; the HTTP backend builds its auto builder with it, so HTTP/2's stream tasks run where every other task does. `RuntimeTimer` sleeps on the app's `Timer`, so the HTTP/1.1 header-read timeout of the HTTP backend and of the WebSocket server, which hyper panics on when set without a timer, is timed by the app's clock: hyper's `Sleep` must be `Sync` and a `BoxFuture` is not, so each sleep sits in a `Mutex` reached only through `&mut`, and `sleep_until` measures its deadline against the app clock's `now`, which hyper reads through `Timer::now` too, so a test's fake clock is the one both read. `FuturesIo` is both directions, as `TokioIo` is, and lives in `compat.rs`, a module holding it alone. Into hyper, `futures-io` reads into initialized memory and hyper hands out uninitialized memory, so each read zeroes hyper's whole unfilled region in place through `ReadBufCursor::as_mut`, a pending poll included, hands it to the reader as `&mut [u8]`, checks the count the reader answers against the slice it was offered, and `advance`s past it. The region is zeroed whole, and on every poll, because hyper's `ReadBuf` records how much of its buffer is initialized and `ReadBufCursor` exposes no reading of it: `as_mut` answers the whole unfilled region and `advance` raises the initialized mark to the filled one, so a wrapper that zeroed once and tracked the initialized region would have nothing to track against. The slice the reader receives is exactly that region, every byte of it written by the loop before the read, so the `&mut [u8]` never covers a byte still uninitialized; the cost is the cursor's API's. The two `unsafe` calls carry their safety arguments beside them: `as_mut` requires that no byte that may be initialized is uninitialized, which a loop that only writes keeps; the cast to `&mut [u8]` keeps the length and the layout, which `MaybeUninit<u8>` and `u8` share, and is valid because the loop has written every element; and `advance(n)` requires the first `n` unfilled bytes initialized, which the loop did for all of them. The count check is the one line the argument for `advance` cannot do without: `AsyncRead` is a safe trait, so a reader reporting more bytes than its slice holds is a bug in safe code that `advance` must not trust, and such a reader panics in `FuturesIo`, "a futures-io reader reported 17 bytes read into a 16-byte buffer", rather than hyper panicking slicing its own buffer (F389); std takes the same stance one layer down, `Read::read_buf`'s default handing the count to `BorrowedCursor::advance_checked`, which asserts it against the initialized unfilled region with no message, while `default_read_to_end` itself asserts nothing. The message is `FuturesIo`'s own, and its test expects it whole. The wrapper holds no buffer, so a connection holds nothing of its own between reads; the zeroing is a cost the smol path pays per read and the tokio listener, handing hyper `TokioIo`, does not. The module is listed `pure-rust` in `unsafe-allowed.txt`, and its four tests, a `futures-io` source read into hyper `ReadBuf`s over fresh uninitialized memory with no socket in sight, run under Miri in CI, which reports a byte read before it was written (§0, 112). Out of hyper, an upgraded connection, it needs no zeroing, and both servers build `Upgraded::from_futures` over it. The backend reaches the runtime through `AppService::runtime()`, carried from `Mounted::runtime()` in `prepare` beside the timer, rather than a fifth parameter on `Backend::bind`. The gRPC server keeps hyper-util's `TokioExecutor` and `TokioTimer` on its `http2::Builder`, tonic being tokio-only, and serves through `Serve<TokioListener>`, its accept loop and connections on the app's runtime like the others' (§6.2).

The loop depends on hyper with no features, for the I/O, executor and timer traits, on `futures-io` and on `fw-transport`, and names no runtime; hyper depends on tokio with `sync` unconditionally, for a `oneshot` inside its upgrade future, so tokio's synchronisation primitives are in its tree and in every hyper server's, with no reactor, executor or timer compiled (F383, §8). `fw-http` depends on neither hyper nor tokio: `Backend::bind` receives listeners, a TLS configuration and a service, and what accepts on them, and with which TLS crate, is the backend's listener's. A listener written outside the workspace is `adopt` and `accept` around its runtime's sockets and TLS crate, its stream on hyper's traits directly or through `FuturesIo`; a backend written outside the workspace has the same shape as this one, conversion plus the drain mapping, and builds its `Upgraded` with `from_futures`. An application that runs inside another framework's server embeds instead (§3.8).

`BackendLimits` is enforced in `prepare`: asking a backend for something it declares it can't do is a `Configure` error naming the limit. One entry is `upgrades`: a backend that cannot hand over a per-request upgraded I/O declares `upgrades: false`, and `prepare` refuses a gateway on its port. `fw-http-hyper` declares no limit: h2c, per-request upgrades, inherited sockets and port 0 all work on it, and the conformance suite confirms that before release.

### 3.8 Embedding [16]

A `Backend` owns sockets. An embedding owns none: a host application binds, accepts and parses, and the app runs inside it, nested under a path or as the host's fallback, with the host's own middleware around it and the host keeping its own server setup. Routing, extraction, pre-dispatch, dispatch and error rendering run inside the app either way, so controllers move between the backend and a host unchanged.

**Engines and adapters.** An engine parses HTTP off the wire: framing, keep-alive, HTTP/2 streams, upgrades. Three are in play, hyper 1.x, actix-http, and the hyper 0.14 under rocket 0.5, and the framework talks to none of them directly. `fw-http-hyper` is the case where the app owns the sockets. actix-http owns no sockets in this design: an application wanting actix's per-core runtime model embeds in an actix-web host, where the app's pipeline runs inside actix's single-threaded workers and the model is kept. The five adapters are the case where the host owns the sockets, and they split by how they connect:

- **axum** is the one tower embed. The adapter names `type HostRequest<'r> = http::request::Parts;` and hands the host `fw_http::embed::Service<Axum>`, a cheap-clone `tower::Service<http::Request<B>>` over `AppService` whose `Error` is `Infallible`. The impl exists for an `A` whose `HostRequest<'r>` is `Parts` for every `'r`: the head is the only request a copy on a tower host can read, and the restriction is what keeps a `forward` on such a host from declaring a value it never copies. Its `call` runs every `Embedded::forward` copy on the request's head, adds what they inserted to the head's extensions, and builds the app's `Request` from the host's. `ConnInfo` is read from the request's `http::Extensions`, and one carrying only the HTTP version is built when none is there; an adapter whose host keeps the peer elsewhere, axum in `ConnectInfo`, inserts a `ConnInfo` from a layer of its own ahead of the service, which keeps `fw-http` free of any host's types. That layer also inserts `embed::OriginalPath`, built from the host's `OriginalUri`. What it writes is a host extension, axum declaring `host_extensions: true`, and `Host<T>` reads it as it reads any other. The tower path calls `Embed::take_upgrade(&mut http::Extensions) -> Option<OnUpgrade>` on every request, a defaulted associated function answering `None`, and keeps the answer as the `Request`'s `upgrade` only where `A::limits().upgrades` holds. axum's adapter overrides it: it removes `hyper::upgrade::OnUpgrade` from the extensions and converts the upgraded I/O through `TokioIo` and `Upgraded::from_tokio`, so `hyper` and `hyper-util` are the adapter's dependencies, as they already are salvo's, and `fw-http` names no host's type; hyper 1 depends on tokio unconditionally, so any hyper type in `fw-http` would put tokio in its tree. A tower host declaring `upgrades` that leaves the default hands the app no upgrade, which its conformance run's upgrade scenario reports: the scenario requires a 101 and an echoed frame where the host declares `upgrades` and no 101 where it does not, so the declaration is asserted in both directions. The response body is mapped back. `embed::Service<A>` is a type apart from `fw_http::Service`, the inner service a pre-dispatch layer wraps (§3.4), which answers a bare 500 outside the stage.
- **salvo, poem, actix-web and rocket** are native embeds: each adapter implements the host's own handler trait (`salvo::Handler`, `poem::Endpoint`, actix-web's `HttpServiceFactory`, rocket's `Handler`), builds the app's `Request` itself with `conn` and `upgrade` filled from what the host hands it, and calls `embed::Service::respond(&host_request, Request)`, the entry point that takes the host's own request beside the app's. `respond` runs every `Embedded::forward` copy on the host's request before answering, and borrows that request for the call alone, the copies having run before it returns: a rocket handler passes the `&'r Request<'_>` it holds and awaits the answer after the request is gone. Each native adapter names its host's request as its `HostRequest<'r>`: rocket's is `rocket::Request<'r>`, which a rocket handler holds for the lifetime `'r`, and actix's is `HttpRequest`, which borrows nothing and ignores the lifetime. That shape holds on rocket 0.5.1: an `Embed` with `type HostRequest<'r> = rocket::Request<'r>` and `host_extensions: false` compiles on rustc 1.98.1 and 1.88, its rocket `Handler` passing the `&'r Request<'_>` it receives to `Service::respond`. A `forward` copy reading a request header reaches `Host<T>` there, and the handler answers 200 with the header present and 500, `HostMissing`, without it. The copy compiles with its parameter unannotated, `.forward(|req| req.headers().get_one("x-user") ..)`, as it does annotated. `http` 1 requires everything in `Extensions` to be `Clone` and an upgrade future is not, so a host with its own upgrade mechanism cannot reach the app through the tower `call`; the tower `call` converts the request and answers through the path `respond` takes, both running the copies first, so no adapter reaches the app without them. salvo's and poem's tower bridges drop what a native handler reads, the peer address on both and the upgrade future and original URI on poem, and salvo's sits behind a non-default feature. actix's request payload is `!Send` while the app's body must be `Send`, so the adapter forwards payload chunks through a bounded channel from actix's worker-local task. rocket 0.5 is on `http` 0.2, and the adapter converts at its edge.

| Host      | Exposed as                                                                                                            | Mounting                                                                                     |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| axum      | `tower::Service` (`fw_http::embed::Service<Axum>`, aliased `fw_http_axum::Service`), behind `fw_http_axum::HostLayer` | `Router::nest_service("/api", HostLayer.layer(handle.service()))` or `.fallback_service(..)` |
| salvo     | `salvo::Handler` (`fw_http_salvo::handler(&handle)`)                                                                  | nested under a path or as the catch-all                                                      |
| poem      | `poem::Endpoint` (`fw_http_poem::endpoint(&handle)`)                                                                  | nested under a path or as the fallback                                                       |
| actix-web | `HttpServiceFactory` and `ServiceFactory<ServiceRequest>` (`fw_http_actix::scope(path, &handle)`, an `ActixScope`)    | `App::service(scope("/api", &handle))` or `App::default_service(scope("", &handle))`         |
| rocket    | `rocket::Handler`, one catch-all route per method (`fw_http_rocket::routes(&handle)`)                                 | `rocket.mount("/api", routes(&handle))`                                                      |

**`Embedded<A: Embed>`.** The embedding is a second `Server` implementation, generic over its adapter as `Server<B: Backend>` is over its backend, and it binds nothing: the app still goes through `listen()`, `prepare` still builds the route table, checks CORS and validates every `Path<T>`, and `Embedded::prepare` then checks the app against `A::limits()`. `Server::bound` answers nothing, so `App<Bound>::addresses()` is empty; port 0, inherited sockets and `fw dev --listen` are the host's business. Each adapter crate exports its aliases (`fw_http_axum::{Embedded, Handle, Service}`) and the functions that hand the app to its host. `Embedded::handle()` answers the `embed::Handle<A>`, as `App::handle()` answers the `AppHandle`: `Clone + Send + Sync`, usable before `listen()` returns, carrying `service()`, `host(fut)`, `stopping()`, `app()`, `register_listener()` and `listeners_closed()`. `Handle<A>` and `Service<A>` carry the host as a type parameter: each `forward` copy is typed over `A::HostRequest<'r>`, and running it needs that type at the call. `Stopping` carries none.

```rust
pub trait Embed: Send + Sync + 'static {
    const NAME: &'static str;
    type HostRequest<'r>;                             // the host's request as its handlers receive it, borrowed for one call
    fn limits() -> EmbedLimits;                       // documented limits, checked in `prepare`
    const STRIPS_PREFIX: bool = true;                 // the host removes `.nested_at` before its handler sees the path; `false` has `Service::respond` strip it
    fn builtin_forwards(embedded: Embedded<Self>) -> Embedded<Self> where Self: Sized { embedded }   // the adapter's own `forward` registrations; `Embedded::new` passes the fresh server through it
    fn take_upgrade(extensions: &mut http::Extensions) -> Option<OnUpgrade> { None }   // the tower path's upgrade; a hyper host's adapter converts hyper's `OnUpgrade` here. A host declaring `upgrades: true` implements it, unless it builds the app's request itself for `respond` and sets `upgrade` there, as salvo's, poem's and rocket's do
}

impl<A: Embed> Embedded<A> {
    pub fn forward<T: Clone + Send + Sync + 'static>(
        self,
        copy: impl for<'r> Fn(&A::HostRequest<'r>) -> Option<T> + Send + Sync + 'static,
    ) -> Self;                                        // records `T` as supplied and stores the copy
}

impl<A: Embed> Service<A> {
    pub fn respond(&self, host: &A::HostRequest<'_>, req: Request) -> impl Future<Output = Response> + Send + use<A>;
}

impl<A, B> tower::Service<http::Request<B>> for Service<A>
where
    A: for<'r> Embed<HostRequest<'r> = http::request::Parts>,
    B: http_body::Body<Data = Bytes> + Send + 'static,
    B::Error: Into<BoxError>,
{ .. }
```

```rust
let server = fw_http_axum::Embedded::new()           // Embedded<Axum>
    .nested_at("/api")                               // the prefix the host strips
    .peer_addr(true)                                 // the host supplies `ConnectInfo`
    .body_limit(4 * MB);                             // app-level settings only
let embedded = server.handle();                      // `embed::Handle<Axum>`, aliased `fw_http_axum::Handle`: Clone + Send + Sync, usable before `listen()` returns

let app = App::builder(AppModule).runtime(fw_runtime_tokio::Tokio::current()).wire()?   // a server needs the runtime, not the clock alone (§8)
    .connect().await?
    .bind(server)
    .listen().await?;

let router = axum::Router::new()
    .route("/legacy", get(legacy))
    .nest_service("/api", fw_http_axum::HostLayer.layer(embedded.service()))   // the layer inserts `ConnInfo` and `OriginalPath`
    .into_make_service_with_connect_info::<SocketAddr>();   // what `.peer_addr(true)` relies on
fw_http_axum::run(app, &embedded, axum::serve(listener, router), fw_runtime_tokio::shutdown_signal()).await?;
```

`Embedded` carries the five app-level settings `Server<B>` has, `body_limit`, `max_inflight`, `shed_retry_after`, `challenge` and `timeout_grace`, plus three the adapter reads, `nested_at`, `peer_addr` and `on_miss`, and the copies `forward::<T>(..)` registers (below), all set before `listen()` so `prepare` sees them. `.nested_at` is normalized to a leading `/` and no trailing one; `/` or an empty string means not nested; a prefix carrying a parameter, or one that does not parse as a route, is refused in `prepare`. The host's settings, the endpoint, `tls`, `h2c`, `max_concurrent_streams`, `header_timeout` and `handshake_timeout`, have no method on it, so writing one is E0599 rather than a setting ignored; `prepare` refuses a zero `max_inflight` or `timeout_grace` on it as on a backend (§3.6). `Server<B>::prepare` and `Embedded<A>::prepare` call one crate-private function that builds the stage, the router, the upgrade paths and the admission, taking the parts both have as plain arguments, so the conformance suite compares one route table with itself. `EmbedLimits` and `BackendLimits` stay separate structs, which keeps each builder's compile-error story exact.

The handle moves through three states, `Unbound → Bound → Closed`, and the state a request meets decides its answer. In `Unbound`, before `listen()` has returned, a request is answered 503 with `Retry-After` and a problem document naming the state ("the application is not yet listening"), rendered from the settings every builder method copies into the handle's shared state, since no `AppHandle` exists yet; starting the host after the app's bind is the host's responsibility. In `Bound` the app serves. In `Closed`, after `Embedded::close`, a request is answered the drain's 503 with `Connection: close`. A `listen()` that fails after this server bound closes it, so a failed app does not keep serving through the handle. An answer given in `Unbound` or `Closed` carries `Routing::Unrouted`.

**Prefix.** The app sees the request with the nest prefix stripped: on axum `/api/users/1` arrives as `/users/1` and `/api` as `/`. Two hosts strip it themselves, axum's `nest_service` and poem's `Route::nest`, and their adapters declare `Embed::STRIPS_PREFIX` as `true`, its default. salvo hands its handler the full `uri().path()`, actix's `web::scope` leaves `req.path()` whole with the rest in `match_info`, and rocket's `mount` leaves `req.uri()` whole with the tail in a `<path..>` segment, so those three adapters declare `false`, under which `embed::Service::respond` strips the normalized `.nested_at` from the path, keeping the query, before the app routes. The rule holds by construction: the adapter that strips declares it, and the one place that strips reads the declaration. A request those adapters receive outside the prefix is the host's misconfiguration. `respond` marks it with a crate-private `OutsidePrefix` extension, which routing answers as the app's 404 with `Routing::NotFound` before the router runs, so no in-app route matches it by accident, and logs it at `warn` once per embedding with the host, the path and the prefix. No adapter compares `.nested_at` with the host's own nesting: on a host that strips the prefix itself, a wrong `.nested_at` shows in `HttpCx::mount_prefix()` and the joined route alone. `.nested_at("/api")` tells the app, which routes on the stripped path. `HttpCx::route()` is the in-app pattern routing matched, `/users/{id}`. The span's name and its `http.route`, and `Routing::Matched::route`, carry the joined route, `/api/users/{id}`, under which `/api` joined with `/` is `/api` (§2.9). `HttpCx::mount_prefix()` answers the normalized prefix, empty when not nested and on a backend, so `format!("{}{path}", cx.mount_prefix())` builds a `Location` header for an app path starting with `/` without doubling a slash; a method with no argument cannot join an arbitrary path. The host's original path crosses as `embed::OriginalPath`, built with `OriginalPath::new(..)` or `From<&http::Uri>`, which keeps the URI's path and drops its query, and read back with `as_str()`. It is one of the adapter's built-in values, a `forward` the adapter registers in `Embed::builtin_forwards` (below), rocket's reading `req.uri().path()`; on axum the adapter's `HostLayer` ahead of the service inserts it into the request's `http::Extensions`, built from the host's `OriginalUri`, a host extension under `host_extensions: true`. The span's `url.path` records it when present and the path the app received otherwise, on a backend as well, where nothing outside the app can insert one: axum delivers both `/api` and `/api/` as `/`, and the original is not recoverable from the stripped one. Only the span reads it inside the framework; `Routing::Matched::route`, `HttpCx::route()` and `HttpCx::mount_prefix()` are unaffected, and a handler reads it as `Host<OriginalPath>`, a type the `host_extensions: false` check counts as supplied through the adapter's forward. The embedded app may own `/`, which is `/api` from outside, and the route table's trailing-slash rule decides `/api/` against `/api` as it does unembedded.

**The host and the app.** The app's `Execution` opens inside the app's service, so host middleware runs before any execution exists and never touches one. Information crosses the boundary in two places:

- _Host to app, through request extensions._ A host layer writes a value into the request's `http::Extensions`. The app reads it with the `Host<T>` extractor, `Host<T>(pub T)` with `FromCall<Http>` for `T: Clone + Send + Sync + 'static`, or copies it into the execution with the pre-dispatch entry `.adopt::<T>()`, so guards and services read it as `Ext<T>`. `adopt` is an unscoped entry: it copies `T` into the execution's extensions when the request carries one and passes the request on unchanged when not, and it runs at its place in declaration order, so a tower layer written before it can be its source. A value missing is a deployment fault rather than a bad request: `Host<T>` fails with `ExtractError::HostMissing { param: "host", type_name }`, which classifies as `Internal` with its message withheld, the type name in the error's `Display` and not in the body, and `Option<Host<T>>` is the spelling for a value that may be absent, `Option<P>` answering `None` for `HostMissing` as for `Missing`. Where the host's store is neither `http::Extensions` nor enumerable, actix's request store and rocket's `local_cache`, the adapter declares `host_extensions: false`. A value in that store crosses through a copy the embedding registers, and `prepare` refuses each `Host<T>` a handler reads and each `adopt::<T>()` entry that no copy and no declared entry reaches (below). `Host<T>` is found by a probe: `#[fw_http::get]` and its siblings emit one autoref-ranked probe per parameter, which records the `TypeName` of a `Host<T>` or `Option<Host<T>>` on the handler's record for `Embedded::prepare` to read. The probe sees direct parameters only, so a custom extractor calling `Host::<T>::from_call` inside escapes the refusal and fails at the call with `HostMissing`.
- _App to host, through response extensions._ Every response the app gives carries one `fw_http::Routing`, `#[non_exhaustive]`, and a response without one is the host's own: nested or as the fallback, a request the host routed elsewhere has none, and presence tells "the app answered without routing" from "the app never saw this request". `Matched { route, handler }`: a handler answered; `route` is an `Arc<str>` holding the pattern as the host sees it, the `.nested_at` prefix and the controller's prefix applied (`/api/users/{id}`), and `handler` the `Arc<HandlerInfo>` that `AppHandle::handlers()` lists, with the transport key, the controller, the method name and the metadata. `Options { route }`: the path matched a route and the router answered the 204 with `Allow` on its behalf, `route` the same value `Matched` carries, which a metric keyed on the variant does not count as an error. `NotFound` and `MethodNotAllowed`: the two misses, the second the 405 alone; a `HEAD` answered from a `GET` handler is `Matched`. `Unrouted`: the app answered before routing decided. The refusal renderer sets it on a load-shedding refusal, the drain's 503 and the embedding's 503 before `listen()` and after `close`, and every other response leaving the service with no decision recorded gains it on the way out: a response an unscoped pre-dispatch entry gave without calling `next`, one whose `Err` or panic the global error handlers rendered, and an upgrade request an upgrade handler took, which exposes no `HandlerInfo` for `Matched` to name. A response already carrying a `Routing` keeps it, so the decision rides a response a pre-dispatch entry rebuilt. rocket's `Response` has no extensions; there the value lives in the request's local cache, where a fairing's `on_response` reads it.

**Host values under `host_extensions: false`.** The host's store does not reach the app, so a host value enters the request's extensions through a copy the embedding registers: `Embedded::forward::<T>(copy)`, with `copy: impl for<'r> Fn(&A::HostRequest<'r>) -> Option<T> + Send + Sync + 'static`, actix's `|req: &HttpRequest| req.extensions().get::<CurrentUser>().cloned()`. `Embed::HostRequest<'r>` is the host's own request as its handlers receive it, borrowed for one call, which is how rocket hands its request over; a request borrowing nothing ignores the lifetime. The method records `T` as supplied and stores the copy, so a declared type is a copied type and no call declares a value nothing copies. An adapter's built-in values are `forward` registrations in its `Embed::builtin_forwards(Embedded<Self>) -> Embedded<Self>`, which `Embedded::new()` passes the fresh server through, and the forward is the insertion: rocket's registers `.forward(|req: &rocket::Request<'_>| Some(OriginalPath::new(req.uri().path().as_str())))`, and salvo's, poem's and actix's register `OriginalPath` the same way, while axum's `HostLayer` inserts it ahead of the service. An adapter on a `host_extensions: false` host inserts a value into the request through a `forward` and through nothing else, and the registration the check counts is the code that supplies the value. `respond` runs a built-in forward as it runs any copy. Each adapter's documentation lists its built-in forwards.
