The copies run on every request before the app sees it, in `Service::respond` on the host's request and in the tower `call` on the request's head. `None` inserts nothing. A copy that panics inserts nothing, is logged at `error` with the host and the type, and the request goes on: the copy runs in the host's task before any execution exists, so no error handler can be offered the panic, and the handler reading the value answers `HostMissing`. `prepare` moves the registered copies into the slot every handle shares once the app is accepted, so a handle taken before `.forward(..)` runs them too; before then the list is empty, and a request is answered 503 regardless.

A pre-dispatch entry that inserts `T` itself is declared with `PreDispatch::supplies::<T>()` written after it (§3.3), and `prepare` reads the declaration where the entry runs. A `Host<T>` read is checked per route: `T` reaches it through a `forward` copy, through a `supplies` on any unscoped entry, or through a `supplies` on a scoped entry whose prebuilt stack the route runs. An `adopt::<T>()` is reached by a `forward` copy or by a `supplies` on an unscoped entry earlier in stage order, modules in collection order and entries as written; a scoped entry runs after routing, so its declaration reaches no `adopt`. An unscoped entry's `exclude` is not consulted: it matches the request path as that entry receives it, which an entry after it may rewrite before routing, and comparing it with route patterns would refuse a route every request reaches through a rewrite. The cost is that a `supplies` after an excluding entry lifts the refusal for the routes it excludes too, and a handler there reading `Host<T>` answers 500 per request. The `supplies` documentation states that cost and names the two placements that avoid it: the supplying entry where its exclusion covers none of the routes that read the value, or a scoped entry, whose exclusions are applied per route in `prepare`.

Each refusal names what reads the value and why nothing reaches it. `prepare` answers its failures as one `PrepareError` (DESIGN §10.2) holding every type they name as a `TypeName`, the `T` of each `Host<T>` and `adopt::<T>()` and the controller of each handler a refusal names, and each failure's text is written when the startup report is built, against the names of every transport's failures (DESIGN §10.1): a type prints cut to its last path segment, `Host<User>`, and in full only where that one report would print two different types alike, `Host<a::User>` beside `Host<b::User>`, or two controllers named `Api` answering one route. The route table's failures take the same path: "`embed::Api::user` and `embed::other::Api::user` both answer `GET /users/{id}`". For a route: "`Api::maybe` on `GET /maybe` reads `Host<User>`, and the rocket embedding declares `host_extensions: false`: the `.supplies::<User>()` at src/main.rs:227:83 follows a scoped entry whose scope does not cover `/maybe`, so it does not reach this route". The route is the app's own pattern, the one scopes are matched against, and the refusals come in the router's precedence order. With no `supplies` of `T` anywhere the reason reads "nothing supplies it. A value the host keeps is copied in with `Embedded::forward::<User>(..)`, and a pre-dispatch entry inserting it is declared with `.supplies::<User>()` after it". For an `adopt`, the refusal names its source location and every reason that applies, joined by `;`: a `supplies` on an unscoped entry at or after it "follows an entry that runs after this `adopt`, which then finds nothing; write the `adopt` after it", one on a scoped entry "follows a scoped entry, which runs after routing and so after every `adopt`", and with neither the "nothing supplies it" text. When the stage or the route table fails, `prepare` reports those failures and leaves the `Host<T>` reads unchecked, since which routes a scoped entry covers is then unknown; the `adopt` check needs only the metadata and runs regardless. A `Host<T>` refusal therefore appears once the stage's own failures are fixed.

Errors render inside the app: host middleware sees the finished response, problem details through the app's error handlers, never a `BoxError`, so the app's error shape is the same embedded or not. Panics are caught inside the app on every host, a body the host polls included. `ExecBody::poll_frame` runs the inner poll under a panic catch. On a panic it marks the body ended, reports `StreamOutcome::CutOff(exec.cancel_reason())` (the first report wins, and a `Tracked` inside reporting the same on its drop changes nothing), drops the panicked body under a second catch, logs at `error`, and answers the error frame, after which the body is empty. The `PanicRecovered` it logs, stage `Handler`, is built by resuming the payload inside the core's own panic catch and polling that future once, which completes on the first poll because nothing in it awaits. Resuming runs no panic hook, so the panic is reported once, where it happened, and `PanicRecovered`'s constructor stays crate-private. Host code that wants the app's services holds the `AppHandle` and calls `handle.execute(..)` for anything execution-scoped or `handle.get::<T>()` for a singleton, which is how an existing application adopts the container one route at a time.

**Misses.** Nested, the app answers everything under its prefix, misses included: its 404 and 405 go through its global error handlers with `NoRoute` and `MethodNotAllowed` as on the backend, and the host answers everything else. As the fallback, the app answers whatever the host did not match, and its 404 is final. Unscoped pre-dispatch entries run for every request that reaches the app, in both modes. Handing a miss back to the host needs a host that supports fallthrough, which rocket does (`Outcome::Forward` with the request's original `Data`, unread) and a tower service cannot, so `.on_miss(Miss::Forward)` is refused in `prepare` on every adapter whose limits declare `forward_miss: false`. Under `Miss::Forward` the decision is per request and the app's. The service wraps the request body in a watcher that records the first `poll_frame` and keeps the path as the client sent it; an unscoped entry is opaque to `prepare`, and whether one consumed the body or rewrote the path is known only after it ran. A `NotFound` miss with the body never polled and the path unchanged is answered with the `NoRoute` 404 problem document carrying `embed::Forwardable` in its extensions and `Routing::NotFound`, and the error handlers are skipped: the host answers that request, and a host ignoring the marker still sends a 404. `Forwardable` tells the adapter the original request is intact for the host, and the rocket adapter forwards on it. Any other miss is the app's own 404 without the marker, logged at `warn`. A 405 is never forwarded: a route of the app matches the path, and the resource is the app's. Under `Miss::Final` no watcher is built. rocket's own routes outrank an unranked catch-all, so the forward matters once the app's routes are mounted with a rank above them.

**Limits.** Each adapter declares `EmbedLimits`, checked in `prepare` as `BackendLimits` is and shaped like it: `#[non_exhaustive]` with public fields, `EmbedLimits::NONE` and one `const fn` per row, with `request_body`, `disconnect` and the three drain rows as enums (`RequestBody::{Streamed, Buffered(u64)}`, `Disconnect::{AtClose, AtNextWrite}`, `DrainPending::{Served, Closed}`, `DrainAbandoned::{Released, Window}`, `DrainHttp2::{GoAway, Reset}`). `prepare` reads `peer_addr`, `upgrades`, `forward_miss` and `host_extensions`; `tls_info`, `request_body`, `disconnect`, `drain_pending`, `drain_abandoned` and `drain_http2` are read by the conformance suite alone. A host's drain behavior is declared and asserted rather than noted in its documentation: a note asserts nothing, and a host's next version changes the behavior with nothing to catch it, which is how actix-web 4.15 moved from answering a half-arrived request to closing it:

| Limit             | What varies                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Refused in `prepare`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `peer_addr`       | axum supplies the peer address only through `ConnectInfo`, which `into_make_service_with_connect_info` inserts; the native hosts read it off their request                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | a non-optional `Dep<ClientAddr>` on a handler's reachable path, found through `Mounted::handlers_reading::<ClientAddr>()` (X16) and refused naming the path from the handler to the binding that reads it, ``Peer::peer (Http) → Audit (execution) → Dep<ClientAddr> (field `addr`) reads `ClientAddr`, and the rocket embedding supplies no peer address: read `Option<Dep<ClientAddr>>`, or call `.peer_addr(true)` when the host provides it``; the head step is written from the reader's `handler()` and `transport()` when the report is built, and the controller, the transport and `ClientAddr` enter the report's names, so each prints in full only where the report prints a different type alike |
| `upgrades`        | the hyper hosts leave `OnUpgrade` in the request's extensions; rocket takes the hyper upgrade itself and hands the adapter an `IoStream` through its `IoHandler`, on two conditions, the app's 101 names `websocket` and rocket writes the two upgrade headers itself, and rocket 0.5 keeps no request's protocol version, so the adapter hands the app every request as HTTP/1.1 and a gateway inside rocket answers an HTTP/1.0 upgrade with 101, which RFC 6455 §4.2.1 forbids and the adapter cannot detect, where every other host answers 400, a limit no declaration states and rocket's crate docs carry (F382); actix's upgrade is a payload/body pair rather than a per-request future, and the actix adapter declares `upgrades: false`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | a gateway on the HTTP transport under an adapter declaring `false`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `forward_miss`    | rocket only                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | `Miss::Forward` elsewhere                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `host_extensions` | `http::Extensions` on the hyper hosts, salvo's `Request::extensions` among them; actix's store and rocket's `local_cache` are not enumerable, and a value in them crosses through an `Embedded::forward` copy over the host's request, the adapter's built-in values through forwards its constructor registers                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | `Host<T>` where `false`, for a `T` no `Embedded::forward` copies and no `PreDispatch::supplies` reaching the route declares; `adopt::<T>()` for a `T` no copy and no unscoped `supplies` before it declares                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `tls_info`        | whether the host terminates TLS and says so                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | nothing; `ConnInfo::tls` is `None`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `request_body`    | `Streamed`, or `Buffered(limit)`: rocket's `Data` must be read inside the handler future, so the rocket adapter reads `body_limit + 1` bytes of it under `Handle::body_limit()`, lazily at the app body's first poll, and hands them over as one frame; a body over the limit is the same 413 as everywhere else, under a route whose own limit is higher an error frame follows, and a body the app never polls leaves `Data` unread for a forwarded miss. `Embed::limits()` is an associated function with no instance to read, so the variant reports `Buffered(HttpConfig::default().body_limit)`, 2 MiB                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | nothing; the 413 scenarios hold byte-identical                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `disconnect`      | `AtClose` where the host drops the response body at the disconnect, `AtNextWrite` where it drops it at the next failed write; on actix the response is a `MessageBody` over the app's `Send` body, polled on the worker, `BodySize::Sized` where the size is exact, and dropped at the next write that fails                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | nothing; the cancellation scenario reads it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `drain_pending`   | whether a request whose head is still arriving when the host's graceful stop begins reaches the app: `Served` where it does, and the app answers it 503 with `Connection: close`; `Closed` where the host closes the connection first and the client gets no answer. From actix-web 4.15 actix's graceful stop reaches every HTTP/1 connection, and a connection with no complete request in progress closes at once, so a client caught mid-request at the moment of shutdown gets a closed connection rather than the app's 503, and a request pipelined behind one in flight is dropped the same way; hyper counts a connection's first request as in progress once it has read some of it, and closes a connection it has read nothing from as idle (F377)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | nothing; the HTTP/1.1 drain scenario reads it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `drain_abandoned` | how long the host's graceful stop lasts when a response in flight as it begins is abandoned by the client: `Released` where the stop ends once the host drops the response at its declared `disconnect` moment; `Window` where it lasts the whole drain window however soon the host drops it. Once hyper's server has finished, rocket's launch waits out its whole `shutdown.grace` while anything still holds the server, and a response the client abandoned during the drain holds it; `run` sets the grace to the app's drain window, so a client that leaves mid-response during shutdown makes the app's `close` take that whole window and not more. An idle keep-alive connection closes when the drain begins on every host                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | nothing; the abandoned-response scenario reads it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `drain_http2`     | what the host's graceful stop does with an HTTP/2 connection: `GoAway` where it sends GOAWAY with `NO_ERROR` when its stop begins and closes the connection once its streams end, so a client opens a new connection for its next request; `Reset` where it sends none and the connection stays open, carrying requests to the draining app, each answered 503, until the host's stop deadline, when it is reset. actix's stop sends no GOAWAY. The adapter builds actix-web without its `http2` feature, so on its own it serves HTTP/1.1 alone, and Cargo unifies features, so any crate in the application enabling actix-web's `http2` turns it on there too, after which a server listening with `listen_auto_h2c` or over TLS with ALPN serves HTTP/2; actix therefore declares `Reset` in every build, and a host that serves no HTTP/2 declares what it would do were it enabled. While such a connection is open the app's `close` takes the whole window, `shutdown_timeout` being the drain window | nothing; the HTTP/2 drain and GOAWAY scenarios read it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**What each adapter declares.** The suite and the adapters are written against one record:

| Adapter   | `HostRequest<'r>`                                                                                                                 | `peer_addr`                             | `upgrades`                                    | `forward_miss` | `host_extensions`                                                                                            | `tls_info` | `request_body`                                | `disconnect`  | `drain_pending`        | `drain_abandoned` | `drain_http2`         |
| --------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
| axum      | `http::request::Parts`, the tower bound                                                                                           | `false` unless `.peer_addr(true)`       | `true`: hyper's `OnUpgrade` in the extensions | `false`        | `true`                                                                                                       | `false`    | `Streamed`                                    | `AtClose`     | `Served`               | `Released`        | `GoAway`              |
| salvo     | `fw_http_salvo::SalvoRequest<'r>`, a struct holding `&'r salvo::Request` and `&'r salvo::Depot`, so a `forward` copy reads either | `true` (`Request::remote_addr`)         | `true`: `OnUpgrade` left in the extensions    | `false`        | `true`: `Request::extensions` is copied; a value a middleware put in the `Depot` crosses through a `forward` | `false`    | `Streamed`                                    | `AtClose`     | `Served`               | `Released`        | `GoAway`              |
| poem      | `poem::Request`, owned, the lifetime ignored                                                                                      | `true` (`remote_addr`)                  | `true`: `take_upgrade`                        | `false`        | `true`: `Request::extensions`                                                                                | `false`    | `Streamed`                                    | `AtNextWrite` | `Served`               | `Released`        | `GoAway`              |
| actix-web | `actix_web::HttpRequest`, borrowing nothing                                                                                       | `true` (`peer_addr`, `connection_info`) | `false` (decision 10)                         | `false`        | `false`; of the app's response extensions only `Routing` is copied into actix's store                        | `false`    | `Streamed`, the payload pumped off the worker | `AtNextWrite` | `Closed` (decision 32) | `Released`        | `Reset` (decision 32) |
| rocket    | `rocket::Request<'r>`                                                                                                             | `true` (`remote`, `client_ip`)          | `true`: `IoHandler`; HTTP/1.0 upgraded (F382) | `true`         | `false`                                                                                                      | `false`    | `Buffered(body_limit)`                        | `AtNextWrite` | `Served`               | `Window`          | `GoAway`              |

`AtNextWrite` on poem and rocket is declared from what those hosts were observed to do, not from a documented guarantee; the conformance suite's cancellation scenario is where it is checked, and the limits table's second direction catches a wrong declaration either way. The three drain rows are declared the same way, from what each host was observed to do, and each scenario checks its row in both directions: actix declaring `Served` fails the HTTP/1.1 drain scenario and axum declaring `Closed` fails it the other way, rocket declaring `Released` and axum declaring `Window` each fail the abandoned-response scenario, and actix's h2c host declaring `GoAway` and axum declaring `Reset` each fail the GOAWAY scenario. A `SalvoRequest` is a struct rather than a tuple because it names its fields and can grow.


The actix adapter also maps a `Connection: close` header onto the response head's connection-type flag, since actix-http's HTTP/1 encoder writes the connection line from the flag and skips the header; hyper honours the header on HTTP/1.1 and strips it on HTTP/2, where GOAWAY carries the drain.

**Shutdown.** The app is the one owner of the shutdown trigger, `serve(signal)` or `AppHandle::close` as DESIGN §9.5 requires, and the host's own signal handling is turned off (actix `disable_signals()`, rocket `shutdown.ctrlc = false`). `Handle::stopping()` is a `'static` future that `Embedded::drain` resolves, and that `Embedded::close` also resolves for an app closed without a drain. It resolves at the moment the core's `draining()` does, and it is the signal adapters wire to the host's graceful stop, axum's `with_graceful_shutdown`, salvo's `stop_graceful`, actix's `ServerHandle::stop(true)`, rocket's `Shutdown::notify()`, because it is available before `listen()` returns and needs no `AppHandle`. `Embedded::drain` resolves it and returns at once; an embedding cannot cut a connection, so the host's lingering connections are `close`'s business. A host that keeps its listener until its connections end registers it with `Handle::register_listener()`, which counts one listener registered and open and answers a `HostListener` whose drop reports it closed. `Handle::listeners_closed()` answers `None` while nothing was registered on that handle, and otherwise a future resolving once every registered listener has closed, which the adapter's `run` awaits before telling the host to stop. The count covers a handle that sees more than one listener, a server rebuilt or a value built and dropped before `run`: `run` waits for the one inside its server whichever else exists, and a listener dropped unused reports itself closed by its drop. `Handle::host(fut)` takes `&self` and installs the host's server future in a slot, which `run` does before calling `app.serve(signal)`. `Embedded::serve` waits for the slot when it is empty and polls the future; `Embedded::close` awaits the completion notice when `serve` holds the future, and drops one installed and never polled; no task is spawned. The embedding dropped without `close` does the same: its `Drop` sets the slot `Released` and drops an installed host future after the slot's lock is released, the host's listener with it, and then calls `release` on every upgrade handler it prepared (X21), so an app bound over an embedding and dropped unserved keeps no listener and no singleton past the embedding's last handle. A second `host` call, or one after `close` or after the drop, answers `Err` and drops the future, so a later installation cannot hold the app again (157). When the host future ends, `serve` reads `AppHandle::phase()`. In `Running` the shutdown has not begun, and a host that ended `Ok` leaves the app with nothing serving it, a failure reading "the `A::NAME` host server stopped before the shutdown began"; a host `Err` is a failure in any phase, "the `A::NAME` host server failed: ..". Either way `serve` answers `Err` and the app shuts down under "transport `Http` failed: ..", as it does for a dead backend. A host stopping during the before-shutdown stage (`Stopping`) is after the trigger. For axum, `run` takes `axum::serve::Serve` and attaches `with_graceful_shutdown(stopping)` itself; a `WithGracefulShutdown` the user built would be a second signal owner, and `run`'s parameter type does not accept one.

Each adapter's `run` takes the host object before its terminal call, so it can attach the stop signal and the drain bound, awaits `app.serve(signal)` and answers `Result<Shutdown, BoxError>`; four are `async fn`s, and actix's is a plain `fn` answering a `Send` future, for the reason its bullet gives. A `run` whose `Handle::host` refuses the host closes the app, since the app is bound by then and nothing would serve it:

- axum: `run(app, &handle, serve: axum::serve::Serve<L, M, S>, signal)`, attaching `with_graceful_shutdown(handle.stopping())`.
- salvo: `run(app, &handle, server: salvo::Server<Closing<A>>, service: salvo::Service, signal)`, the server the caller's, built over `fw_http_salvo::Closing::new(&handle, acceptor)`, which the parameter type requires, so `with_http_builder`, `http1_mut`, `http2_mut` and `fuse_factory` stay the caller's to set. `Closing<A>` is a public `salvo::conn::Acceptor` over the acceptor it wraps: its `accept` races the inner accept against the handle's `stopping()`, and once that resolves it drops the inner acceptor, closing the listener, and pends from then on, so a connection arriving during the drain is refused as on the other hosts; `holdings()` answers a copy taken at construction. salvo's own `try_serve` keeps its acceptor, and so the bound listener, until every connection has closed or the stop bound passes, under which a connection arriving during the drain is completed by the kernel and never served. `Closing::new` registers the acceptor with the handle through `Handle::register_listener` and holds the `HostListener` beside the inner acceptor, the acceptor dropped first, so the listener is closed before it is reported closed. `run` takes `server.handle()`, serves with `try_serve`, and calls `stop_graceful(drain)` in the first poll that finds `handle.listeners_closed()` resolved, whether or not the server has been polled since: salvo's loop selects between its acceptor and its command channel in random order, and a stop read with the acceptor still alive would keep it, and the bound listener, inside `try_serve` until its connections end; a stop sent once the acceptor is gone depends on no poll order of salvo's. A `Closing` built from another embedding's handle is refused before serving: `handle.listeners_closed()` then answers `None`, and `run` closes the app and answers `Err` naming `Closing::new(&handle, acceptor)` from the handle passed to `run`. A second `Closing` built from `run`'s handle and kept outside the server holds the stop until it is dropped, the app's `close` then bounded by the core's close bound. salvo 0.92 has no `serve_with_graceful_shutdown`, and the crate enables salvo's `server-handle` feature.
- poem: `run(app, &handle, server: poem::Server<L, A>, endpoint, signal)`, calling `run_with_graceful_shutdown(endpoint, handle.stopping(), Some(drain))`.
- actix-web: `run(app, &handle, server: HttpServer<F, I, S, B>, signal) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shutdown, BoxError>> + Send + use<F, I, S, B, Sig>`, a plain `fn`. actix's `HttpServer` holds `Rc`s and is `!Send`, while the server its `.run()` yields is `Send`, so `run` does the builder work, `.disable_signals().shutdown_timeout(secs).run()`, and the `Handle::host` installation in its body, installing a future that awaits `handle.stopping()`, calls `ServerHandle::stop(true)` and then awaits the server, and answers a future over `app.serve(signal)` holding the app, the signal and the installation's result and nothing `!Send`, which `tokio::spawn` takes as it takes the other four; a refused installation closes the app inside that future. A caller writing `run(..).await` reads no difference. Like actix itself, `run` must be called inside a tokio runtime.
- rocket: `run(app, &handle, rocket: Rocket<Build>, signal)`, setting `shutdown.ctrlc = false`, `shutdown.signals = []` (rocket otherwise handles SIGTERM on Unix itself) and `shutdown.grace` before `ignite()`, taking the `Shutdown` handle off the ignited rocket and installing a future that notifies it on `stopping()` then awaits `launch()`. An ignite failure is installed as a host future failing at once, so the app shuts down naming the error rather than staying bound with nothing serving it; rocket's errors cross as their `Display`, which marks them handled.

The drain window is one clock, set once by the user: `run` reads `AppHandle::drain_timeout()` (X17) through `Handle::app()`, which answers the `AppHandle` once `prepare` has run, and passes it to the hosts that take a stop bound, salvo's `stop_graceful`, actix's `shutdown_timeout`, rocket's `grace`. The accessor reports the window in force, ten seconds unset and zero on an app without a `Timer`, where the drain is zero-length. actix's `shutdown_timeout` takes whole seconds as a `u64` and rocket's `grace` and `mercy` as a `u32`, so on those two hosts the window is rounded up to the second and the host's copy of the clock exceeds the app's by under a second. axum's drain has no bound of its own, and the app's `close` bound contains it: `close` runs under what is left of `shutdown_timeout`, or under `hook_timeout`, ten seconds unset, with no cap (DESIGN §9.5), so a host still stopping past that is recorded `ShutdownFailure::Close` with `TimedOut` and the shutdown report says so. What a host's stop takes inside the window is the host's, declared in the limits table: a `Released` host ends once an abandoned response is dropped, a `Window` host takes the whole window for it, and a host under `DrainHttp2::Reset` takes the whole window while an HTTP/2 connection is open. A request arriving once `Execution::open` is refused is answered 503 with `Connection: close` as on the backend (§3.6). §10 maps each step.

**Conformance.** `fw-http-conformance` runs one scenario list against the hyper backend and against every adapter in both modes, nested and fallback. Its shape is the RPC suite's (§5.2): a `Host` trait, `type Harness: Harness`, the runtime half, `start(app: App<Connected>, mode: Nested | Fallback) -> Self`, which binds the suite's app into the host, runs `listen()` and serves it, `base_url(&self)`, `limits() -> EmbedLimits`, `connections_read(&self) -> Option<usize>`, how many connections the host's server has accepted and read from, each counted at its first read, or `None` from a server that cannot count them, and `stop(self)`, one implementation per adapter crate in its `tests/`, the hyper backend as the reference `Host`, and the macro `http_conformance_suite!(HostType)` stamping every scenario per implementation in both modes, each a plain `#[test]` run through `Harness::block_on`. The suite names no runtime. `Harness` is the runtime suite's shape (§8) with the suite's two additions: `type Runtime: Runtime`, `fn runtime() -> Self::Runtime` and `fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output`, plus `type Listener: fw_server_hyper::Listener`, the listener the reference host accepts on, and `type Stream`, the client end of one connection on `futures-io`'s traits, opened by `fn connect(addr: SocketAddr)`. The runtime half is a type the `Host` names rather than three methods on `Host` itself, as the WebSocket suite has them, because the reference host compared against in `same_as_reference` must run on the host's runtime and on that runtime's listener, so it is `HyperHost<H::Harness>`, one line per host. `OnTokio`, behind the suite's `tokio` feature, is every tokio host's: a multi-thread tokio runtime per scenario, `TokioListener` and tokio's `TcpStream` behind `compat`. `OnSmol`, behind `smol`, is `fw_runtime_smol::Smol` over an `async-executor` `Executor` per scenario, `Smol::new(..).with_workers(3).block_on(fut)` running it on the test's thread and three more and `runtime()` answering `Smol::current()`, as `fw-runtime-smol`'s own suite and the RPC suite run (§8), `SmolListener` and `async-net`'s `TcpStream`; the hyper backend runs the suite on it in `fw-http-hyper`'s `tests/conformance_smol.rs`, declaring the reference's one scenario in both modes, and passes the other 44 of the 46 stamped. The suite offers `ReadCount`, with `wrap(stream) -> Counted<S>` behind `tokio` for an embed host that holds each accepted stream through its acceptor or listener: axum's host wraps under a no-op `tap_io`, the one wrapper axum gives `ConnectInfo<SocketAddr>` for, and salvo's and poem's through their own acceptor and listener; the hyper reference answers `fw-server-hyper`'s own count through `HyperOn::read_count()`; actix takes a listener and gives no hold on a stream, so its host counts in `on_connect`, as its worker starts each connection, which its `DrainPending::Closed` branch tolerates by never finishing the head; rocket 0.5 binds and accepts inside `launch` and answers `None` (F378). `FW_CONFORMANCE_PARALLEL` bounds how many of the stamped scenarios run at once, both modes counted together, read as the RPC suite reads it (§5.2), the slot taken by blocking the test thread on a `std` condition variable before `block_on`, as the WebSocket suite's is. The client is hyper's: a request is one HTTP/1.1 client connection over the harness's stream, with `Host` and, unless the exchange names one, `accept: */*`, the whole exchange bounded by `PATIENCE` on the app's clock and a timeout a `Failure::TimedOut`; `drain_http2` holds its connection through hyper's HTTP/2 client with prior knowledge, its tasks on `RuntimeExecutor`; `drain_goaway` keeps `h2`, which reports the GOAWAY frame, over the stream seen through `tokio-util`'s `compat`, which converts traits and starts nothing. Every sleep, deadline and task in the suite is the app's `Timer` and `Runtime`; the suite's own tree reaches tokio through hyper, `h2` and `tokio-util` alone (F383, §8). The suite's surface beside the trait is `app(runtime)`, `app_for(EmbedLimits, runtime)` (the app without its upgrade handler where `upgrades` is `false`, which `prepare` would otherwise refuse; its `/endless` takes the clock as a parameter, `timer: Dep<dyn Timer>` beside `probe`, `Suite` being a unit struct, and its echo upgrade handler spawns on the runtime it takes from `AppHandle::runtime()` in `prepare`), `PREFIX`, `HyperHost<R>`, `report(error: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> String`, which joins the error's text with each cause under `source()`, a colon and a space between, skipping a cause whose text the message already carries, and the contract through which a host's test middleware writes `Routing` into the response header `ROUTING_HEADER` as `routing_label` spells it and copies a `HostValue` read from `HOST_VALUE_HEADER` into its own store, with `ORIGIN` for the preflight. Every startup path of a `Host` fails through `startup_failed!` with `report`'s text, the suite's app's wiring and connect, the reference host's `listen`, and each host's `listen`, listener, address and adoption, so a scenario failing while its host starts says what failed and why; the rocket host awaits its serving task and reports `run`'s answer, where a lift-off channel would report only that the launch sent nothing, and a task that ends without lifting off fails the same way. `startup_failed!` and `failures_dir()` are the RPC suite's (§5.2): the message goes to a file of its own under `failures_dir()` before the panic, and CI's `test` job, when it fails, prints every file there into the job log and uploads the directory as the artifact `conformance-failures-test`. The suite's app drains in four seconds, set by `app_for`: a `Window` host takes all of it, and half of it still covers a `Released` host dropping a response at its next write.

Two rules hold over every scenario. **Nothing passes on silence.** A request the client's own timeout ends fails the scenario it ends, the suite's I/O primitives (`Running::send`, `Raw::read_until`, `Raw::read_to_close`) failing it with the message that a timeout is neither an answer nor a refusal, and so does a wait for a close or a frame that does not arrive in time; a scenario about a timeout is the one place a timeout is an answer. **A scenario that cannot apply to a host is declared, not skipped.** `http_conformance_suite!(HostType; not_applicable { scenario: "reason", .. })` stamps each named scenario `#[ignore = "not applicable: <reason>"]`, so the test report counts it as ignored rather than passed; a declared name that is no scenario fails to compile; a scenario run on a host it does not apply to fails rather than returning, so a host leaving out a declaration it needs fails, and `cargo test -- --ignored` runs the declared ones, which fail the same way. The declaration sits in the stamping macro because libtest cannot skip at run time, `macro_rules!` cannot read a trait item, and the `Host` trait is frozen.

Twenty-three scenarios per mode: a routing hit; a 404 with `NoRoute`; a 405 with `Allow`; `OPTIONS` answered 204; `HEAD` answered from `GET`; each extraction failure's status, 400, 413, 415 and 422, with its problem document; an error reshaped by an error handler; a domain error an error handler answers with a value of its own, `GET /recover` answered 200 with the substitute item as JSON through `Json(..).into_reply(cx)`; an unscoped entry answering a preflight; SSE with an `error` event; a disconnect mid-stream firing `Disconnected` at the declared `Disconnect` moment; a 101 upgrade with one frame echoed where `upgrades`; `Host<T>` present, and absent as a 500, one scenario sending the same two requests on every host, `host_extensions` deciding only whether the assertions name the host's request extensions or the `Embedded::forward` copy `start` registers on a host declaring `false`, the reference running the absent half alone, having no host to write the value; `Routing` in the response extensions, and on rocket in the request's local cache through a test fairing, since every declared capability is asserted, the reference declaring it not applicable, having no host around the app to read `Routing`; the 503 after `close`, accepting no listener as well as a 503 with `Connection: close`; and four drain scenarios. `drain_http1` writes half a request head, waits for `Host::connections_read` to pass the value it read before connecting, and starts `close`: a host closing its listener at the drain resets a connection still in its backlog, and hyper closes as idle one it has read nothing from, so the count is what shows the connection in progress, and no accept order is assumed; where the host declares `DrainPending::Served` it finishes the head at once and requires the 503 with `Connection: close`, which the app's 503 carries itself, so no wait for the host's stop is needed; where `Closed` it never finishes the head and requires the connection to close with nothing written, since a head finished before the host processes its stop would reach the app. A host answering `None` fails the scenario with a message naming the declaration, and declares it not applicable: rocket does, its server reporting no connection (F378). `drain_http2` holds an HTTP/2 connection open through the drain with an endless stream and sends a request during it through a client with prior knowledge: where `GoAway` the request is answered 503 on the held connection or refused on the new connection the client opens after GOAWAY; where `Reset` it has to be answered 503, no GOAWAY telling the client to leave the held connection; either way it ends within half the drain window, a request that ends only when the host's own stop deadline cuts it having waited in silence. `drain_goaway` drives an `h2` client directly, opens the endless stream, starts the drain and polls `SendRequest::ready()` until it fails: where `GoAway` the failure has to be a remote GOAWAY with `NO_ERROR` within the patience, which is how an HTTP/2 client learns to stop sending; where `Reset` the connection has to keep taking requests until it fails with no GOAWAY received, no sooner than the drain window and within the window plus the patience. `drain_abandoned` opens an SSE stream, starts the drain, drops the client and times the app's `close`, which waits for the host: under half the window where `Released`, at least the whole window where `Window`. Four scenarios cover what a host could get wrong in carrying the app's bytes. `chunked_body_over_the_limit` writes a `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` request with no `Content-Length` to a route limited to 16 bytes: a body within it is answered 200 and one over it 413 with a problem document, the limit met as the chunks arrive. `path_parameter_percent_decoded` requests `/echo/a%20b%2Fc%2520` and requires `a b/c%20`, the parameter decoded once after the path is split, so an encoded slash stays inside its segment and an encoded percent sign is not decoded again, as the reference reads it. `trailing_slash_insignificant` requests `/hit` and `/hit/` and requires the same answer and the same recorded route. `sse_delivered_as_produced` reads the first event of a handler that writes its second only once the scenario opens a gate, which it does after reading the first, so a host that holds frames back until the response ends fails when its read runs out of patience. `Host::start` returns once the app listens and every adapter's `run` serves the host only after `listen()`, so the 503 before `listen()` is unreachable through `Host` and is not run; a `Host` method for a host started before `listen()` does not exist. Where a backend cannot do what a host does, a scenario checks whether the host is the reference by `TypeId` and runs the half that applies, since the frozen `Host` trait cannot say it. The suite asserts byte-identical responses wherever a scenario depends on no declared limit. `Routing` is asserted outside the byte-identical rule. The limits table is checked in the other direction too: an adapter that passes a scenario it declares unsupported fails, so the declared limits stay honest, and an adapter declaring `forward_miss` that answers a `Forwardable` 404 itself fails the same way. The actix crate runs the suite twice: its default target on a host listening with `listen`, which serves HTTP/1.1 alone and declares `drain_http2` and `drain_goaway` not applicable for that reason, and a second target, `conformance_http2`, behind a test-only `conformance-http2` feature enabling `actix-web/http2`, on a host listening with `listen_auto_h2c` and declaring nothing not applicable, so the `Reset` declaration is asserted on a build that serves HTTP/2 rather than assumed; the feature is a suite feature, described as one in the manifest and the crate doc: it changes nothing in the adapter, and an application serving HTTP/2 enables actix-web's `http2` itself.

---

## 4. WebSocket

### 4.1 API [22]–[26]

```rust
#[module(imports = [fw_ws::WsModule::for_root()], controllers = [ChatGateway])]   // registers the hand-off, binds `Rooms` and the broadcast adapter
pub struct ChatModule;

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct ChatSession { nick: Mutex<Option<String>> }

#[routes]
#[fw_ws::gateway(path = "/chat", namespace = "lobby", event = "event",
                 session = ChatSession, connect_guards(TokenGuard))]
impl ChatGateway {
    #[fw_ws::message("chat.send")]
    #[guards(value = RateLimit::per_second(5))]
    async fn send(&self, msg: Payload<ChatMessage>, session: Session<ChatSession>, rooms: Dep<Rooms>)
        -> Result<Ack, ChatError>
    {
        rooms.gateway::<ChatGateway>().to_room("lobby").except([session.conn_id()]).emit("chat.message", &msg.0).await?;
        Ok(Ack::default())
    }

    #[fw_ws::message("chat.history")]
    async fn history(self: Arc<Self>, q: Payload<HistoryQuery>) -> impl Stream<Item = Result<ChatMessage, ChatError>> {
        self.store.page(q.0)                                   // captures the Arc; the macro appends `+ use<>` (§2.3)
    }
}

impl fw_ws::OnConnect for ChatGateway {                        // after the connect guards; may refuse
    async fn on_connect(&self, cx: &ConnectCx) -> Result<(), ConnectRefused> {
        cx.conn().join("lobby").await;                         // `cx.ext::<CurrentUser>()` reads what the guards wrote
        Ok(())
    }
}

impl fw_ws::OnDisconnect for ChatGateway {
    async fn on_disconnect(&self, conn: &Connection, why: DisconnectReason) { self.presence.leave(conn.id()).await; }
}

impl fw_ws::AfterInit for ChatGateway {
    async fn after_init(&self, gw: GatewayRef) { tracing::info!(path = gw.path(), "chat ready"); }
}
```

`#[fw_ws::gateway(path = "/..", namespace = .., event = .., codec = msgpack, subprotocols = [..], refuse = handshake, overflow = drop_oldest, port = http | own, session = T | session_with = .., message_limit = .., max_connections = .., max_inflight = .., max_outbound = .., ping_interval = .., pong_timeout = .., connect_guards(..))]` sits on the impl next to `#[routes]`. `#[routes]` passes it through untouched, and it then emits `impl fw_ws::GatewayConfig`, the trait carrying what the attribute declares: `settings() -> GatewaySettings`, `connect_guards(&mut EnhancerSpec<WsConnect>)`, `session() -> SessionFactory` and `mount_gateway(&mut Mount<'_>)`. `GatewaySettings::at(path)` with one setter per field is the value form, its `message_limit` an `Option<u64>` that defers to the server or `WsModule` when unset. A gateway written by hand implements `GatewayConfig` and `fw_ws::Gateway: GatewayConfig`, whose `on_message(&self, &Connection, Frame)` receives each data message as it arrived, text or binary, with `on_connect`, `on_disconnect`, `after_init` and `mount` defaulted on the trait; the attributed gateway's hooks are instead the traits below, found by probing the concrete type, which a generic default cannot do. A hand-written gateway's instance is resolved once per connection, in the connection phase's execution, and kept while the connection lasts. Messages reach `on_message` one at a time, in order, on a task of their own, one queued or running counting against `max_inflight`; a panic in `on_message` closes 1011; work that outlives a message runs in an execution the gateway opens through `Connection::open_execution`. A hand-written gateway that also declares `#[message]` handlers is refused in `prepare`, since it reads every message raw. The connection hooks are traits on the gateway type, `OnConnect`, `OnDisconnect` and `AfterInit`, following the core's rule that a role comes from the traits a type implements: they are not handlers, receive no `__handler`, and impl-level enhancers do not reach them; an impl-level `#[guards]` applies to message handlers alone. `connect_guards(..)` on the gateway attribute is the one spelling for connect guards, and its entries are an enhancer attribute's: a type, a DI key the module binds; `value = expr`; or `with = |..| ..` and `with(<scope>) = |..| ..` closures, each closure's non-`async` body wrapped in `async move` through `fw_handler_codegen::util::wrap_async` as `#[guards(with = ..)]` wraps one, so one closure compiles in both attributes. An entry carrying a transport key is refused at the key, every entry being a `Guard<WsConnect>`. The connect handler is mounted by `fw-ws` through `Mount::once`, not by a method, so no `__FW_KEY_*` constant is `"ws_connect"`, and an impl-level `#[guards(ws_connect = ..)]` fails the key assertion (X1) with "is not the key of any handler's transport in this impl".

**Two transports.** `Ws` covers message handlers (one execution per message). `WsConnect` covers the connection phase, with key `"ws_connect"`: its `Cx` is `ConnectCx` and its reply is admit or refuse. `fw-ws` mounts the connect handler itself, one per gateway, with the gateway attribute's `connect_guards(..)` as its guards; its body calls `OnConnect` when the type implements it, which `fw-ws` detects by probing the concrete type. `WsConnect` declares `Transport::BUILDS_CONTROLLER = false`, so `dispatch` does not build the gateway ahead of the chain: an attributed gateway is resolved in the connection phase's execution only to call its `OnConnect`, and a hand-written one by its connect handler, which that execution then keeps for the connection's messages. A gateway implementing no `OnConnect` whose dependencies need a message's execution, an `Ext` a message guard writes, connects, and a failure to build a gateway at connect passes through the connect interceptors. Connect guards are ordinary `Guard<WsConnect>` implementations, running through `dispatch` like any guard, so refusals, error handlers, kinds and panics all work the same at connect time. A connection isn't an execution. The connect phase and each message are; `on_disconnect` runs as a terminal execution without guards, its failures and panics logged; `after_init` is a once-per-gateway lifecycle call, not an execution.

**X20: the mounted handlers of a second marker.** `Server::Transport` is one associated type, and a server's `prepare` receives `Mounted<'_, T>` for that one marker, so a `Server<Transport = Ws>` would never see the connect handlers mounted under `WsConnect`. `Mounted::handlers_of::<U: Transport>()` answers another marker's mounted handlers: `GatewayTable::own_port` reads `mounted.handlers()` for the message handlers and `mounted.handlers_of::<WsConnect>()` for the connect handlers, pairing them by controller key. `AppHandle::mounted::<T: Transport>() -> Result<Vec<MountedHandler<T>>, RuntimeMissing>` is the same read for code holding an `AppHandle` alone, which is what the `UpgradeHandler` on the HTTP port holds (§3.5): a same-port gateway finds its handlers, their enhancer tiers and their handler values through it, and is refused as `listen()` refuses a transport on an app with no runtime (X31, §8). Both are additive core changes.

`#[routes]` doesn't know the impl is a gateway, so each `fw_ws::message` mount function calls `<Self as GatewayConfig>::mount_gateway(m)` under **X15, `Mount::once::<K>(..)`**, which makes the call idempotent per controller type. A gateway with no message handlers would mount nothing, and the gateway attribute refuses that case at compile time. A `#[message]` handler written by a `macro_rules!` call inside the impl is not seen, since an attribute macro reads the impl unexpanded, as `#[routes]` reads it, and such an impl is refused as a gateway with no handler.

**Which port.** `GatewaySettings::port: Port { Http, Own }`, written `port = http | own` on the attribute, selects which server serves a gateway; `Http` is the default. The hand-off serves the `Http` gateways on the HTTP server's port and on an embedding host declaring `upgrades`, and `fw_ws_hyper::Server` serves the `Own` gateways on its own port, `GatewayTable::own_port` refusing a server with none to serve. No gateway is served on both: serving every gateway on both ports would expose one on a port its author did not choose, and neither server can learn at `prepare` whether the other is bound. For the same reason a `port = own` gateway in an application that binds no `fw_ws_hyper::Server` is reachable by nothing, and nothing reports it: a wiring-time check needs the server's existence, which no module sees.

**X32: the serving surface.** A server is socket code around three calls of `fw-ws`'s, and both shipped servers are written over them. `GatewayTable::own_port(server, &mounted, &defaults, &mut failures) -> GatewayTable` is a standalone server's `prepare` step: the `port = own` gateways built from `Mounted`'s message handlers paired with `handlers_of::<WsConnect>()`, every zero default checked under `server`'s name, the hub taken from `WsModule`'s metadata or an in-memory one of the table's own, which no `Dep<Rooms>` reaches, and the absence of any such gateway refused. It pushes onto the caller's `Failures`, so a server's own failures, its endpoints, TLS and timeouts, are reported in the one `Configure` error, and it builds the table either way; a server reports the failures and binds nothing when any was pushed. `paths()` lists the gateway paths, prefixes joined. `start()` is broadcast delivery, once whichever server starts it, and each gateway's `AfterInit`, each a task on the app's runtime, which a server calls once bound. `handshake(head, peer) -> Handshake` is the decision on one upgrade request, made from `http::request::Parts` alone and in this order: the gateway at the path, 404 when none; RFC 6455 §4.2.1's checks, 405 with `Allow: GET` for a method other than GET, 400 for HTTP/1.0, for a missing `Connection: Upgrade`, `Upgrade: websocket` or `Sec-WebSocket-Key` and for a malformed key, 426 with `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13` for another version; the subprotocol and the accept key; 503 once the table's drain has begun; and under `refuse = handshake` the connection phase, whose refusal is 401 with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` or 403. It is async and answers a value because the connection phase runs inside it, as a task on the table's tracker whose answer the handshake awaits through a oneshot: a server that drops the handshake's future while `OnConnect` runs, as hyper drops a request whose client has gone, leaves the phase to finish, and the drain counts it as it counts a connection mid-upgrade (F371); a phase the table's close aborts answers the handshake 503. `Handshake::Switch(Switch)` carries the connection it admitted, registered in the rooms with its session built, from the decision to the driver, and `Handshake::Refuse(Refusal)` carries `status()`, `reason()` and the headers the status calls for, written by `Refusal::into_response()` as an `http::Response<String>` whose body is the reason as `text/plain; charset=utf-8`, which each server maps onto its own body type. `Switch::response()` is the 101 as an `http::Response<()>`: `Upgrade`, `Connection`, `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` and the subprotocol chosen, no extension negotiated. `Switch::serve(upgraded)` is the connection driver. It takes a future of the upgraded stream, `U: Future<Output = Result<Io, BoxError>> + Send + 'static` with `Io: futures_io::AsyncRead + AsyncWrite + Unpin + Send + 'static`, and spawns the connection's task on the app's runtime under the table's tracker before the future resolves: hyper hands over an upgraded connection only once the 101 has been written, and the hand-off's `OnUpgrade` is such a future too, so a driver taking the stream would have each server spawn that wait itself, outside the tracker the drain counts; a server holding the stream already passes `async move { Ok(io) }`. The task awaits the stream, an `Err` ending the connection before it opens, logged at `debug`, runs the connection phase unless the handshake ran it, then the read loop, keep-alive, the 1001 drain and `on_disconnect` for a connection that connected (§4.2). The slot under `max_connections` is taken inside the connection phase, in the call `connect` hands `fw::dispatch`, which runs once every connect guard has admitted and before the handler's `OnConnect`: a free slot is kept for the connection, and with none the call answers a refusal of kind `Unavailable`, `connect` returning `Full` whatever an interceptor made of that answer; an interceptor that answers `Admitted` without calling the handler takes no slot in the call, and `connect` takes one after `dispatch`, `Full` if none is free. The session and the hub registration still come first, and neither is a hook. Under `refuse = close` the phase runs after the 101 and a full gateway closes 1013, "too many connections"; under `refuse = handshake` it runs before the 101 and a full gateway answers a `Switch` decided `Full`, which upgrades and closes 1013 the same way. A guard's refusal holds no slot in either mode, so a guard-refused connection on a full gateway closes with its guard's 1008, and a connection refused for capacity runs no hook: it never connected, so there is nothing to pair with `on_disconnect`. The slot lives in `Admitted` and is freed after `on_disconnect` and the unregistering. One rule holds on every path: a connection whose `OnConnect` ran gets `on_disconnect`, and leaves the rooms after it, so the hook sees the connection's rooms as it does on the served path. Under `refuse = handshake` the phase has run before a `Switch` exists, so a `Switch` dropped unserved, as when writing the 101 fails, runs `on_disconnect` with `Lost` for the connection it admitted and then releases it, on a task the tracker counts, spawned from its `Drop`; a `Switch` served an upgrade future that fails, hyper's shape, where the 101 is written after `serve` and the future fails when the write does, does the same; and a connection the handshake decided `Full`, its guards having admitted it and no slot being free, is closed 1013 after the 101 and runs no hook, its `OnConnect` never having run. Under `refuse = close` nothing has run before the 101, and a dropped `Switch` runs nothing. The release is asynchronous on the drop path, so a room broadcast between the drop and the release still reaches the connection's queue, which nothing writes. `drain(token)` and `close()` reach every connection served through the table, since the table owns the tracker: the first returns once every connection has ended, the second aborts what is left, waits for the tasks and stops broadcast delivery. `GatewayDefaults` is what `WsModule` and `fw_ws_hyper::Server` carry for what a gateway's attribute leaves unset, `message_limit`, `max_connections`, `max_inflight`, `max_outbound`, `ping_interval` and `pong_timeout`, one builder method each, and for the one setting that is the server's rather than a gateway's, `server_max_inflight`, the messages in flight across every connection of the server (§4.2), so a server on another stack carries the same seven; its `messages_read()` hands out the `MessagesRead` every table built from those defaults counts into, how many data messages the connections have read off their sockets, which a server hands out before it moves into the app, as `fw_ws_hyper::Server::messages_read` does, and its `answer_hold(..)` sets the `AnswerHold` the connections of those tables await between each answer and its queueing (143); the count, its `get`, the export, both accessors, `AnswerHold::new` and `answer_hold` compile under `fw-ws`'s and `fw-ws-hyper`'s `conformance-probe` feature alone, for the conformance tests and not an application feature, which each crate's tests turn on through its dev-dependency on itself, and without it `MessagesRead` stays a crate-private zero-sized type whose `add` does nothing and `AnswerHold` an unexported empty type whose wait returns at once, so the read loop, the tracker and `message` keep one shape (§4.2). The hand-off builds its table from `AppHandle::mounted` under `WsModule`'s defaults and serves through the same `handshake` and `serve` (§3.5); `fw-ws`'s `tests/table.rs` is the third server, a test-local `Server` with no socket over a `tokio::io::duplex` pipe, and its `tests/conformance_pipe.rs` the fourth, a `Host` of the conformance suite over a `piper` pipe on smol (below); `table.rs` pins each unserved path's hooks over a pipe whose client end is dropped first, one record per connection, `[Connected, Disconnected(Lost)]` for a failed 101 and for a failed upgrade, no hook under `refuse = close`, no hook for a connection over `max_connections` in either mode, the record holding the slot holder's two hooks alone, a guard-refused connection on a full `refuse = close` gateway closing 1008 and an admitted one 1013 with neither running a hook, and the handshake's 503 once the drain has begun, refused before any connection phase. Nothing in the surface names hyper, tokio or a socket. Every server is held to the surface's behaviour by the conformance suite below, which `fw-ws-hyper`'s server and the hand-off both run.

**Conformance.** `fw-ws-conformance` runs one scenario list against every WebSocket server through a `Host` trait the server's crate implements in its `tests/`. Its runtime half is the runtime suite's `Harness` (§8): `type Runtime: Runtime`, `fn runtime() -> Self::Runtime` and `fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output`, so each stamped test is a plain `#[test]` and the scenario builds the suite's app on the host's runtime inside the future `block_on` runs, every wait bounded by that runtime's `Timer`, five seconds (`PATIENCE`). Its server half is four values and five calls: `type Stream`, the client end of one connection on `futures-io`'s `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`, which a smol server answers with `async-net`'s stream and a tokio server with its `TcpStream` behind a `futures-io` adapter, a TLS server performing its client handshake in `connect`; `const PORT: Port`, the gateways the server serves; `const CLOSES_IDLE_AT_DRAIN: bool`, `false` unless declared, whether the server closes a connection idle between requests when its drain begins rather than keeping it and answering a request that then arrives on it, which every hyper-based host declares, hyper's graceful shutdown closing such a connection; `fn upgrades() -> bool`, required, whether the server hands a gateway on its port the connection a 101 upgrades, `true` on the standalone server and on `fw-http-hyper`, and on an embed host what its adapter's `EmbedLimits::upgrades` declares, read as `<A as Embed>::limits().upgrades` rather than copied, since `limits()` is not `const`; `fn bind(app: App<Connected>) -> (App<Connected>, Self)`, which binds the server under test on a port the OS chooses, so no two scenarios contend for one, and hands back the host value the scenario reads the server through; `fn connections_read(&self) -> Option<usize>`, required, how many connections the server has accepted and read from, each counted at its first read, which the hyper hosts answer from a `ReadCount` (§3.7) and a server that cannot count answers `None`, failing the drain scenario with a message naming the declaration; `fn serve(&self, app: App<Bound>) -> impl Future<Output = Serving>`, defaulted to the addresses `App<Bound>::addresses()` reports and `App::serve` until a close, which an embed host overrides to bind its own listener, wrap it in the HTTP suite's `ReadCount` where its acceptor allows, and serve through its adapter's `run`, the suite's close through `AppHandle::close` ending that `run`; and `fn connect(addresses: &[BoundAddr]) -> impl Future<Output = io::Result<Self::Stream>>`, one connection to the addresses `serve` answered. `Serving { addresses, until_closed }` is what `serve` answers; the suite spawns `until_closed` on the app's runtime, awaits it when it stops the app, and fails a host that serves on no address. Everything else is the suite's: the app, its gateways, `listen()`, the drain, which is the core's, run by the suite's `AppHandle::close` in a four-second window (`DRAIN`), and the client, `async-tungstenite` with no runtime feature over the host's stream, the suite writing the upgrade request itself and reading the answer as the server wrote it, a refusal's body with neither `Content-Length` nor chunked coding read to the connection's close, where RFC 9112 §6.3 ends it (F381), so no server's own client sits between the suite and the wire. `ws_conformance_suite!(HostType)` stamps one `#[test]` per scenario; `ws_conformance_suite!(HostType; not_applicable { scenario: "reason", .. })` declares the scenarios that cannot apply under the rules the HTTP suite states (§3.8); and `ws_conformance_suite!(HostType; without_upgrades)` stamps a host declaring no upgrades, under which the declaration scenario first requires `upgrades()` to answer `false` and every other scenario is ignored as not applicable, the host serving no gateway on its port, so a host declaring upgrades under that arm fails the requirement and one declaring none under the plain arm fails thirty scenarios at `listen()`; `startup_failed!`, `failures_dir()` and `report` are the RPC suite's (§5.2). `FW_CONFORMANCE_PARALLEL` is read as the HTTP suite reads it, the slot taken by blocking the test thread on a `std` condition variable before the scenario's runtime starts, since the other suites' tokio semaphore would put tokio in the tree. The suite depends on `fw`, `fw-transport`, `fw-ws`, `async-tungstenite` with `handshake` alone, `event-listener`, `futures-io`, `futures-util` with `io` and `serde_json`, and `cargo tree -e normal -i tokio` prints nothing for it (§8). Nothing in the trait or in any public signature of the crate names hyper, tokio or a socket type.

The gateways are declared once per `Port`. `port = own` is a word in the gateway attribute, so one gateway type cannot serve both servers; the suite's app writes its nine gateways inside a `macro_rules!` that takes the word and stamps them into two modules, and its root module imports `WsModule::for_root()` and registers the set `Host::PORT` names. Every limit a scenario reads is set on the gateway's own attribute, so a server's `GatewayDefaults` and `WsModule`'s change nothing the suite asserts: `/echo`, plain; `/versioned`, `subprotocols = ["v2.chat", "v1.chat"]`; `/strict`, `refuse = handshake` with a connect guard on `x-token` and an `OnConnect` refusing `Unauthorized`; `/refused`, a connect guard and an `OnConnect` refusing as its `x-refuse` header names; `/small`, `message_limit = 128` and `max_connections = 1`; `/serial`, `max_inflight = 1`; `/outbound`, `max_outbound = 1`; `/heartbeat`, a 100 ms `ping_interval` and a 150 ms `pong_timeout`; `/streams`, `on_stream_end` reporters and an interceptor that discards the handler's stream.

Thirty-one scenarios in seven groups. Handshake, ten: the upgrade as the host declares it, on a host declaring upgrades a 101 to `/echo` and a message answered, on one declaring none `listen()` refusing the suite's app as `StartupError::Configure` whose text names "declares `upgrades: false`", the sentence `fw-http`'s limits check writes; a 101 carrying RFC 6455 §1.3's `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, `Upgrade` and `Connection`, then a round trip on the socket; a path without a gateway, 404; a method other than GET, 405 with `Allow: GET`; HTTP/1.0, 400 with a plain-text reason, RFC 6455 §4.2.1 requiring HTTP/1.1, a scenario of its own so a host that cannot refuse it declares that case alone; a malformed upgrade, 400 for `Upgrade: h2c`, for no `Connection: Upgrade` and for no `Sec-WebSocket-Key`, each with a plain-text reason, every case keeping its `Upgrade` header, since a request without one on the HTTP server's port is an HTTP request and never reaches the hand-off; another version, 426 with `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13`; the drain's refusal: a connection idle between requests, shown accepted by `GET /nowhere` answered 404 on it, and an idle `/echo` connection are opened first; a fresh connection then carries the upgrade head up to its `Sec-WebSocket-Key` line, and the scenario waits for `connections_read` to pass the value it read before that connection, starts the close, waits for the idle `/echo` connection's 1001, which shows the drain has begun, sends the rest of the head and requires 503, the handshake's plain-text refusal on `Port::Own` and the status alone on `Port::Http` (F368);
