A scenario asserts kinds and reason strings, never message text. The suite closes its client apps rather than dropping them, so the client module's destroy hook runs in every scenario (§5.4).

### 5.3 Links [30], written without macros

```rust
pub trait Link: Send + Sync + 'static {
    const NAME: &'static str;
    fn capabilities(&self) -> Capabilities;

    /// What can fail before any I/O: endpoint text, `Tls`, a broker URL. Called from `Server::prepare` with the app,
    /// whose root module's full type path is the default competing-consumer group (§5.2). It reports `usable`'s refusal beside its own
    /// where that refusal applies to a server; a client's link reports it where the client is built, and the rest from its first `connect`.
    fn prepare(&mut self, app: &AppHandle) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), BoxError>> + Send { async { Ok(()) } }
    /// What the link refuses before any I/O and without an app: on a tokio-based link, being built outside a runtime and given none;
    /// on the TCP links, a client endpoint that is not an IP address and port, an inherited socket, or `tls` set (138); on the UDP link,
    /// a client endpoint that is not an IP address and port, or an inherited one (142).
    /// `RpcClient::new` calls it and refuses the client as `UnusableLink`, `RpcClientModule`'s init hook calls it and fails `connect`;
    /// it runs when a client or a server takes the link, not when the link is built (§5.4).
    fn usable(&self) -> Result<(), BoxError> { Ok(()) }
    /// The server's in-flight bound, 1,024 at `Default`, handed over beside `prepare`. A link declaring `native_backpressure`
    /// stops taking requests from its broker at it, RabbitMQ's prefetch and Kafka's pause; the server frees a call's place
    /// before it settles the call's `Ack`, so such a link never hands over one past the bound (§5.2). Every other link ignores it.
    fn max_inflight(&mut self, count: Count) {}
    /// Server side: subscribe to the given patterns, all-or-nothing. Called from `Server::bind`.
    fn listen(&self, patterns: &[Pattern]) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Inbound, BoxError>> + Send;
    /// Client side: connect. `RpcClient` calls it lazily, on its first call and again after the connection is lost, passing `runtime`,
    /// the runtime the client was built on: its app's inside an app, the one given to `RpcClient::new` outside one. A link that needs a
    /// runtime for its client side's tasks spawns them there unless it was given one of its own; a link that carries its own runtime ignores it.
    /// A misconfiguration only the connect can see, an `mqtts://` or `tls://` store yielding no root, a `tls://` NATS roots file that cannot
    /// be written, a `tls://` NATS link in a process linking two rustls providers and installing none, or a `tls://` NATS roots' load
    /// outlasting `roots_timeout`, is answered `Misconfigured`, which the client maps to `Internal` and asks again on the next call: no retry
    /// mends the first three, and a later call mends the last once the load has ended. Any other failure it maps to `Unavailable` (§5.2,
    /// 135, 139, 145, 150, 156).
    fn connect(&self, runtime: &Arc<dyn Runtime>) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Outbound, BoxError>> + Send;
    /// The link's own close signal (below). Called from `Server::drain`; the inbound stream ends once nothing more
    /// will arrive, and a link whose drain cannot promise that declares `confirms_drain(false)`.
    fn drain(&self) -> impl Future<Output = ()> + Send;
    fn close(&self) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), BoxError>> + Send;
    /// The addresses bound, for `App<Bound>::addresses()`; a broker link answers none.
    fn bound(&self) -> Vec<BoundAddr> { Vec::new() }
}

pub type Inbound = BoxStream<'static, Delivery>;
pub struct Delivery { pub frame: Frame, pub reply: Option<ReplyPath>, pub ack: Ack }   // `reply` is `None` for an event, and for a `cancel` the link raises itself
impl ReplyPath {
    pub fn new(send: impl Fn(Frame) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<(), BoxError>> + Send + Sync + 'static) -> Self;
    pub fn peer(self, peer: SocketAddr) -> Self;                                         // the caller's address, seeded as `LinkInfo::peer`; TCP and UDP set it
    pub fn send(&self, frame: Frame) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<(), BoxError>>;
}
impl Ack {
    pub fn new(settle: impl FnOnce(bool) + Send + 'static) -> Self;                      // `true` acknowledges, `false` rejects without requeue: the broker never hands the delivery over again
    pub fn none() -> Self;                                                               // a broker that acknowledges nothing
    pub fn ack(self); pub fn reject(self);
}

/// On TCP, UDP, Redis, RabbitMQ and Kafka, frames go out in the order their sends were called: each frame takes its place in the
/// writer's queue when `send` is called, before the returned future is polled, so a streamed request's `in` items arrive in order
/// with `in_end` last and a `cancel` follows the request it names. NATS and MQTT hand each frame to their client library's one
/// command channel as the send is polled. No link writes through a task per frame. A streamed request's `in`, `in_end` and `cancel`
/// on a broker are held until the server acknowledges the `open` and then sent in their own order, a `cancel` alone. The same
/// holds for a server's `ReplyPath`s.
pub struct Outbound {
    pub send: Box<dyn Fn(Pattern, Frame, Option<ReplyTo>) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<(), BoxError>> + Send + Sync>,
    pub replies: BoxStream<'static, Frame>,
}
pub struct ReplyTo { pub id: u64 }                                                       // the correlation a link maps onto its own mechanism

#[non_exhaustive]
pub struct Capabilities {
    pub binary: bool,                 // the codec carries raw bytes
    pub max_frame: Option<u64>,       // `None` for no limit of its own, or one not yet read off the broker
    pub ordering: Ordering,
    pub shapes: &'static [Shape],     // `ALL_SHAPES`, or `UNARY_ONLY`
    pub native_backpressure: bool,    // AMQP prefetch, Kafka pause
    pub delivery: DeliveryMode,
    pub miss_signal: bool,            // a request to a pattern nothing subscribes to is reported to the caller
    pub holds_unserved: bool,         // the broker keeps a request for a subscribed pattern while no instance consumes it, for the next instance
    pub durable_replies: bool,        // the broker keeps a reply published while the client's connection is down, read once it reconnects
    pub confirms_drain: bool,         // the link's drain returns only once nothing more is on its way to the server; `true` unless declared, and a link declaring `false` can lose a request already on its way
    pub ordered_control: bool,        // a request and its control frames travel one ordered lane end to end, so a `cancel` reaches the server after the request it names
}
impl Capabilities { pub const fn new(delivery: DeliveryMode) -> Self; /* one `const fn` setter per field */ }

pub struct NoDestination { pub pattern: String }   // the miss signal, failing a client `send`; `RpcClient` answers `Unavailable`, `reason: "no_destination"`
pub struct FrameTooLarge { pub size: u64, pub limit: u64 }   // a frame over the link's limit, refused before it is sent
pub struct FrameUnencodable { pub codec: Codec, pub source: BoxError }   // a frame the codec cannot encode, from `Codec::encode_frame`; `Display` carries the cause and `source()` answers it
impl Codec { pub fn encode_frame(self, frame: &Frame) -> Result<Bytes, FrameUnencodable>; pub fn decode_frame(self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Frame, BoxError>; }
```

Four rules bind every link beyond its signatures. The `id`s a link delivers are unique among the calls in flight on one inbound stream, so an `in`, `in_end` or `cancel` reaches the call its `req` or `open` started: TCP and UDP map each caller's ids to ids of their own and write the caller's back on the reply path, and a broker link keeps a table from the native correlation to a local `u64` that the client rewrites back. A link that loses a caller with calls in flight, a TCP connection closing, delivers `cancel` for each with `reply: None`, which the server reads as `Disconnected`; a `cancel` the caller sent carries its reply path and is `ClientCancelled`; no broker loses one caller apart from the others. A reply `send` that fails with `FrameTooLarge` or `FrameUnencodable` is replaced by an `err` of kind `internal` under the same `id`, written at once rather than left to the caller's own `Timeout`; the second is the server's own code failing and is logged at `error` with the encoder's complaint, the first stays silent, and any other send failure means the caller is gone and cancels the call `Disconnected`, logged at `debug`. `Codec::encode_frame` is where an encoding failure is typed, a `d` that is no item of the codec, JSON bytes on a CBOR link or bytes that are no JSON on a JSON link: a link encoding its reply frames with it and passing the error on with `?` reports the failure with no change of its own, and a link encoding some other way builds the value itself, its fields public as `FrameTooLarge`'s are. The `err` reaches the caller on every link: TCP and UDP forget the id mapping only after a terminal frame is sent, and the failed frame was never sent; a broker link releases the call from its table before encoding, which removes the control lane's entry and not the reply path. A reply stream whose item the codec cannot encode ends `internal` after the items before it, the failed `item` replaced the same way. The codec is read off `Capabilities::binary`, CBOR when `true` and JSON otherwise, through a crate-private `Codec::of`; a third codec needs a field. `new`, the one constructor, sets `holds_unserved`, `durable_replies` and `ordered_control` to `false` and `confirms_drain` to `true`, the one capability it sets `true`: a link that declares nothing is held to the confirmed drain, so a declaration left out fails the drain-window scenario rather than loosening it. RabbitMQ and Kafka declare the first, an AMQP queue and a Kafka topic holding what no consumer takes; Kafka alone the second, its reply topic holding what a disconnected client has not read; TCP and Redis declare `ordered_control`, a request and its control frames travelling one lane end to end there, a connection on TCP and one publisher with one Pub/Sub connection on Redis, so the ordered-cancel scenario runs where it is declared and is not applicable elsewhere (§5.2); NATS and UDP declare `confirms_drain(false)`, each for a reason of its own: async-nats removes a drained subscription before the server has processed the `UNSUB` and discards what arrives for it afterwards, and UDP's `close` answers the requests its socket already holds, but a datagram arriving after the socket closes reaches no one, nothing telling a caller to stop sending; a connected client socket may learn of it through an ICMP port unreachable, which is often filtered and is not relied on. Each names what a caller sees: under `holds_unserved` a caller reaching a draining or stopped server sees its own `Timeout`, and `miss_signal` covers only a pattern never subscribed; under `durable_replies` a call waiting when the client loses its connection is answered once the client reconnects, where every other link fails it `Unavailable`; under `confirms_drain(false)` a caller reaching a draining server can see its own `Timeout` rather than `Unavailable`, and once the server has closed a miss is reported as on any link with `miss_signal`.

`fw_rpc::Server<L: Link>` implements the core `Server`. `Server::new(link)` carries `max_inflight: Count`, 1,024 at `Default` (§2.8) and refused at `Max(0)` in `prepare` with the HTTP server's hint, and `timeout_grace: Bound`, one second at `Default`, the window the error handlers get after a `deadline-ms` passes (§5.2), refused at `After(Duration::ZERO)` with the HTTP server's hint; `max_frame: u64` is the link's. In `prepare` it reads the app's runtime through `Mounted::runtime()`, which answers it with no `Option`: `listen()` has refused an app binding any transport with no runtime before any `prepare` runs (X31, §8), so the server carries no check of its own. It calls `Link::prepare` with the app and `Link::max_inflight` with its count, and checks each handler's shape against `capabilities()`, so a streamed shape on UDP is a `Configure` error, and each handler's `PayloadKind` against `binary`; a frame bigger than `max_frame` is refused at runtime with the error above. `bound` reports what the link reports, so a TCP or UDP server on port 0 shows its port in `App<Bound>::addresses()`. Over `max_inflight` the shed `err` of kind `unavailable` carries a `RetryAfter` detail of one second. `fw-rpc` has no runtime of its own: `serve` spawns each call into a `fw_transport::TaskSet` over the app's `Runtime` (§8) and races its futures through `futures-util`'s `select`, the first future polled first, so the close signal is read before a delivery and a delivery before a reaped task; `close` aborts the set and waits for every abort to take effect, which is when a refusal still being sent has released its count. The close signal and the drain state are one `Watch`, `fw-transport`'s, doc-hidden in its `__private` module and shared with `fw-ws`'s connection tracker (§4.2): a `std` mutex for the value and an `event-listener` event for the wake-up, each listener registered before the value is read so a change between the read and the wait still wakes it; a streamed request's items and each call's reply frames cross `futures-channel` channels; the client's connection lock is `async-lock`'s.

The links are built as `Tcp::new(endpoint)` with `.tls(Tls)`, `.codec(Codec)` and `.max_frame(u64)`, on `fw-rpc-tcp` and on `fw-rpc-tcp-smol`, whose `Tcp` adds `.with_runtime(runtime)`; `Udp::new(endpoint)` with `.codec`; `Nats::url(..)`, a comma-separated list for several servers, with `.group(..)`, `.codec` and `.roots_timeout(Bound)` (150); `Redis::url(..)` with `.codec`; `RabbitMq::url(..)` with `.codec`; `Mqtt::url(..)` with `.group`, `.qos(QoS)` and `.codec`; and `Kafka::brokers(..)` with `.group`, `.reply_topic(..)`, `.topic_partitions(i32)`, `.replication_factor(i32)` and `.codec`. `Tcp::new` and `Udp::new` take text, an `Endpoint` or a `SocketAddr` (§2.7) and bind it in `listen`; a TCP server may listen on an inherited socket through `Endpoint::inherited`, which UDP refuses in `prepare`, the activation adopting listening TCP sockets alone. A constructor taking an already-bound listener, for a supervisor or an embedding host that holds the socket, is not built; the conformance suites need none, binding port 0 and reading `Link::bound()` (§5.2).

**Seven links are tokio-based and each holds a tokio runtime of its own**, a `fw_runtime_tokio::Tokio`, whatever runtime the app or the client was given; `fw-rpc-tcp-smol`, the eighth, holds none (below). The constructor captures the runtime current where the link is built, `Tokio::try_current()`, or none, and `with_handle(h)` on each of the seven replaces it; nothing looks for a runtime later. A link holding none is refused by `Link::usable`, defaulted to `Ok(())`, answered by each of the seven as its runtime check, naming `.with_handle(..)`, and by the TCP links as their client endpoint check too, the smol link's `usable` being that check alone (138), "the TCP link has no tokio runtime: build it inside one, or give it one with `.with_handle(..)`": `prepare` reports it beside its own failures, so a server's `listen()` answers `Configure` before any socket, TCP collecting it with its other `prepare` problems and the other six returning it first; `RpcClient::new` calls it and refuses the client as `UnusableLink` where it is built; and `RpcClientModule`'s init hook calls it and fails the app's `connect` (§5.4). The check runs when a client or a server takes the link, not when it is built, so `Tcp::new(addr).with_handle(h)` written off a runtime passes. Each of the seven ignores the runtime `connect` is handed, naming the parameter `_runtime`: a link built off a runtime and given no handle refuses to connect when its client hands it a tokio runtime too, since `Runtime` offers no downcast by which the link could tell it is tokio's, and each link's `handle.rs` holds it to that refusal. The `Link` module's documentation states the rule for both sides: a server's link reads its app's runtime in `prepare`, `AppHandle::runtime()`, and a client's link receives its client's in `connect`, a link whose sockets belong to no runtime spawning its tasks there and one carrying a runtime of its own ignoring it. The client paths read `usable` rather than `prepare` because `prepare` takes an `AppHandle`, which `RpcClient::new` has none of and which no module hook or factory can reach, the injectables being `Dep`, `Many`, `Ext`, `ModuleRef` and `ExecutionRef`, and because each link's `prepare` checks a server's concerns too, the default group from the root module's path, Kafka's timer, TCP's endpoint resolved for listening. A constructor that panics outside a runtime, as `Tokio::current()` does, would make `Tcp::new(addr).with_handle(h)` unusable off one (64). Every task a link starts spawns on the held handle by name, `Handle::spawn` or `JoinSet::spawn_on`, and no link calls `tokio::spawn`; `tokio::time` is used inside those tasks alone. What needs tokio's context runs on the link's runtime through `Tokio::run` (§8): opening a socket, a connection or a client, which start the library's own tasks on the current runtime, and a library future that uses tokio's timer or spawner when polled, redis's `ConnectionManager`, which answers within a 500 ms response timeout on `tokio::time::timeout`, Kafka's `FutureProducer::send`, which waits on tokio's clock while librdkafka's queue is full, lapin, which takes tokio's current runtime when it connects, and UDP's socket sends. A library call whose future only hands a command to the library's own task, already on the link's runtime, over a channel that needs no runtime stays inline where it is polled: rumqttc's `AsyncClient`, a flume request channel, async-nats's `publish`, `subscribe`, `flush` and `drain`, a tokio `mpsc` command channel, and every link's frame writes, which go over the link's own queue to its writer task (below); MQTT's drain depends on it, its UNSUBSCRIBEs queued at the drain future's first poll, where a `run` task spawned at that poll and aborted by a drop that follows would queue nothing (66). Every link funnels its frames through one writer task per link side, never a task per frame: TCP's writer per connection; UDP's per socket, each client socket's ended by `close`'s epoch or the client dropping its sends and the server socket's once every sender is gone, fed by the client's `send` and, on the server, by the reply path, `refuse` in the receive loop and `final_read` at `close`; one per side on Redis, RabbitMQ and Kafka, fed by the client's `send` and the reply router's `opened`, and by the reply path and `opened` on the server; NATS and MQTT through their library's one command channel, async-nats's connection task and rumqttc's event loop under the client's order lock, their publishes inline. The five writers are fed through one queue, `fw_transport::__private::ordered`, bounded at 64, which fixes a frame's place at the send's call and applies the bound after it: `Sender::send` puts the item in the queue under its lock at the call and answers a `Room` future that resolves once the item is among the first 64 the receiver has not taken, so waiting for room cannot reorder; each link's client `send` encodes the frame and queues it in the closure's body, before the `BoxFuture` it returns is polled, each reply path does the same, forgetting a finished call's id at the queueing, and the server writers' `write` helpers queue and then return the wait. Frames therefore go out in the order their sends were called, not the order their futures were first polled, under which a request waiting for room had its permit assigned while its task was not running and a `cancel` polled next took the place the writer freed and pushed first (F380); a semaphore acquired in order fixes the place at the acquire, which is the poll, a credit the writer returns needs the same ticket at the call, and either still needs the queue to take the item at the call, so the queue does both in one place. It is runtime-free, a `std` mutex and `event-listener` as `Watch` is, cancel-safe on the receiving side, and an item stays queued when its `Room` is dropped, so a request whose call timed out mid-send is followed by its `cancel` rather than lost, as on TCP; a dropped receiver fails the waiting sends `Closed` and refuses new ones, and `try_send` refuses past the bound, for TCP's `goaway`. A waiting send's frame sits in the queue from its call, so the queue's length past 64 is the number of sends waiting for room, each of which held its frame before, and the writer still takes 64 ahead of any wait. The `Room`, and on Redis the writer's answer through a oneshot as well, the `PUBLISH`'s receiver count being its miss signal, poll without a runtime. The writer runs on the link's runtime, spawned where `listen` or `connect` builds the side, so I/O stays on the link's runtime and results are handed back. RabbitMQ's writer awaits `basic_publish`, which lapin answers once the frames are written to its connection in call order, then pushes the `PublisherConfirm` into a `FuturesUnordered` it polls between jobs; Kafka's queues each record with `send_result`, retrying `QueueFull` every 100 ms for up to 5 s as `FutureProducer::send` does, and pushes the `DeliveryFuture`: order is fixed when the frame is queued with the library, and a writer awaiting each round trip before the next would cap a link at one publish per round trip. Redis has no split between queueing and answering a `PUBLISH`, the miss signal being its answer, so its writer awaits each in turn. On RabbitMQ and Kafka no task per call publishes beside the writer: an `in` or `in_end` for a call whose `opened` has not arrived is held in the call's entry, the reply router sends `Job::Opened(call)` down the same queue, and the writer publishes the held frames before any job queued after it; a `cancel` before `opened` replaces what was held with itself, which `Job::Opened` then publishes alone, and an entry still cancelled after `CANCEL_HOLD` is dropped (F376, F379, §5.2). NATS and MQTT keep their per-call pumps, which publish through the library's one channel. RabbitMQ's `Ack` settles on a task of its own per delivery and Kafka's stores its offset in place, neither a frame; an acknowledgement is created after the call's last reply has answered, so it follows that reply either way. `Tokio::run` stays for `listen`, `connect`, the drains and the closes. What can still reorder is one race: a `cancel` on a broker's control lane that the broker delivers ahead of the request it names (U17, §5.2). Every stream a link hands out reads a channel that needs no runtime, fed by a task on the link's runtime: TCP's and UDP's client reply lanes each have a task reading the socket into a queue of 64 frames, which ends at the link's `close`, at the connection's end, or once the lane is dropped (67); the brokers' streams are channel receivers fed by their lanes. `listen` and `connect` run their I/O alone through `run`, which answers the connection, the subscriptions and the consumers; the side is built, its tasks spawned and the link's state written after `run` answers, in the caller's poll, with no await between, so a `listen` or `connect` dropped while `run` is under way aborts the task and drops what it opened. MQTT spawns its event loop before the broker answers, and the loop's `JoinHandle` reaches the link's state only after the SUBACK; `connect` and `listen` hold the loop's `AbortHandle` in an `AbortOnDrop` from the spawn until the broker's answer and disarm it once the handle is in the link's state, whose `Drop` aborts the loop when the link drops (152), so a `connect` or `listen` dropped before then, a call's timeout cutting `connect` short, aborts the loop as `task.abort()` would, where a detached loop kept its connection and reply subscription until the process ended (F369); `tests/abandoned_connect.rs` stands a socket in for the broker, since only a broker that answers late shows the leak and rumqttc's own connect timeout would end a loop no CONNACK reaches, and requires the connection to end with no SUBSCRIBE on it, for `connect` and for `listen`. Kafka's blocking librdkafka calls keep their threads of their own (57), the close's synchronous offset commit among them (F370), `blocking` carrying `fetch_metadata` and the offset reads and `Detached` a consumer's drop, the server's producer's, which `listen` holds in a `Detached` from its creation (F430, 155), and the admin client's, which `create_topics` holds in a `Detached` from its creation: rdkafka's drop joins the client's polling thread, which reads its stop flag only once a 100 ms poll of its queue comes back empty, and on the `run` task it held a worker of the link's runtime 102 to 110 ms per `connect` and twice per `listen`, every task scheduled there with it; nothing waits for the drop, the topics existing once `create_topics` returns (F413, 133); the reply consumer `connect` creates is held in a `Detached` from its creation too, and `route_replies` takes the `Detached`, so a `subscribe` or a producer creation failing after the consumer exists drops it on that thread (F419, 141); `anchor` waits on the app's `Timer` between retries inside the `run` task, so a smol app's timer is awaited on a tokio worker, `async-io`'s timers firing whichever executor waits on them. No link resolves a host name on the runtime's worker: the TCP and UDP clients take an IP address and port and resolve none, `Endpoint::parse` being `SocketAddr`'s parse, the TCP and UDP links refusing a host name in `usable` (F416, 138, 142); NATS, Redis and MQTT resolve through their libraries' `tokio::net::lookup_host`, on tokio's blocking pool; RabbitMQ through async-rs's `to_socket_addrs` under its `spawn_blocking`, `hickory-dns` being off; Kafka on librdkafka's broker threads, the link leaving `client.dns.lookup` unset; and the gRPC channel through hyper-util's `GaiResolver`, on tokio's blocking pool (§6.3). The TLS loads run off the worker: an `mqtts://` MQTT link reads the store once per link, on its runtime's blocking pool, a server's in `prepare` and a client's at its first connect, 71 ms warm and 2.3 s cold on macOS against microseconds for `mqtt://`, and `listen` and every connect after use what it kept (F414, 134); the process reads it once for every NATS link while any link holds the load, `nats://` included, on the blocking pool of the link that starts it, and writes the roots to a file async-nats reads on tokio's blocking pool at each connection and reconnect that uses TLS, where async-nats 0.46 read the store on the polling thread whenever it was handed a `ClientConfig` or named no certificate file, 76.7 to 77.2 ms a connection after a first of 1.57 s, and upgrades a `nats://` connection whose server requires TLS whatever the scheme; a server's `listen` and a `tls://` client's connect wait for the load under `roots_timeout` and a `nats://` client waits for none, a connection it makes before the load ends being handed no file (F417, F423, F427, 139, 144, 147, 148, 150); RabbitMQ's `amqps://` path is not read. `Runtime` is `Timer + Spawn` and offers no way to run blocking work off a worker, a blocking call spawned through it holding a worker as one polled inline does, and gains none until a crate at the runtime-free or runtime-neutral level needs one; the TCP and UDP clients resolving a host name, which the smol link could do only through an async resolver or blocking work off the worker, would be the first (F416, 133; §8). The `Link` module's documentation states the rule: the futures and streams a link hands out are polled on whatever executor drives the server or the client, which need not be the runtime the link's I/O belongs to, so a link tied to one runs its I/O and its tasks on that runtime itself and hands the results back; the conformance suite calls a client from a plain thread that no runtime runs (§5.2).

**The two TCP links share one wire, `fw-rpc-tcp-core`**, an implementation crate for link authors that both depend on: everything but the sockets. Its crate docs and its manifest's description say so, "For link authors, not applications": a TCP link over another runtime's sockets is built on it, as the two are, application code names `fw_rpc_tcp::Tcp` or `fw_rpc_tcp_smol::Tcp` and not this crate, and its names and shapes follow what the links need and change with them. It holds the framing and its frame limit, `prepare`'s checks and the capabilities, the server's state with its call-id map, the reply path and the writer queue, the accept loop with its drain and close phases, each connection's reader, writer and late `goaway`, the post-drain forwarder, and the client connection's writer, reply reader and send, over `futures-io`'s traits. A link hands `Core::listen` the runtime and an `adopt` closure that turns `fw-net`'s `BoundListener` and the loaded `ServerConfig` into an `Accept`, whose `accept()` answers an `Incoming` carrying the peer and a handshake yielding a `Reader` and a `Writer`, ready at once for a plain connection and the TLS handshake for one with TLS, run on the connection's own task; and `Core::connect` the runtime and the two halves of a connected socket. Every task the core starts is spawned on the `Runtime` the link hands it, the accept back-off slept on that runtime's timer; `fw-transport`'s `Watch` carries the phase, the held-call count and the client epoch, its `TaskSet` the server's connections and a `FuturesUnordered` of `TaskHandle`s the client writers, `futures-util`'s `select_biased!` picks between the close signal and a read, a client's reply lane ends when its stream is dropped through a oneshot's cancellation, and the forwarder takes a slot with `poll_ready` before `try_send`, so a delivery refused by a gone receiver comes back to be answered `unavailable`. The drain behaviour, the late `goaway` (F366) and the stream ending once the draining server holds no call, is one implementation on both links. `fw-rpc-tcp` is that core over tokio's sockets: it adopts the listener under its handle's `enter()`, connects through `Tokio::run`, hands the core tokio's halves through `tokio-util`'s `compat`, which wraps each read's slice in tokio's `ReadBuf` and starts nothing, and spawns through its own `Tokio` as the core's `Runtime`, so a panic in one of its tasks ends it `Panicked` as on every runtime. Its public API, error texts and capabilities are the ones above.

**`fw-rpc-tcp-smol` is the same core over `async-net`'s sockets**, the type `Tcp` with `Link::NAME` `"tcp"` as the tokio link's, since the wire is one: a server's `LinkInfo` names the wire whichever crate carries it, and a client of either link is answered by a server of the other, which `fw-rpc-tcp`'s `tests/interop.rs` holds for a unary call and a streamed reply each way, the smol link given no runtime on either side and its tasks on the tokio runtime there, the app's as a server and the client's as a client. Its TLS is `futures-rustls`'s acceptor over `fw-net`'s `Arc<ServerConfig>`, as `fw-listener-smol`'s is; a plain stream is cloned into its two halves, as `async-net` streams allow, and a TLS stream split through `futures-util`'s `split`, a lock between the halves, as tokio's `split` is on the tokio link's TLS. Its sockets belong to no runtime, `async-io` driving them from its reactor thread whichever executor polls them, so only the link's tasks need one, and they run on the runtime the link runs under: a server's link given none takes its app's in `prepare`, `AppHandle::runtime()`, the app's redacting wrapper, and a client's link given none spawns on the runtime `connect` is handed, its client's, the app's inside an app through `RpcClientModule` and `RpcClient::new`'s outside one, so a smol client link needs nothing named on it (F386); `with_runtime(..)` names another in place of either, `fw_runtime_smol::Smol` or any `Runtime`. No client is refused, `usable` is not overridden, and the one refusal left is a server's, in `prepare`, when its app has no runtime and the link was given none: "the smol TCP link's server has no runtime for its tasks: its app has none and the link was given none with `.with_runtime(..)`". The tokio links capture the runtime current where they are built; smol has none to capture, so the runtime arrives through the SPI instead. Its tests beside the three suites are the tokio link's where it has one: `runtime.rs`, whose runtime a client's and a server's tasks run on, a client link given none outside an app spawning on `RpcClient::new`'s runtime, the link's two tasks and the client's router and close, four exactly, and inside an app on the app's, a client link given its own keeping the link's two tasks there and the client's two on the client's, `connect` called directly spawning on the handed runtime, and a server's link on its app's or on its own; `late_goaway.rs`, TLS through `futures-rustls`; `drain_end.rs`; `client_close.rs`, the client links of the three suites and of those two tests given no runtime.

Each broker's TLS is its client library's, selected by the URL scheme in the right column and enabled as a feature of the link crate; both TCP links take `fw_net::Tls` (§2.7) on their server side, and their clients speak plain TCP. An `mqtts://` link builds its TLS configuration from the platform's roots once per link, on its runtime's blocking pool, a server's in `prepare` and a client's at its first connect, and keeps what the load answered, a failure included: a store yielding no root fails a server's `bind` as `StartupError::Configure` before `listen` connects and each client call `Internal` with `reason: "misconfigured_link"`, through `Misconfigured` (§5.2), and a load yielding roots beside errors keeps the roots and logs the errors at `warn`. The configuration's crypto provider is the process's installed one, or `aws-lc-rs` where none is, and the load draws once on its random source, so the provider's one-time initialisation, about 20 ms in a debug build, runs off the worker with the load (134). The process loads the platform's roots for every NATS link once while any link holds the load, `nats://` included, since async-nats upgrades a `nats://` connection whose server's `INFO` requires TLS and the link cannot know before connecting whether one will: off the worker, on the blocking pool of the link that first needs them, a server's in `prepare` and a client's at its first connect, the load writes those a root store accepts as PEM to one file in the OS temp directory, `fw-rpc-nats-roots-<pid>-<n>.pem`, and each link hands the file to every connection it makes once the load has ended through async-nats's `add_root_certificates`, which async-nats reads on tokio's blocking pool at each connection and reconnect that uses TLS in place of its own read of the store, a connection that stays plain never reading it (139, 144, 147). A server's `listen` waits for the load on either scheme, and so does a `tls://` client's connect, each under `Nats::roots_timeout`, 30 s at `Bound::Default`: async-nats reconnects a connection with the options it was made with, so a server's one connection made without the file would read the store at every reconnect for the app's life. On expiry a `tls://` link is refused as `Misconfigured`, and a `nats://` server connects without the file and logs one `warn`. A `nats://` client waits for nothing: a connection it makes before the load ends is handed no file at its connect or its reconnects, so if its server upgrades it, async-nats reads the platform's store on the thread polling it each time, and its next connection after a lost one is made afresh (F423, 148, 150). The file is removed once the last link and connection holding the load have dropped it, and a link needing the roots after that loads them again; a process killed before the drop leaves its one file in the temp directory, the roots being public data and the name unique, so a leftover costs only space (139). Over `tls://`, a store yielding no root, a file that cannot be written, a load outlasting `roots_timeout`, or a process whose build links both of rustls's crypto providers and installs neither is refused as `Misconfigured`, the last naming `CryptoProvider::install_default`, where async-nats's `ClientConfig::builder()` panicked the connection (139, 145, 150), and a later call mends the load outlasting `roots_timeout` once the load has ended (F432, 156); over `nats://` a load that failed is logged at `warn` once and the link connects without the file (144), and a server whose load ends unanswered, the runtime it ran on having shut down, logs that at `warn` and connects without it (F431, 156). A zero `roots_timeout` is refused in `Link::usable`, so a client is refused where it is built, `RpcClient::new` answering `UnusableLink` and `RpcClientModule`'s init hook failing `connect` with it, and a server's `prepare`, which calls `usable` first, refuses it as `Configure` (150). A server's link bound through an app drops, and its hold on the file with it, once the app has closed and `serve` has returned, or once the `App` value and every `close` claim held at its drop have gone (146, 149, 153). Two cases are open: a `nats://` connection a server upgrades, in a build linking both providers with neither installed, still panics inside async-nats (F422, 145), and a `nats://` connection made without the file and upgraded by its server, a client's made before the load ends or a server's whose load outlasted `roots_timeout`, reads the store on its polling thread (F423, 148, 150). Links connect lazily: the server side at `bind`, the client side on its first call. A broker link connects once, in `listen` or `connect`, and does not retry: an unreachable broker fails `bind` as `StartupError::Bind`, one report at startup, and a retry window is a `Bound` to add when a deployment needs one. Kafka's committed-offsets read at `bind` is the one retry inside it, on the three coordinator codes alone and within the read's own 10 s timeout (above): the broker is reachable and its coordinator is still loading or moving, an error librdkafka classes retriable, so the retry hides no configuration error and the one report at startup stands; each attempt runs on a thread of its own and the wait between attempts is the app's `Timer`, which `Link::prepare` reads from the `AppHandle` it is handed. After `bind`, a server side keeps its own reconnect: async-nats, lapin with auto-recovery on the server connection, and librdkafka reconnect inside their clients, and the Redis and MQTT links reconnect in their read loops. A client side carries no call across a reconnect. Each link but Kafka's ends its reply lane when its connection drops, NATS on async-nats's `Disconnected` event, Redis when its Pub/Sub stream ends, MQTT on a connection error after the first CONNACK, and RabbitMQ on its reply consumer's error, its client connection opened without lapin's auto-recovery, since a recovery that re-consumes `amq.rabbitmq.reply-to` on a new channel loses the replies addressed to the old one. A reply published during the gap is lost on all four, and ending the lane reports that loss; a reconnect finishing before the reply would answer short outages and leave longer ones to the caller's `Timeout`, with nothing reporting what was lost. `RpcClient` then fails every call waiting on the lane `Unavailable`, and the next call connects through a fresh `Link::connect` (§5.4). Kafka's client keeps librdkafka's reconnect: its reply topic holds a reply published while the client is out, read once it reconnects, which the link declares as `durable_replies`. Over the server's in-flight limit, 1,024 unset, TCP, UDP, NATS, Redis and MQTT refuse with `err` of kind `unavailable` and `RetryAfter`, and RabbitMQ and Kafka stop taking requests (§5.2).

**Shutdown:** `Link::drain` is the link's own close signal; a broker link's returns once the broker has confirmed that it stopped routing to the instance, and a link that cannot confirm it declares `confirms_drain(false)`. Every refusal a link or the server writes because it is draining or closing reads "the server is shutting down", the phrase HTTP's 503 carries (§10). TCP closes its listener and sends `goaway` on every connection without waiting for room in a writer's queue, a connection registering after that sending its own (above), and finishes the calls in flight; every connection's deliveries pass through one forwarder, which hands them to the server until the link is draining and holds no call, counted across connections, then ends the inbound stream and answers what arrives afterwards itself, a request or streamed request `err` of kind `unavailable` on its reply path, which also forgets the id, and anything else, naming no call, dropped. A `cancel` forgets its id before it is queued and a closing connection forgets its orphans before their `cancel`s are queued, so both release the count only after the queueing, and the forwarder reads its queue before it looks at the count, so nothing queued before the count reached zero is answered by the link in place of the server; ending the stream only when every connection had closed would hold the drain to its deadline while a client keeps an idle connection open. UDP sends nothing and keeps receiving, so a `cancel` still arrives; its receive loop, the one sender of deliveries, ends the inbound stream between datagrams once the link is draining and holds no call, and refuses a request arriving afterwards under the sender's own id until `close`, which aborts the receive task and then reads what the socket's buffer already holds, answering each request found there `unavailable` before the socket is dropped. NATS drains each pattern subscription; async-nats queues the `UNSUB` and removes the subscription on its connection task's next poll, without waiting for the server to process it, and discards a message for a removed subscription, so a request the server routed to this instance before it processed the `UNSUB` can be lost on its way in, its caller seeing its own `Timeout` rather than the drain's `Unavailable`. async-nats 0.46 offers no public path that unsubscribes, waits for the server and still delivers what arrives before the server has processed the `UNSUB`: `flush` resolves on the client's own write, with no `PING` sent, `unsubscribe` removes the subscription at once, and the command channel is crate-private, so an unsubscribe followed by a flush loses every such request where the drain loses some. The link declares the window as `confirms_drain(false)`. AMQP cancels its consumers (`basic.cancel`) and awaits each `basic.cancel-ok`, which the broker sends after every delivery to that consumer, the consumer receiving until then. Redis sends one `UNSUBSCRIBE` for its patterns and awaits the reply, every pushed message handed to the inbound stream before the reply resolves the request; Redis runs the whole command before replying, so the reply already follows the unsubscribe of every channel. The server lane may read a pushed message after the drain's watcher has ended the inbound stream: the lane hands each frame over under the lock the watcher takes the sender under, the watcher ending the stream only while no call is held, and a `req` or `open` the ended stream no longer takes is answered `err` of kind `unavailable`, "the server is shutting down", on its reply channel under the caller's wire id, published on the lane itself before its next message is read; a delivery the sender refuses is released and answered the same way, and a control frame or an event read then is dropped. `close` takes the sender before it clears the table, so no call is held once it is. MQTT unsubscribes each `$share` filter and waits for the broker's UNSUBACK to each, under the drain's deadline and no bound of its own: the broker writes every PUBLISH it routed before processing an UNSUBSCRIBE ahead of the UNSUBACK and the event loop reads in order, so once every UNSUBACK is in, nothing more is routed here and what was routed has reached the link. MQTT 5 §3.10.4 lets a broker deliver after the UNSUBACK a publish it held back for the instance's flow control, so both sides of the link announce a Receive Maximum of 65,535, MQTT 5's largest, in their CONNECT: a broker then holds back nothing until that many publishes are unacknowledged to the instance. rumqttc acknowledges a publish as its event loop reads it, so the window bounds only what is on its way, and the server's own admission, `Server::max_inflight` when set, refuses what it will not take; MQTT 5 reads an absent Receive Maximum as 65,535, but Mosquitto 2.0 then applies its own `max_inflight_messages`, 20 unset, and holds the rest back. A request is lost at shutdown only when more are outstanding to the instance than the broker's flow control allows, the announced 65,535 or a smaller cap the broker applies itself; `confirms_drain` stays `true`, a boolean being unable to express that bound, and the drain scenarios hold the link to the confirmed drain below it. A filter is matched to its UNSUBACK by order, the server side unsubscribing nowhere else and rumqttc taking requests in the order they were queued: the event loop moves the oldest queued filter under the packet id its `Outgoing::Unsubscribe` reports and removes it on the UNSUBACK with that id. An UNSUBACK refusing a filter is logged at `warn` naming the filter and the reason and counts as answered, since the broker goes on routing and nothing before `close` changes that; a CONNACK without a session present releases every outstanding filter, the new session holding no shared subscription, and the loop resubscribes only the control topic while draining. A drain dropped at the deadline before every UNSUBACK is in logs at `warn` the filters still outstanding, since until the broker confirms it can route requests to this instance; the log fires from the drain future's own drop, the core's deadline path having no logger and knowing no filter. Kafka pauses its assignment and commits asynchronously, and has nothing to confirm: a group member pulls, and no broker routes to it. `pause` is local to librdkafka, which bumps the partition's version barrier before returning and drops prefetched records of an older version, the partitions staying assigned until the consumer leaves the group at `close`; offsets are stored only when a handler settles and the drain's and close's commits commit stored offsets, so a record never handed over stays in the topic and the next member resumes from it after the rebalance, the hold `holds_unserved` declares, and a record polled before the pause and dropped after the inbound stream ended is redelivered the same way unless a later offset on its partition is stored first, offsets being cumulative per partition. The control lane stays open and the inbound stream ends once the draining server holds no call, since a held call can still receive its items or a `cancel`; on MQTT only after the UNSUBACKs, so a request routed before them reaches the core and is refused by the dispatcher rather than by the link. `Server::drain` then waits, once `Link::drain` has returned, for the inbound stream to end and for every refusal spawned to be sent, under the one drain deadline: what reaches the server during the drain opens no execution, so the core's wait for live executions does not cover it, and a refusal is small and fast, so a bound of its own would add a knob and protect nothing the deadline does not. The core awaits each server's drain future inside the window and drops it at the deadline. The wait is for a settled state, the stream not read or ended with no refusal outstanding: `serve` marks the stream read while it holds it, through a guard cleared when `serve` returns or is dropped, so a server that never served waits for nothing; the end is marked when the stream returns `None`; and a refusal is counted from its spawn to the end or abort of its send, the dispatcher's three refusal sites, over the in-flight limit, a call during the drain and an unhandled pattern during the drain, going through one path. The serve loop routes deliveries in order and counts a refusal as it accepts the delivery, so every refusal for a delivery the stream yielded is counted before the end is marked; a shed refusal spawned before the drain is counted too, and waiting for one costs nothing the window does not already allow. At `close`, the serve loop takes without waiting every delivery the inbound stream has ready and drops it, a dropped delivery's `Ack` settling nothing, so AMQP and Kafka redeliver it, reads the refusals not yet sent, and logs at `warn` when either count is nonzero, "the RPC server closed before answering every call that reached it; the drain's deadline passed first", with the link, `refusals_unsent` and `deliveries_unread`; a call still running was cancelled at the drain's end and is counted once, in the shutdown's report. It then aborts the tasks. In-flight calls drain under the core's rules meanwhile.

`Link::close` runs under the core's `close` bound, closing the connections and committing synchronously on Kafka; that commit, `commit_consumer_state(CommitMode::Sync)`, runs through `blocking` on a thread of its own and is awaited, as every other blocking librdkafka call in the link is, a failed commit logged at `debug` and a panicked one at `warn`: run in place it held the thread polling `close` without bound against a frozen broker, librdkafka waiting on a synchronous commit past its request timeout (F370), and the link's `close_commits_off_the_runtime_thread_polling_it` pauses the broker's container with an offset stored and requires a task beside `close` on a current-thread runtime to keep ticking. On NATS, `close` subscribes each connection still connected to a fresh inbox, publishes an empty message there and waits for it to come back before draining the connection: async-nats's `publish` and `drain` only queue commands for the connection's task, and a task that finds its command channel closed exits without writing what it already took, so a `close` that drained and dropped the last `Client` at once could lose the replies of the calls the drain let finish. NATS routes one connection's messages in order, so the echo shows every earlier one was routed; `Client::flush` would show async-nats's own write and not the server's routing. A connection that drops during the round trip leaves `close` waiting until the core's `close` bound drops it, recorded `ShutdownFailure::Close` with `TimedOut`. On MQTT, the server side's `close` queues a DISCONNECT and waits for its connection's event loop to report it written before ending the loop: rumqttc's `publish` and `disconnect` only queue requests, which the loop writes in order, so the report shows every reply queued earlier, a drained call's or a refusal sent during the drain, was written ahead of it, where aborting the loop at once could drop them. A connection that fails after `close` ends the loop instead of reconnecting, and a broker that stays reachable but never takes the DISCONNECT leaves `close` to the core's bound. On Kafka, `close` drops each consumer on a thread of its own: a librdkafka consumer's drop leaves the group and polls until the broker confirms, about a tenth of a second with the broker up and without bound once it is gone, and on a runtime worker it stalls every task scheduled there, while a `spawn_blocking` task would hold the runtime's shutdown instead; a thread that cannot be spawned drops the consumer where it is, logged at `warn`. The client side's `close` signals its reply router and awaits it, the router dropping the reply consumer before it ends, so the consumer leaves its group while the broker is there to answer, and then takes the producer out of the slot the send closure reads and awaits its drop on a thread of its own, librdkafka purging, flushing for up to 500 ms and destroying the handle, which closes the client's last connection; a send afterwards fails until the next call connects anew. A router dropped before it ends, its client never closed and the runtime shutting down, still drops its consumer on a thread of its own. The server's group and control consumers are dropped with their last reference and not awaited: once the broker is gone that drop blocks without bound, holding its thread and librdkafka's and neither the tokio runtime's shutdown nor the process's exit. The server's producer drops where its writer ends, after `close` or after a dropped link's side has gone, on a thread of its own through `Detached`, and `close` does not wait for it (F430, 155). On TCP, `close` advances a client epoch every client connection subscribed to when it was made: each writer, owned by the link, shuts its half of the socket on it and is awaited, and the reply lane ends with it, so the peer reads the end of the connection, the waiting calls fail `Unavailable`, and a call made afterwards connects on a new subscription. The server side's `close` aborts the connection tasks and, once the accept task has ended, clears the map holding each connection's writer sender, since an aborted task never removes its own: every writer then ends, shutting its half of the socket, so a peer that sent a call as the server closed reads a FIN and its reply lane ends `Unavailable` rather than waiting out its own `Timeout`. On UDP the reply lane owns the client socket and ends on the same epoch, releasing the socket; the send closure holds a `Weak` and fails once it cannot upgrade, and a call made afterwards binds a new socket. On Redis the client's `close` takes the `PUBLISH` connection out of its slot beside aborting the Pub/Sub lane, the `RpcClient` keeping a connection's send half until its next call replaces it. A link dropped without `close`, as the `App` value's drop leaves a server's (149), aborts every loop it spawned that holds a socket or a connection, each held by the link through a handle that aborts on drop and not by the state the loop holds: TCP's accept loop and forwarding task and UDP's receive task and writer as an `Owned` in the link, the broker links' read loops, lanes and routers, the RabbitMQ client's writer among them, through a `Drop` on their `State`, the Kafka client's producer dropped on a thread of its own, and NATS's lanes and routers through an `AbortOnDrop` in its state; every broker server side's drop clears its held calls, whose reply paths hold the writer's queue or the connection's client, and each drain's watcher holds the side weakly, so a server dropped holding a call closes its connections too (F428, F429, 47, 151, 152, 154). A TCP server's listener and accepted connections close and its address can be bound again, a UDP server's socket closes, and a broker link's connections close, its subscriptions, consumers and group memberships going with them at the broker. The drop runs none of `close`'s steps: no DISCONNECT, UNSUBSCRIBE or synchronous commit is written.

### 5.4 Client [31]

```rust
#[module(imports = [RpcClientModule::for_root(fw_rpc_nats::Nats::url("nats://bus:4222")).timeout(Bound::After(Duration::from_secs(2))).keyed::<Billing>()])]
pub struct OrdersModule;

#[injectable]
pub struct Checkout { billing: Dep<RpcClient, Billing> }

impl Checkout {
    async fn finish(&self, order: &Order) -> Result<Invoice, RpcError> {
        self.billing.request::<_, Invoice>("invoices.create", &NewInvoice::from(order))
            .header("tenant", order.tenant())
            .timeout(Duration::from_secs(2))
            .await
    }
}
```

The client offers `request(pattern, &req)`, `emit(pattern, &data)`, `stream(pattern, &req)`, which answers a stream, `send_stream(pattern, items)` and `duplex(pattern, items)`, each an `IntoFuture` builder carrying `.header(name, value)` and `.within(&exec)` and, by shape, its bounds: `request` and `send_stream` answer a `Call` with `.timeout(Duration)`, the whole call, sent as `deadline-ms`; `stream` and `duplex` answer a `StreamCall` with `.idle_timeout(Bound)`, the longest silence the client tolerates between reply frames, not sent, `Default`, which a call that never sets it has, taking the client's, `Unbounded` none for this call whatever the client's, and `After(d)` `d` in place of the client's, and `.deadline(Duration)`, the whole call, sent, the deadline applying only where the call sets it and the idle timeout where the call or the client does; `emit` answers an `Emit` with neither. Each name means one thing on every shape, so `StreamCall` has no `timeout` and `client.stream(..).timeout(d)` is E0599, which a `compile_fail` doctest on the type holds (111). The module's `timeout` is a `Bound`, five seconds at `Default`, the default for a `request` or `send_stream` that sets none and the bound on an `emit`'s publish; it does not reach a stream. The module's `idle_timeout` is a `Bound` too, none at `Default` and at `Unbounded`, the idle timeout of every `stream` and `duplex` that sets none of its own, which a call's `.idle_timeout(Bound::After(d))` replaces, longer or shorter, and `.idle_timeout(Bound::Unbounded)` turns off for that call (X39, 120): a quiet stream, a subscription yielding an event now and then, runs until it ends unless one is set, and a lost connection fails a waiting stream `Unavailable` through the reply lane whatever the idle timeout, so the idle timeout catches only a server that is still connected and has gone silent (118). `.timeout` and `.deadline` take a `Duration`, their move to `Bound`, for §3.4's sake, deferred as F393, so a call cannot turn the client's timeout off, only lengthen it, and one with none is made on a client whose timeout is `Bound::Unbounded`; no startup check sees a per-call value. A caller's `deadline-ms` and a per-call zero each fail the call when it is awaited, before it connects, where a binary payload on a JSON link fails (§5.2), since a builder method answering `Self` can refuse nothing and the await is the first point that can. The header is checked first, one line common to the three shapes where the zero checks are each shape's own: a call of any shape, `emit` included, whose caller set `deadline-ms` with `.header` answers an `RpcError` of kind `BadRequest`, `reason: "reserved_header"`, whatever the value, since the client writes that header from the call's bound and the mistake is setting it at all, its message quoting the value to 64 characters, marked cut short past that, as the server's `bad_deadline` quotes one, and naming what to write instead, `.timeout` or `.within` on a `Call`, `.deadline` or `.within` on a `StreamCall`, and for an `Emit` that an event is sent with no deadline (F395, 124). The zero checks follow: `.timeout(Duration::ZERO)`, `.deadline(Duration::ZERO)` and `.idle_timeout(Bound::After(Duration::ZERO))` each answer an `RpcError` of kind `BadRequest`, `reason: "zero_timeout"`, whose message is the `ZeroTimeout`'s and whose `source`, `RpcError` implementing `Error::source` for the client's own typed refusals, is the `ZeroTimeout`; nothing connects and no frame is sent, so the server never sees the call (F392, 120). The `ZeroTimeout` names the setter, the zero as the setter takes it, the link and what to write instead: "`StreamCall::idle_timeout(Bound::After(Duration::ZERO))` on the tcp link would time out the stream; write `Bound::Unbounded` to turn the timeout off", and for the two `Duration` setters, where that spelling does not compile, "`Call::timeout(Duration::ZERO)` on the tcp link would time out the call; leave `.timeout` unset for the client's timeout, or make the call on a client whose timeout is `Bound::Unbounded`" and "`StreamCall::deadline(Duration::ZERO)` on the tcp link would time out the stream; leave `.deadline` unset for no deadline". The client has no retry policy: no path in it repeats a call, every refusal of its own and every `err` a server answers is returned at once, and its one loop, registering a call on a second connection when the first's reply lane ended between the hand-over and the registration (below), runs before any frame is sent and repeats none, so a `BadRequest` from any of its four sources, a reserved header, a zero bound, a frame the link refuses as too large or a server's `bad_request`, is attempted once; `fw-rpc`'s unit tests hold each to it, the reserved header's finding no connect made and no frame sent an hour on. A module has no `prepare`, so `RpcClientModule::timeout(Bound::After(Duration::ZERO))`, and `RpcClientModule::idle_timeout` with the same zero, which would end every stream before its first frame, is recorded through `ModuleDef::try_value` as a `ZeroTimeout`, the error `RpcClient::timeout` and `RpcClient::idle_timeout` answer, with the setter in its sentence and what the zero would end, "every call" or "every stream", a module with both at zero reporting the timeout's, and reported by `wire()` beside every other wiring error as a `WiringError::ValueFailed` whose `Redacted` downcasts to it, naming the link and pointing at `Bound::Unbounded`; a zero on a module is visible there, and `wire()` comes before `prepare`, so one report still precedes any socket. The module's init hook calls its link's `usable`, so a link that can never connect, a tokio-based one built outside a runtime and given none, fails the app's `connect` as `ConnectError::Hook { reason: Errored(..) }` carrying an `UnusableLink` whose sentence names `RpcClientModule::for_root`, rather than failing each call `Unavailable` (§5.3). Each `for_root` is its own module, labelled `RpcClientModule`, so two clients of one link type are two imports; the client is a singleton reading `Dep<dyn Runtime>`, so an application without a runtime, one given `.timer(..)` alone included, fails `wire()` naming the missing binding, with the help line the core writes for that key, "set one on the app with `.runtime(..)`, which sets its timer too", and for a missing `dyn Timer` "set one on the app with `.timer(..)`, or with `.runtime(..)`, which sets both"; the line is the core's rendering of `WiringError::Missing` for any binding reading either key, since a module registers before the app's builder is known and cannot tell a timer-only app from one with a runtime, and the factory reading the `Dep` is what fails. The runtime's `Timer` half times every call.
