## 6. gRPC

### 6.1 Generation and API [34][36]

```rust
// build.rs
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    fw_build::configure().file_descriptor_set_path("users.bin").compile(&["proto/users.proto"], &["proto"])?;   // a vendored protoc: no system protoc
    Ok(())
}

// src/pb.rs
fw_grpc::include_proto!("users.v1");
```

The build step is `fw-build`: tonic-prost-build over a vendored `protoc` binary, behind a default-on `vendored-protoc` feature that yields to a `PROTOC` environment variable; that meets [34]'s "no system protoc", and a pure-Rust compiler is a later swap behind the same `configure()` API. `configure()` carries `out_dir(..)`, `OUT_DIR` unset, `file_descriptor_set_path(..)`, relative to the package root, `build_client(bool)`, `true` unset, and `compile(&protos, &includes)`. For every RPC method, generation emits the messages (prost), a client (tonic), a file descriptor set (for reflection) and a marker type; no server trait is generated, tonic's generator running with `build_server(false)`, since handlers bind to the markers and the dispatcher calls them by path. The markers are written by a `ServiceGenerator` wrapping tonic's, which prost-build takes through `Config::service_generator`: after each service the wrapper appends `pub struct GetUser; impl fw_grpc::Method for GetUser { .. }` per method under a module named by tonic-build's own snake-casing, `user_service` beside `user_service_client`, so the two agree character for character, the module carrying `#[allow(clippy::module_inception)]`, since a wrapper module named as the service, `mod users { include_proto!("users.v1"); }` for the service `Users`, holds `users::users`, which clippy would report in the user's crate on a module the user cannot rename (§1), and, with clients on, the `fw_grpc::GrpcClient` impl for the client, through which `GrpcClientModule` builds it (§6.3); a message path prost made relative gains `super::`. `fw_grpc::include_proto!("users.v1")` includes `$OUT_DIR/users.v1.rs`, where the markers sit. The descriptor set comes from `file_descriptor_set_path`, and the package's file then ends with `pub const FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET: &[u8] = include_bytes!(..)` of the absolute path, since a relative one would resolve against `OUT_DIR`; `Server::file_descriptor_set(pb::FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET)` hands it to reflection (§6.2). The generated code names `tonic`, `tonic-prost` and `prost`, and `prost-types` where a proto uses a well-known type, so the crate running the build step depends on those beside `fw-grpc`.

```rust
pub struct GetUser;
impl fw_grpc::Method for GetUser {
    const PATH: &'static str = "/users.v1.UserService/GetUser";
    const SHAPE: Shape = Shape::Unary;
    type Request = GetUserRequest;
    type Response = User;
}
```

Handlers bind to a marker, and the attribute checks the signature against the marker's types and shape at the concrete site, so a mismatch fails to compile:

```rust
#[routes]
#[guards(grpc = TokenGuard)]                                               // reads a bearer token off `GrpcMetadata`
impl UsersGrpc {
    #[fw_grpc::method(pb::user_service::GetUser)]
    async fn get_user(&self, req: Message<pb::GetUserRequest>) -> Result<Response<pb::User>, UserError> {
        let user = self.users.find(req.0.id).await?;
        Ok(Response::new(user.into()).metadata("x-cache", "miss"))      // reply metadata [35]
    }

    #[fw_grpc::method(pb::user_service::WatchUsers)]
    async fn watch(&self, req: Request<pb::WatchRequest>, cx: GrpcCx)  // the whole request, and the context
        -> Result<impl Stream<Item = Result<pb::UserEvent, UserError>>, UserError> { /* ... */ }

    #[fw_grpc::method(pb::user_service::ImportUsers)]
    async fn import(&self, rows: Streaming<pb::UserRow>) -> Result<pb::ImportSummary, UserError> { /* ... */ }
}
```

`Message<T>`, `Request<T>` and `Streaming<T>` each declare `CONSUMES_BODY = true`, so a handler taking two of them fails the pairwise check naming both (§2.2). The marker checks are const generics at the concrete site: the attribute writes, beside each `#[method]` handler, a hidden `__fw_grpc_<name>` method taking the same parameters, in which one `ParamProbe::<M, P>` per body-consuming parameter takes `{ streams_request(M::SHAPE) }` and the reply probe takes `{ streams_reply(M::SHAPE) }`, and a mismatch in message type or shape leaves `ParamCheck::matches` or `Checked::checked` uncallable, an E0599 whose type spells what the handler declares beside what the marker requires: `Checked<(Shaped<true>, UserEvent), (Shaped<false>, User)>` is a stream of `UserEvent` returned for a unary method replying `User`. The reply probe is spanned at the return type, the `impl` token for an `impl Stream<..>` return, since on stable a span over several tokens keeps the first one's, and at the method's name for a handler with no return type; spanned at the signature's output as a whole, the caret would sit on the `-` of `->`. A handler reading no message is accepted, its request unread. The hidden method answers a crate-local `Answer`, which the generated call reads as the handler's `IntoReply<Grpc>` value, through a six-arm autoref probe, each arm one reference deeper than the priority reads, the first that applies winning: a `Result` of a reply stream whose error converts into a `CallError`, then one whose error boxes, then a bare stream; then the same three over a reply value. The streams come first, so a type that is both is answered as a stream. The detour exists because a handler answers a prost message or a stream of them, and neither can implement `IntoReply<Grpc>`: a blanket in `fw-grpc` over the foreign `prost::Message` is refused by the orphan rule, and a message `fw-build` wrote cannot cover `()` or a `prost_types` message. What a handler returns, then: the reply message, `()`, `Response<T>` with `.metadata(key, value)` for reply metadata, a stream of `Result<M, E>` with `E: Into<CallError>`, or a `Result` of any of those; the error implements `Classify`, or is a `tonic::Status`, which the probe boxes unchanged and the wire sends as it stands (§6.2). Three public traits name those sets, and `GrpcCx::reply` and `reply_stream` take them (§6.2): `IntoGrpcReply` is a reply of one message, a prost message or `Response<T>` around one, `()` among them as `google.protobuf.Empty`; `IntoGrpcStream` is a reply stream, any stream of `IntoGrpcItem`s or `Response<S>` around one; `IntoGrpcItem` is one item, `Result<T, E>` with `E: Into<CallError>`. They are conversion traits consuming their value, so each follows Rust's `Into*` convention, as `IntoReply` does, and is named after its one method: `into_grpc_reply`, `into_grpc_stream` and `into_grpc_item`. None is sealed: the probe's value arms are blanket over the traits, so a type implementing `IntoGrpcReply` is a value a handler may return. `fw_net::Tls` verifies no client certificate, so a guard that would read the peer's certificate has nothing to read; client authentication is a later `fw-net` item, where it serves every transport at once, and the example guard reads a token.

**How a marker becomes a service.** tonic's generated `UserService` trait is never implemented. `fw-grpc` builds one tower service that dispatches on `:path` to the marker's call. It does not go through `tonic::server::Grpc::unary` and its siblings: those decode the message before the service runs, which would run the guards after a decode, against §2.2, and answer an unencoded `Response<M>` where the pre-dispatch stage's reply is the encoded `http::Response` an interceptor reads. The dispatcher uses the two pieces `Grpc` composes instead, `Streaming::new_request` under the extractors and `EncodeBody::new_server` for replies, so the message is decoded by the extractor that reads it and encoded at the reply. A path off the table answers UNIMPLEMENTED, as the gRPC specification requires; the dispatcher writes it and offers it to no error handler, as HTTP's `OPTIONS` 204 is offered to none. Two handlers for one `PATH` are a `Configure` error.

### 6.2 Wire behavior [35]

- **Engine:** `fw_grpc::Server::new(endpoint)` is an HTTP/2 server over `fw-server-hyper` (§3.7) on `fw-listener-tokio`'s listener, `Serve<TokioListener>`, tonic being tokio-only: `fw-net` endpoints and inherited sockets, `fw_net::Tls` with ALPN `h2`, hyper's `http2::Builder` per connection, so TLS and socket activation have one story and one vocabulary with HTTP. Its accept loop and connections run on the app's runtime as the other two servers' do; the builder keeps hyper-util's `TokioExecutor` and `TokioTimer`, so a gRPC server bound on an app whose runtime is not tokio's fails `listen()` at `bind`, the listener refusing to adopt (§3.7). tonic's own `transport::Server` is not used: it owns its socket, its TLS and its limits, which would be a second vocabulary for each.
- **Reply:** `fw_grpc::Reply` is `http::Response<tonic::body::Body>`. An interceptor reads and writes reply metadata through its headers and cannot read the message, which is what lets one enhancer list serve every method of a service. An error handler claiming an error with `Ok` builds that `Reply` through the context, in the three forms a reply takes. `GrpcCx::reply(value)` takes an `IntoGrpcReply` (§6.1), the message or `Response<T>` around it with reply metadata, encoded as a handler returning it is. `GrpcCx::reply_stream(stream)` takes an `IntoGrpcStream`, each `Ok` item written as a message and an `Err` item run through the matched handler's error handlers on the late path and written in the trailers. `GrpcCx::reply_status(status)` is a trailers-only `tonic::Status`, which claims the error when answered with `Ok`; the same `Status` returned as the error is offered to the next handler and sent as it stands when none claims it. The handler path and the three methods share one encoder. They sit on the context rather than on `Reply` because `Reply` is a type alias of `http::Response`, which takes no inherent constructor in `fw-grpc`, and because a stream reply needs the call for its late path. `IntoReply<Grpc>` for `Response<T>` over a message and over a stream would overlap, a foreign type being free to implement both `prost::Message` and `Stream`, and `GrpcCx::reply(impl Into<Response<T>>)` is ambiguous for a `Response<T>` argument between the reflexive `From` and `From<T> for Response<T>`. A stream item's `Err` goes through `dispatch_late` (§2.3) and is written as the trailers `grpc-status`, `grpc-message` and `grpc-status-details-bin`, gRPC's mid-stream error form: once data frames have been sent the status travels in the trailers. A reply stream reports its end where the dispatcher writes it: `encode_stream` builds its body over the bare items and marks the reply with a private `Streamed` extension, and the dispatcher's outermost body, the one that holds the execution and the in-flight permit, reports once for a marked reply, whichever comes first: `Completed` as it yields trailers carrying `grpc-status: 0`; `CutOff` with the execution's reason as it yields trailers with any other status, an `Err` item's included, as it ends without trailers or fails, as the deadline's DEADLINE_EXCEEDED or a panic's INTERNAL ends it, or as it is dropped before any of these, `ClientCancelled` written before the report, so a caller abandoning the reply is `CutOff(ClientCancelled)` (§2.6). A marked reply an interceptor discards is never handed to that body and reports nothing; an interceptor answering `cx.reply(..)` answers an unmarked single message. A hand-built body and the health and reflection services' replies are not tracked.
- **Pre-dispatch:** gRPC is HTTP/2, and `http::Request` and `http::Response` are already its types, so `fw_grpc::PreDispatch`, a name for `fw_http::PreDispatch<Grpc>` (X23, §3.4), takes `.apply`, `.apply_for`, `.layer` and `.layer_for` as HTTP's does, scoped by method path (`/users.v1.UserService/*`). A layer that answers with a non-200 HTTP status is not a valid gRPC response, so the transport translates such a response with the specification's HTTP-to-status table and the client receives a proper `grpc-status`:

  | HTTP status        | gRPC code         |
  | ------------------ | ----------------- |
  | 400                | INTERNAL          |
  | 401                | UNAUTHENTICATED   |
  | 403                | PERMISSION_DENIED |
  | 404                | UNIMPLEMENTED     |
  | 429, 502, 503, 504 | UNAVAILABLE       |
  | any other          | UNKNOWN           |

- **Deadlines:** `fw-grpc` parses `grpc-timeout` itself, first of all in the dispatcher's `call`, tonic's server being outside its path and the header reaching the dispatcher as hyper parsed it: `PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md`'s grammar, a `TimeoutValue` of one to eight ASCII digits, the specification's positive integer of at most eight, and a `TimeoutUnit` in `H`, `M`, `S`, `m`, `u` or `n`, into the execution deadline. A value off that grammar, an overflowing or nine-digit amount, a non-numeric or negative one, the empty value, a missing, lowercase or unknown unit, is answered INTERNAL, the code grpc-go 1.84.0 answers each with, its message quoting up to 64 characters of the value, marked cut short past that, before admission and before any execution opens, so no pre-dispatch stage, span, handler or error handler runs: before admission because the refusal is permanent and a caller told UNAVAILABLE first would retry a call the server will never run, and before routing because grpc-go reads the header before it routes, which refuses the health and reflection services, reached through the same `call`, the same way (F396, 125). A zero amount, `0S`, `0n`, `00000000H` or any other unit, is on the grammar's digits and is a budget already spent: it is answered DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, "the call's deadline passed", at the same point, as grpc-go answers it, with no handler run and no error handler offered the `Timeout`, where RPC's `deadline-ms: 0` opens its execution and polls the handler once (§5.2; F399, 125; the difference is F401, deferred). A positive amount, `1n` among them, opens the execution with that much left, and the pipeline is polled once before the expired sleep. When the deadline passes first, the pipeline is dropped, the execution is cancelled with `Deadline`, and the error handlers run with a `Timeout` `CallError` under `Server::timeout_grace` (§2.4): their answer is the reply, an unclaimed `Timeout` is DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, and when the grace passes first DEADLINE_EXCEEDED is written without them. A caller past its deadline has stopped waiting, and the handlers still run, because the grace bounds them and running them is what lets an application log, count or reshape its timeouts on every transport alike. The deadline is the caller's and starts when the call arrives, so it covers the unscoped pre-dispatch stage, routing, the scoped stage and `dispatch`: routing records the handler it matched, and a deadline passing after routing offers that handler's tiers then the global ones, one passing before routing the global ones alone, with a context rebuilt from the path, metadata and peer the call arrived with and carrying no request. A caller through tonic's `Channel` wraps every call in its own `GrpcTimeout`, which answers CANCELLED at the same deadline, so a tonic client never reads what the handlers answer; a client enforcing no deadline of its own reads it. When the reply comes first, the deadline moves into its body, which ends with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED trailers if the deadline passes while it streams. The reply the error handlers answer is delivered as a single reply: a trailers-only status as it stands, or a body read under the rest of the grace and written as one data frame followed by its trailers. A body whose bytes run past its first length-prefixed message, or one still open when the grace runs out, is a stream, dropped unwritten for a trailers-only DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, the reply's metadata dropped with it and the drop logged at `warn` naming the path (§2.4); a body failing while it is read answers DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, logged at `debug`. The stream is told by its bytes because `Reply` is an erased `http::Response<tonic::body::Body>`, a body an error handler writes by hand carrying no mark of its shape and `GrpcCx::reply` and `reply_stream` producing the same erased `Reply`, and on the wire a server stream of one message and a unary reply are the same bytes. A stream whose items come readily is ended at its second message, one that yields an item and then waits at the grace's end, and under an `Unbounded` grace the body is read until its end or its second message. A marked stream the error handlers answered there was the reply: dropped unwritten, or replaced by DEADLINE_EXCEEDED after a failed read, it reports `CutOff(Deadline)`, as on HTTP and RPC (§2.6); a single message they answered within the grace keeps its mark through the buffered body and reports `Completed` at its trailers.
- **Errors:** kinds map to canonical codes per §2.4; `fw_grpc::code_for(kind)` is the table and `fw_grpc::to_status(&CallError) -> Status` the rendering. `CallError::with_grpc_code(i32)` names a canonical code in place of the kind's, `google.rpc.Code`'s number, read back by `grpc_code()`: an error naming a resource that exists writes `.with_grpc_code(6)` for ALREADY_EXISTS where `Conflict` maps to ABORTED, the kind still deciding every other transport's rendering; a code outside 1 to 16, `OK` included, is ignored. The code is an `i32` because `fw-transport` depends on no gRPC crate. A `tonic::Status` returned as the error, by a handler or by an error handler, reaches the wire as it stands: the rendering downcasts what the error handlers left to `Status` before anything else, since `from_boxed` would answer `Internal` for a type it does not recognise, and the error handlers see the `Status` first, so nothing bypasses them; it is the one way to name a code outside the eleven kinds without a `CallError`. `Details` are packed into a `google.rpc.Status` and sent in `grpc-status-details-bin` through tonic-types, whose `ErrorDetails` takes the design's variants one to one: `FieldViolations` through `set_bad_request`, `ErrorInfo` through `set_error_info`, `RetryAfter` through `set_retry_info`, `Help` through `set_help`, and `StatusExt::with_error_details` writes the trailer. `ErrorDetails` holds one of each message, so every `FieldViolations` detail's violations go into the one `BadRequest` and every `Help` detail's links into the one `Help`, and the first `ErrorInfo` and the first `RetryAfter` are kept. `Detail::Json` has no setter: a `prost_types::Value` built from the `serde_json::Value` is packed in a `prost_types::Any` with type URL `type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Value` and appended to the `Status.details` list by hand. An error with no details sends no trailer.
- **Cancellation:** `ClientCancelled` fires for every abandonment hyper reports, the call's future dropped before it answered and the reply body dropped before its end (§2.6).
- **Message size and compression:** the extractors decode under tonic's own 4 MiB limit, and a larger message fails extraction as `ExtractError::TooLarge`, INVALID_ARGUMENT; the server carries no message-size setting. A request whose `grpc-encoding` is not `identity` answers UNIMPLEMENTED with `grpc-accept-encoding: identity` before dispatch, as the compression specification prescribes.
- **Load shedding and settings:** `fw_grpc::Server::new(endpoint)` carries `.endpoint(..)` for a further endpoint, `tls: fw_net::Tls`, `max_inflight: Count`, 1,024 calls at `Default` (§2.8), `max_per_connection: Count`, no bound of its own at `Default`, the server's applying, and `max_concurrent_streams: Count`, each refusing `Max(0)` in `prepare` with the HTTP server's hint, `handshake_timeout: Bound`, 30 seconds at `Default`, and `timeout_grace: Bound`, one second at `Default`, each refusing `After(Duration::ZERO)` the same way, plus `reflection(bool)` and `file_descriptor_set(&'static [u8])` below. `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` bounds each connection, and excess streams get `REFUSED_STREAM`. Over the server's in-flight limit or the connection's, a call gets UNAVAILABLE, "the server is at its in-flight limit", and during the drain UNAVAILABLE, "the server is shutting down", each before an execution opens and with no `Retry-After`; clients treat it as retryable.
- **Health:** `tonic_health::server::health_reporter()` answers the `HealthReporter`, and `GrpcHealth::module()` binds it as `Dep<GrpcHealth>` for an application that sets status per service through `set_service_status`; without the module the server keeps a reporter of its own and health still answers. The known services are those the handlers' paths name. `grpc.health.v1` reports SERVING for every known service after `bind`, overwriting what an init hook set, and at `drain` sets the overall status `""` and each known service NOT_SERVING before the accept loop's drain, so a client polling health stops sending before the GOAWAY; the write for `""` is a floor the server keeps when `GrpcHealth::delegate_overall` has handed the status to another writer, so `""` reads NOT_SERVING once the drain begins however that writer behaved. It stays SERVING through the before-shutdown stage, consistent with `is_draining()`. Health and reflection are routed after the unscoped pre-dispatch entries, with no scoped entries and no error handlers, since no handler matched.
- **Reflection:** `grpc.reflection.v1` and `v1alpha`, from the descriptor set `Server::file_descriptor_set(pb::FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET)` hands over, through `tonic_reflection::server::Builder::configure().register_encoded_file_descriptor_set(..)` and its `build_v1()` and `build_v1alpha()`. Both are added to the route table in debug builds and behind `reflection(true)` in release builds (decision 7). With reflection on and no set, the two services serve, describing only themselves; a set that does not decode is a `Configure` failure.
- **Shutdown:** GOAWAY through `fw-server-hyper`'s drain, then the core's drain and close.
- **Scope:** gRPC serves on its own port. Nothing routes an `application/grpc` request arriving on the HTTP server's port, or on an embedding host, to the gRPC server. The extension point, if that is ever wanted, is a hand-off like `UpgradeHandler` keyed by path and content type rather than by `Upgrade`, on `Server<B>` and on `Embedded<A>` alike.

### 6.3 Clients [36]

```rust
imports = [GrpcClientModule::<pb::UserServiceClient<Channel>>::for_root(
    GrpcEndpoint::new("https://users:443").tls(ClientTls::system_roots()),
).keyed::<UsersApi>()]

#[injectable]
pub struct Profile { users: Dep<pb::UserServiceClient<Channel>, UsersApi> }
```

`GrpcClientModule::<C>::for_root(GrpcEndpoint)` binds the tonic client `C` under its own type and exports it; `C` implements `fw_grpc::GrpcClient`, `from_channel(Channel)`, which `fw-build` writes for every client it generates. `GrpcEndpoint::new(uri)` takes `.tls(ClientTls::system_roots())` or `.tls(ClientTls::ca_pem(..))` for a private CA, and an `https` URI without `.tls` trusts the platform's roots. The URI is parsed through `ModuleDef::try_value`, so a bad one is a wiring error reported by `wire()`; the client is built through `try_singleton`, so the roots load and the channel is built when the app connects. The channel connects lazily (tonic's `connect_lazy`), so `connect` does no network I/O. `fw_grpc::outgoing(&exec, request) -> Result<tonic::Request<T>, tonic::Status>` sets tonic's `Request::set_timeout` from the execution's remaining deadline, read on tokio's clock, which `fw-runtime-tokio`'s `Timer` reads too. A deadline already passed is refused there, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, "the calling execution's deadline has passed", with no request built and nothing sent: `outgoing` is the one point ulo touches an outgoing gRPC call, the generated client and its `Channel` being tonic's, so it is the one place the call can be stopped before the request exists, and the status is the code the callee would answer and the type the call itself fails with, so `outgoing(&exec, request)?` and the call's own `?` are one error type in a handler, where an error of ulo's would have a caller handle two for one call (F407, 127). Sent instead with the shortest `grpc-timeout`, `1n`, such a call reaches a callee that opens it with a nanosecond left and polls the pipeline once (§6.2), so a handler answering without awaiting runs and is answered while the caller is told it timed out. The remaining time is held between one nanosecond, a floor the encoder alone needs since `outgoing` hands it no zero, and `99999999H`, the longest value the grammar holds, about 11,415 years, since tonic 0.14.6 panics past it and a deadline that far off is reachable, an RPC server opening an execution `deadline-ms` from now up to `u64::MAX` milliseconds and a handler forwarding it (F405, 126). Within that, tonic writes the finest unit whose truncated amount fits eight digits, `n`, `u`, `m`, `S`, `M` then `H`, so no positive remainder encodes as zero and the callee's deadline is up to one unit before the caller's, exact under 100 ms, where grpc-go's encoder rounds up. Truncation is kept (126): rounding down is the conservative direction for a propagated deadline, the callee giving up no later than the caller, so its timeout can reach a caller still waiting, where rounding up lets the callee work on for up to a unit after the caller has given up; interoperability decides nothing here, every value on the grammar being accepted by grpc-go and by this server alike, only a receiver's behaviour ever having been at issue; and the loss is one unit of an amount that overflowed the finer unit's eight digits, under one part in a hundred thousand of the remaining time, 999 ns of 100 ms at the worst. A unit test sweeps 4,016 durations through the encoder and reads each back with the server's own parser. `outgoing` writes the header when it is called, through `Request::set_timeout`, which puts it in the request's metadata at once, before the generated client is called, and a `GrpcClientModule` channel connects lazily on its first call, which follows, so that call gives the callee the connect's length beyond its caller's wait: a `Channel` whose connector held each connect 250 ms gave the server a deadline 252.3 to 253.6 ms past the caller's (F410, open on gRPC, §5.4, 129). A ready `Channel` is a free slot in its buffer, not an established connection. The generated client awaits `ready()`, which polls the `Channel`, a tower `Buffer` whose `poll_ready` reserves a permit on its worker's channel and nothing else; the worker polls the inner service's readiness only once it holds a built request, and that service is `Connection`, a fixed stack of `AddOrigin`, `UserAgent`, tonic's `GrpcTimeout` and the optional limits over `Reconnect`, whose `poll_ready` makes the connection, the connector and hyper's HTTP/2 handshake, and is ready only once connected, so the connect is driven by the request after its header was written. The one point after the connect, inside that stack where `GrpcTimeout::call` reads the header to arm tonic's own client timer, takes no layer through `Endpoint`'s API, and the custom connector of `connect_with_connector_lazy` is a `Service<Uri>` that sees no request; making the connection ready before `outgoing` builds the request has no path either, since readiness does not drive the connect, and `Endpoint::connect`, which connects before the buffer is built, covers the first connection alone, `Reconnect` returning to idle when a connection fails and reconnecting at the next request. In tonic 0.14.6 and tower 0.5.3 nothing is built for it, so the limit stands, stated on `outgoing`: on a new or re-established connection a gRPC callee can outlive its caller by the duration of the connect, where RPC measures its stamp with the connection in hand (§5.4). F410 stays open on gRPC, its fix deferred for its cost: a transport service of ulo's own under tonic's generated clients, which take any `T: tonic::client::GrpcService<tonic::body::Body>` with `T::Error: Into<StdError>` and `T::ResponseBody: Body<Data = Bytes> + Send + 'static` in place of `Channel`, so tonic's codegen and codecs stay; the service owns its connection, reconnects itself and stamps after hyper's `http2::SendRequest::ready()`, as the RPC links stamp with the connection in hand and as grpc-go stamps once it has picked an established transport. It takes over the connection lifecycle, TLS, HTTP/2 settings and keep-alive from tonic's `Channel`, and whether `ready()` resolves only once the connection is established and has room for a stream has not been read; a tonic whose `GrpcTimeout`, sitting after the connect, rewrote the header there would make the service unnecessary. The limit is pinned so that it grows no larger: `a_new_connection_gives_the_server_the_connect_beyond_the_caller_s_deadline_and_no_more`, three rounds, each the first call over a `Channel` of its own built with `connect_with_connector_lazy` over a connector that waits 250 ms before an `HttpConnector` and records when each connect began and returned, from an execution with 2 s left forwarded through `outgoing`, the server's handler recording the deadline it was given, asserts that deadline no later than the caller's plus the connect as the connector measured it, plus the request's transit from the connect's end to the server's reading of the header, the recorded deadline less the `grpc-timeout` written, plus 1 ms, which covers what precedes the connect inside tonic, the request's handoff to the buffer's worker, and the header's truncation to its unit; a stamp written earlier than the call, or a longer wait before tonic starts the connect, fails it. Measured, the server's deadline is 252.4 to 256.0 ms past the caller's, the connect 251.6 to 254.3 ms and the transit 0.4 to 2.8 ms, 0.02 to 0.6 ms of the millisecond used, and `outgoing` writing 50 ms more than is left fails every round, 303.4 to 304.9 ms past (132). There is no ambient execution, so nothing forwards it on its own.

## 7. GraphQL [37]

```rust
type ApiSchema = Schema<QueryRoot, EmptyMutation, SubscriptionRoot>;

#[module(
    providers = [
        with = |q: Dep<QueryRoot>, s: Dep<SubscriptionRoot>| Schema::new(q, EmptyMutation, s),   // the schema, `Auto`
        AsyncGraphql<ApiSchema, GqlContext> as dyn Engine,                                      // the engine, under the SPI key, naming its context type
        GqlContext,                                                                             // resolved in this module, per execution
    ],
    exports   = [dyn Engine],
)]
pub struct ApiSchemaModule;

#[module(imports = [
    fw_ws::WsModule::for_root(),                                                               // once per application; the gateway is reachable through it
    GraphqlModule::for_root(GraphqlConfig::at("/graphql").subscriptions("/graphql/ws").engine_from(ApiSchemaModule)),
])]
pub struct ApiModule;

#[injectable(execution)]                                    // built per execution [37]
pub struct GqlContext {
    user: Option<Ext<CurrentUser>>,
    loaders: Dep<Loaders>,
    head: Option<Dep<RequestHead>>,                         // `Some` over HTTP, `None` over the subscription gateway and RPC
}
```

GraphQL names no transport: the specification defines the language, validation and execution, and GraphQL-over-HTTP and graphql-transport-ws are two bindings. The crates follow that split. `fw-graphql` is transport-neutral, holding the `Engine` SPI, `GqlRequest: Deserialize` and `GqlResponse: Serialize`; the two engine adapters depend on it alone, each a `Construct` type reading its schema (`AsyncGraphql<S, C>` reads `Dep<S>`), bound under `dyn Engine` as above so a handler on any transport takes `Dep<dyn Engine>`. `fw-graphql-http` holds the endpoint, the playground and the GraphQL-over-HTTP status rules, and its `GraphqlModule` is the module imported above: it mounts the endpoint controller `.at(path)` and, with `subscriptions(path)`, the `GraphqlWs<Q>` gateway of `fw-graphql-ws` `.at(path)`, both as its own controllers, so `fw-graphql-http` depends on `fw-graphql-ws` and through it on `fw-ws`. The application imports `WsModule` once itself: an import from `GraphqlModule` would make a second `WsModule` identity beside the application's. `GraphqlConfig::engine_from(module)` names where the engine lives: `GraphqlModule` imports that module and reads its exported `dyn Engine`, and a configured module instance works as the import since module identity is by value (DESIGN §8.3). The visibility rule makes the import necessary: a module sees its own bindings, its imports' exports and the globals' exports, and the module that imports `GraphqlModule` is none of those, so without `engine_from` the engine is read from a global module that exports `dyn Engine`, which puts it into every module's view to solve a visibility problem between two. An RPC-only application serves the same engine with an ordinary handler, `#[fw_rpc::message("gql")] async fn gql(&self, req: Payload<GqlRequest>, engine: Dep<dyn Engine>) -> GqlResponse`, and `subscribe`'s stream over RPC's streamed-reply shape.

The engine SPI, written without macros:

```rust
pub trait Engine: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn execute(&self, req: GqlRequest, exec: ExecutionRef) -> BoxFuture<'static, GqlResponse>;
    fn subscribe(&self, req: GqlRequest, exec: ExecutionRef) -> BoxStream<'static, GqlResponse>;
    fn sdl(&self) -> String;
    fn playground_html(&self, endpoint: &str, subscriptions: Option<&str>) -> Option<String>;   // the engine's own page
}

pub struct GqlResponse { outcome: Outcome, data: Option<Value>, errors: Vec<GqlError>, extensions: Option<Value> }   // serialized without `outcome`; built by `executed(..)`, `request_error(..)` or `failed(..)`
pub enum Outcome { Executed, RequestError, Failed }   // whether execution began, or the server could not begin it, which decides the HTTP status
```

**The context is a type parameter of the engine adapter.** async-graphql takes context as `Request::data(D)` for any `D: Any + Send + Sync`, and juniper's `Context` is a type the schema's root types name, so no adapter can know the user's type by convention. `AsyncGraphql<S, C>` with `C: Send + Sync + 'static` keeps the `ModuleRef` of the module that binds it and resolves `module.with_execution(&exec).get::<C>()` per call, built once in the call's execution, so the context is resolved with the engine's module's visibility and need not be exported to the module serving the endpoint; it inserts the context with `Request::data` as a `Dep<C>`, since the resolver hands back a shared value and `C` is not `Clone`, plus the `ExecutionRef` itself as a second `data`, and `fw_graphql_async::dep::<T>(ctx)` reads `ctx.data::<ExecutionRef>()?.get::<T>()`. `Juniper<Q, M, Sub>` resolves `Q::Context` the same way and hands it over as the context, where the user's `Context` struct holds an `ExecutionRef` field and `fw_graphql_juniper::dep::<T>(ctx)` reads through it. `dep` is therefore engine-specific and lives in each adapter crate under one name. Neither adapter declares `Dep<C>` as a dependency: declaring it would make the engine per-execution under an execution-scoped context, so the binding is read at each call and not checked when the application wires, and a context that is not bound fails each call rather than `wire()`, logged at `error`, answered as `Outcome::Failed`. A resolver that reads the HTTP request does it through the context: the HTTP controller seeds `Dep<RequestHead>` into the execution, so a context built in the call's execution reads it as any execution-scoped binding does, and the SPI needs no HTTP head. The read is a runtime one, which is why a context also built over the subscription gateway or RPC reads `Option<Dep<RequestHead>>`, as the example does. Juniper's `Engine::subscribe` is built on `resolve_into_stream` directly.

- **HTTP:** the endpoint is a controller in `fw-graphql-http`, mounted `.at(config.path)` (§2.5), so role keys and inputs work as for any route, and HTTP guards, interceptors and pre-dispatch entries apply because the endpoint is an HTTP route. It follows GraphQL-over-HTTP, whose rules the endpoint controller applies from `outcome`; the controller is written by hand over the HTTP handler protocol, since `GqlResponse`, `IntoReply` and `Http` are three crates' types and no `IntoReply<Http>` for `GqlResponse` can be written. In `application/graphql-response+json` a request that executed answers 200, errors included, and a request that failed before execution, a document that does not parse or validate, a missing `query`, an unparseable JSON body, answers 400; in the legacy `application/json` media type every response is 200. A `Failed` outcome, a context the server could not build, answers 500 in both: a 400 would tell the client to fix a document it cannot fix. The response media type is negotiated from `Accept` with qualities read per RFC 9110, a type's quality that of the most specific matching range: the response is `application/graphql-response+json` when its quality is nonzero and at least `application/json`'s, and `application/json` otherwise, with no 406. No `Accept`, or only empty ones, negotiates `application/graphql-response+json`, which is how GraphQL-over-HTTP reads it from its 2025-01-01 watershed and what §0.3 leaves to the specification; the consequence is that a client sending no `Accept` receives 400 for a document that does not parse. A POST whose body is not `application/json` is refused with 415. A GET names `query`, `operationName`, `variables` (JSON text) and `extensions` (JSON text) as query parameters, and a GET whose operation is a mutation is refused with 405, built as a `MethodNotAllowed` with `Allow: GET, HEAD, POST, OPTIONS` and offered to the error handlers as the router's 405 is (§3.2), so a 405 has one rule.
- **Subscriptions:** graphql-transport-ws on an `fw-ws` gateway with `event = "type"` and `subprotocols = ["graphql-transport-ws"]` (§4.1). The protocol's `connection_init`, `ping` and `pong` carry no `id` while expecting an answer, and its `complete` from the client cancels an operation, so the `#[fw_ws::message]` convention of §4.2 does not fit and the gateway is a hand-written `Gateway` in `fw-graphql-ws` over `Engine::subscribe`, one for both engines, mounted by `GraphqlModule` at the `subscriptions` path. It owns: the subprotocol echo, a handshake that echoed none closing 4406; `connection_init` once, its payload kept in `Session<ConnectionInit>` for the context builder, a second one closing 4429; `connection_ack`; a `subscribe` before the ack closing 4401; a duplicate `id` closing 4409; an unparseable message closing 4400; an init that does not arrive within `GraphqlConfig::connection_init_timeout(Bound)` closing 4408, 3 seconds at `Default`, the reference server's, `Unbounded` no clock, timed by the app's `Timer` from a task on the app's runtime; `ping` answered with `pong`, and `pong` accepted in both directions; one execution per `subscribe`, opened on the connection with its inputs seeded and run in a task of its own on the app's runtime, whose stream writes `next` items and `complete`, or `error` with an array of GraphQL errors, a `Failed` outcome among them; both tasks spawned through `Connection::runtime()` (§4.1) with their handles dropped, which detaches them, so the crate names no runtime; `complete` from the client cancelling that execution with `ClientCancelled`; and the context built per execution as above. The timeout lives on `GraphqlConfig` because `GatewayConfig::settings()` is a static function: `GraphqlModule` binds it as a module-private value the gateway reads optionally, and a zero is refused through `try_value` when the application wires, with the one hint every zero bound gets. **Connect guards are this gateway's only authorization point.** They run once per connection, and no `Ws` guard, interceptor or error handler runs per operation: the hand-written gateway has no handler for them to wrap, so a `Ws` guard written expecting to run on every message does not run on graphql-transport-ws. An operation's authorization is decided at `connection_init`, from its payload in the session, or inside the resolvers.
- **Playground:** `fw-graphql-http` serves the page `Engine::playground_html` answers, async-graphql's `GraphiQLSource` and juniper's `graphiql_source`, on a GET with `Accept: text/html` and no `query` parameter, under `GraphqlConfig::playground(bool)`, which defaults to `cfg!(debug_assertions)`; an engine answering `None` serves no page.
- **Two engines:** one `GraphqlModule` serves one engine. A second schema is bound under `dyn Engine` with the DI's ordinary qualifier, `dyn Engine @ Admin`, and a second `GraphqlModule` at another path reads it, `GraphqlConfig::at("/admin/graphql").engine::<Admin>().engine_from(AdminSchemaModule)`, as `Dep<dyn Engine, Admin>`; `engine::<E>()` turns a `GraphqlConfig` into a `GraphqlConfig<E>`, the parameter carried by `GraphqlModule<Q>`, the endpoint controller and `GraphqlWs<Q>`. The configuration is the module's identity, so the same configuration imported twice is one module and two paths are two. No GraphQL rule is added for it.

## 8. Runtime [38]

**The core's interface.** The core spawns through a trait as it times through one, and names no runtime:

```rust
pub trait Spawn: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn spawn(&self, fut: BoxFuture<'static, ()>) -> TaskHandle;
}
pub trait Runtime: Timer + Spawn {}
impl<R: Timer + Spawn + ?Sized> Runtime for R {}

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub enum TaskEnd { Finished, Aborted, Panicked(Arc<Redacted>) }   // the panic's message, redacted; cloning shares it. No `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq` or `Hash`
impl TaskEnd { pub fn is_finished(&self) -> bool; pub fn is_aborted(&self) -> bool; pub fn is_panicked(&self) -> bool; }

/// A runtime's own handle to one task, boxed inside a `TaskHandle`; a runtime adapter implements it.
pub trait RuntimeTask: Send + 'static {
    fn abort(&mut self);
    fn poll_ended(&mut self, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()>;   // `Ready` once the future will never be polled again and has been dropped
    fn detach(self: Box<Self>);
}

pub struct TaskHandle { /* private */ }
impl TaskHandle {
    pub fn launch<T: RuntimeTask>(fut: BoxFuture<'static, ()>, start: impl FnOnce(BoxFuture<'static, ()>) -> T) -> TaskHandle;   // the one constructor
    pub fn abort(&self);
}
impl Future for TaskHandle { type Output = TaskEnd; }
impl Drop for TaskHandle { /* detaches */ }

pub fn spawn_with<T, F, R>(runtime: &R, fut: F) -> ValueHandle<T>
where T: Send + 'static, F: Future<Output = T> + Send + 'static, R: Spawn + ?Sized;
impl<T> Future for ValueHandle<T> { type Output = Result<T, TaskEnd>; }   // `Err` is `Aborted` or `Panicked`; polling after the value was taken answers `Err(TaskEnd::Finished)`

// fw_transport
pub struct TaskSet { /* private: Arc<dyn Spawn>, FuturesUnordered<TaskHandle> */ }
impl TaskSet {
    pub fn new(runtime: Arc<dyn Spawn>) -> TaskSet;   // an `Arc<dyn Runtime>` coerces
    pub fn spawn<F: Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'static>(&mut self, fut: F);
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize;  pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool;
    pub fn abort_all(&self);
    pub async fn join_next(&mut self) -> Option<TaskEnd>;   // cancel-safe: dropped before it answers, it takes nothing out
    pub async fn join_all(&mut self);
}
impl Drop for TaskSet { /* aborts every task still in it */ }
```

A handle means the same on every runtime. Dropping it detaches the task rather than stopping it: every fire-and-forget spawn in the hubs would otherwise die the moment its handle went out of scope, and a drain would behave differently by where a handle happened to be dropped. `abort` stops the task at its current await, and awaiting the handle answers how the task ended. A panic is caught inside the task by the core's own `CatchUnwind`, the poll-boundary catch the hook runner and `dispatch` use, which `TaskHandle::launch` wraps the future in before the runtime sees it; `launch` is the one way to build a handle, so a runtime cannot skip the catch, and a runtime that reports a panic itself and one that re-raises it on await answer the same `Panicked`. The payload is converted to a message through `redact_panic`, the conversion `PanicRecovered`'s pipeline, the lifecycle runner's `Outcome::Panicked` and `FailureReason::Panicked` share, and carried as `Panicked(Arc<Redacted>)`. Which registry redacts it depends on where the task was spawned: one spawned through the app's runtime, `Dep<dyn Runtime>` or `AppHandle::runtime()`, reaches the runtime under a second wrapper of the app's own, which carries the graph's redactor and replaces every secret the graph registered (below); one spawned on a bare runtime outside any app, through `TaskHandle::launch` alone, gets `SecretRegistry::default()`, the userinfo strip and nothing more, which the variant's doc states. A runtime reports only whether the task is over, through `poll_ended`: the wrapper records `Finished` or the panic before the spawned future completes, in an `Arc<Mutex<Option<_>>>`, and the handle reads the record once `poll_ended` is `Ready` and answers `Aborted` when nothing was recorded. The handle keeps the `TaskEnd` it first answered and answers a clone of it on every later poll, so two answers to one handle carry one `Arc` and pointer-equal messages; `TaskEnd` is `Clone` and `Debug`, with `Copy`, `PartialEq`, `Eq` and `Hash` left off since comparing panic messages for equality means nothing, and `is_finished()`, `is_aborted()` and `is_panicked()` read the variant where a `matches!` would. The wrapper, `Launched`, also drops the task's future inside `catch_unwind`, through `drop_caught`, on completing and in its own `Drop`, which an abort or a runtime dropping the task runs: a panic raised while the future is dropped never reaches the runtime, is logged at `warn` through `tracing` with its message redacted the same way, and changes nothing recorded, an aborted future reading `Aborted` and a finished one keeping its end. `poll_ended` reports only that the task is over, so no runtime adapter could report that panic through the handle, and uncaught it reached the runtime: tokio caught it in its own cancel and reported it through a `JoinError` the handle never read, and `async-task`, under smol, drops a cancelled future under an abort-on-unwind guard and aborted the process (F374). That `warn` is the core's one log line, and `tracing`, runtime-free and in every transport crate's tree, is its dependency for it. `poll_ended` is `Ready` only once the future has been dropped, never before: a set waiting for all after `abort_all` relies on no part of any task running afterwards, which is what a server's close needs of it. tokio meets the rule, an aborted task's future being dropped before its `JoinHandle` is woken. Once a handle has answered it answers the same end each time, and an `abort` after it changes nothing. `spawn_with` leaves its value in a slot the handle reads once the task's end is `Finished`, the handle's own completion being the wake-up, so the core takes no channel dependency. `TaskSet` replaces the hubs' `JoinSet`: a task runs from `spawn` whether the set is polled or not, polling only collects ends, `join_next` stands as a `select` branch that runs again, and `abort_all` then `join_all` is `shutdown`. Dropping the set aborts what it holds, as the `JoinSet` it replaces did and as the hubs' serve futures rely on when they are dropped; the two drops differ on purpose, the set's owner going away being the signal its tasks have no one left to serve. `Runtime` has no method for blocking work: a blocking call spawned through `Spawn` holds a worker as one polled inline does, the one crate whose library blocks owns its threads (57), and a tokio-based link moves what blocks onto its own runtime's blocking pool or a thread of its own, MQTT's and NATS's trust-store reads and Kafka's librdkafka handles (§5.3). The trait gains a `spawn_blocking` of its own when a crate at the runtime-free or runtime-neutral level needs blocking work, and none does; the TCP and UDP clients resolving a host name would be the first, the smol link having no runtime to hand the resolution to (F416, 133). The blocking connects left are a `nats://` NATS connection its server upgrades after the roots failed to load, a `nats://` client's made before their load ended, and a `nats://` server's whose load outlasted `roots_timeout`, for which async-nats reads the store on the polling thread (144, 148, 150, §5.3).

**The app.** `AppBuilder::runtime(r)` takes an `impl Runtime` and binds in the core's global module, as `dyn Runtime` and as `dyn Timer` upcast, one object: the core's `Clocked`, a wrapper holding `r` as its spawner, `r` upcast as its clock and the app's redactor, so `Dep<dyn Runtime>`, `Dep<dyn Timer>`, `AppHandle::runtime()` and `AppHandle::timer()` answer that one object in every configuration, `Mounted::runtime()` follows it, and every timed behaviour an app given a timer has, an app given a runtime has. The object is the wrapper and not `r`, so nothing reaches `r`'s own type through any of the four, a downcast included, which the documentation of `AppBuilder::runtime` and `AppHandle::runtime` says in a sentence; `Runtime` has no `Any` supertrait, so there is no downcast to attempt and fail. The wrapper is what redacts an app task's panic: `Clocked::spawn` wraps the task's future in the core's own `Launched` carrying the redactor, hands that to `r`'s `spawn`, and makes the handle `r` answers read the inner wrapper's record (`TaskHandle::reading`); the inner wrapper catches the panic, redacts it with the app's secrets and completes, so the runtime's own wrapper around it records `Finished`, which nothing reads, a drop-time panic is caught and logged inside the inner wrapper so the outer one never sees it, and `r`'s `RuntimeTask` still decides when the task is over. The redactor is created with the builder's `AppConfig`, before any graph exists, and set from the graph `wire` built when the app's shared state is made and again on every `load`, for the graph it publishes and for the base graph it puts back on a failed connect; the registry is read when a panic is redacted, not when the task is spawned, so a secret a lazily loaded module registers is replaced in a task spawned before the load that panics after it. The cost is a second `CatchUnwind` and record per task spawned through the app. `.runtime(r)` and `.timer(t)` compose, each overriding only what it sets, in the order written: `.runtime(r)` sets the spawning and the clock, `.timer(t)` the clock alone. `.timer(t).runtime(r)` spawns and times on `r`, through the wrapper. `.runtime(r).timer(t)` spawns on `r` and times with `t`: the builder keeps the runtime as given in a private spawner, and `.timer(t)` binds `dyn Runtime` as a `Clocked` whose `Spawn` half delegates to that spawner and whose `Timer` half to `t`, so `Dep<dyn Runtime>` and `AppHandle::runtime()` sleep and read the time on `t`, `Mounted::runtime()` and `Mounted::timer()`, the runtime upcast, follow it, and the core's waits, the hooks, the constructions, the readiness checks, the drain and the shutdown cap, read `config.timer`, the object `AppHandle::timer()` answers; a transport sleeping through `mounted.runtime()` and the core timing a hook then read one clock, and a test's fake clock governs the transports' timeouts as well as the hooks. `.runtime(r).timer(t1).timer(t2)` composes `r` with `t2`, never with an earlier composition. The cost is identity: after `.runtime(r).timer(t)`, `Dep<dyn Timer>` is `t` and `Dep<dyn Runtime>` the composite, two objects that agree on the clock, where `.runtime(r)` alone binds one; the alternative, `dyn Runtime` staying `r` with `r`'s clock, would have transports that sleep through the runtime on another clock than the core's waits. `TestApp::timer` and `TestApp::runtime` delegate to the same builder. `override_value::<dyn Runtime>` in a `TestApp` is refused as `WiringError::RuntimeOverride` with the hint "set it with `TestApp::runtime(..)`", as the timer's is, since an override would split the one object; `TestApp::runtime` mirrors `TestApp::timer`. `AppHandle::timer()` and `AppHandle::runtime()` answer `Option<&Arc<..>>`, for code holding an `AppHandle` rather than a `Dep`: a link in `Link::prepare`, an embedding's host, a backend through `Mounted::app()`. An app with neither keeps a zero-length drain.

**X31: `RuntimeMissing`.** `listen()` refuses an app that queues any server with no runtime, before any `prepare` runs, as `StartupError::Bind { transport, source }` with a `RuntimeMissing { transport }` in its `source`, `transport` the first queued server's, reading "transport `T` is bound on an app with no `Runtime`; set one with `.runtime(..)`, which sets the app's timer too"; `source.downcast_ref::<RuntimeMissing>()` tells it from a port already taken. An app given `.timer(..)` alone is refused the same way, and one that queues no server, a job or a CLI command, passes `listen()` with the timer alone or with neither. The check is the core's and has no flag on `Server`: every transport spawns its connections and calls through the runtime or hands its upgrades to code that does, so there is no server for which the check is wrong, an embedding, a `Server` that binds no socket, included; and a runtime is a timer, so the refusal of an app with no clock is a subset of it. `AppHandle::mounted` refuses the same way, so an upgrade handler reading its handlers sees the refusal `listen()` would have given, and `Mounted::runtime()` answers the runtime as an `&Arc<dyn Runtime>` with no `Option`, since no server is prepared without one; the RPC and WebSocket servers read it there (§5.3, §4.1). A `dyn Runtime` or `dyn Timer` binding that `wire()` reports missing carries a help line naming the builder method (§5.4).

**A runtime is given, never found.** Inside an app it is `Dep<dyn Runtime>`, which `RpcClientModule` reads (§5.4); outside, an explicit argument, `RpcClient::new(link, runtime)`; from a client to its link, the parameter of `Link::connect`, handed on every connect (§5.3); in a drop, the runtime the value holds, so a client's `cancel` and its link's `close` are spawned on it from whichever thread the drop runs on. Nothing in the core or the hubs calls `tokio::spawn` or looks for a current runtime. A tokio-based link, and `fw-ws-redis`, holds a tokio runtime of its own beside the app's: captured once, where the value is built, or named by `with_handle(h)`, never looked for afterwards, and refused at first use when there is none (§5.3, §4.3). The smol TCP link holds no tokio: its tasks run on the runtime it runs under, a server's on its app's, read from `AppHandle::runtime()` in `prepare`, and a client's on its client's, handed to `connect`, or on the one `with_runtime(..)` names in place of either (§5.3).

**`fw-runtime-tokio`** provides four things:

- `Tokio`: the core's `Runtime` on one tokio runtime, held by its `tokio::runtime::Handle`. `Tokio::current()` captures the runtime current on the calling thread and panics outside one, at that call, as `Handle::current` does; `Tokio::try_current()` answers `None` there instead, which is how a link captures its runtime (§5.3); `Tokio::from_handle(h)` takes one, and `handle()` answers it. `run(fut)` runs a future as a task on the held runtime and answers its output to whichever executor awaits the returned future, a tokio worker, another runtime's or a plain thread with none: the task is spawned at the answer's first poll, so answers created in order and awaited in order run in order; the answer holds the task's `JoinHandle` in a wrapper that aborts on drop, so a dropped `connect` stops its work as an inline future's drop did, a frame's `send` going over the link's writer queue instead (§5.3); a panic in the task resumes where the answer is awaited; and a runtime that has shut down drops the task unrun and answers `Err(Stopped)`, a unit error. The `JoinHandle` is the handoff, since tokio polls one with no runtime context, so no channel stands beside it (65). What a tokio-based link does with tokio's reactor, timer or spawner goes through `run`, so its futures do not depend on the caller's executor. `Spawn` is `Handle::spawn` and the `Timer` half enters the handle before creating a sleep or reading `now`, so a task is spawned on that runtime and a sleep registered with its timer, a paused test clock included, from whichever thread asks, a worker of another runtime or a plain thread with none, as a client's drop may run on. The runtime must outlive what is spawned through it: once it has shut down, a task handed to it is dropped unrun on the spawning thread and its handle answers `Aborted`. `.runtime(fw_runtime_tokio::Tokio::current())` is the spelling; no unit form exists, since one would spawn on whatever runtime was current at the call, which is F360's panic in a drop off a worker thread. Its `RuntimeTask` is the `JoinHandle<()>`: `abort` is `JoinHandle::abort`, `poll_ended` polls it, `detach` drops it.
- `Timer`: the clock alone, sleeps through `tokio::time` and `now()` through `tokio::time::Instant::now().into_std()` on the current runtime, so a paused test clock drives deadlines and sleeps together, as DESIGN §3.9 requires.
- `shutdown_signal()`: SIGINT and SIGTERM on Unix, plus Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Close on Windows. It resolves to `Signal::new("SIGTERM")` and so on.
- `spawn(fut)` and `spawn_in(&exec, fut)`, on the current runtime. The second holds an `ExecutionRef` for the task's lifetime and stops the task on the execution's cancellation.

**`fw-runtime-smol`** provides `Smol`, the core's `Runtime` on an `async-executor` `Executor` the caller owns and runs: `Smol::new(Arc<Executor<'static>>)`, with `executor()` and the `Executor` re-export, and no tokio in its tree. The executor is the caller's and not smol's global one: the `smol` crate's global executor brings `async-net`, `async-fs`, `async-process` and `blocking` and starts threads of its own sized by `SMOL_THREADS`, where a runtime value naming its executor leaves the threads to the caller and lets a test drive it; a task spawned on an executor nothing runs again is never polled, and an executor dropped with tasks in it drops them, each handle answering `Aborted` (69). `Spawn` is `Executor::spawn` through `TaskHandle::launch`, the task kept as a `FallibleTask`, so one its executor dropped unrun answers `None` rather than panicking and reads `Aborted`. `abort` cancels through `Task::cancel`: dropping an `async-task` `Task` marks it cancelled and returns at once, with the future possibly still being polled on another thread or not yet dropped by the executor, which `poll_ended`'s rule forbids, so `abort` takes `cancel()`'s future, which answers only once the task is neither scheduled nor running, polls it once with a noop waker, since the first poll is what marks the task cancelled, so the abort takes effect whether or not the handle is polled again, and keeps it for `poll_ended` to poll to its end; `detach` detaches a running task and drops a cancelling one, whose `Task` drop re-marks it cancelled. A panic reaches `launch`'s catch inside the task, so `async-executor`'s own `propagate_panic` sees none and `Panicked` is reported as on tokio. The `Timer` half is `async_io::Timer::after(d)`, which `async-io`'s reactor fires whichever executor awaits it, and `now()` is `Instant::now()`, the clock it measures against; a duration past `Instant`'s range becomes `Timer::never()` inside `async-io`. The spelling is `.runtime(smol.clone())` with `let smol = Smol::new(Arc::new(Executor::new()))`, and `smol.block_on(fut)` is how `serve` runs: `block_on(&self, fut)` runs the executor on the calling thread while `fut` runs, through `async_io::block_on(executor.run(fut))`, and on the `with_workers(n)` threads, none unset, which start there and are joined before it returns, a panic in `fut` included, through a guard's `Drop`, the stop signal an `event-listener` `Event` beside a flag, registered before the flag is read again; a task still pending when `fut` completes stays on the executor for whatever runs it next, and a worker whose task panicked panics `block_on` once `fut` has completed, unless `fut` is itself panicking. `Smol::current()` answers the runtime on the calling thread and on each worker while `block_on` runs and `None` elsewhere, the previous value restored on the way out, so a nested `block_on` leaves its caller's; `Smol` is `Clone`, the executor and the worker count. `block_on` is also how a test drives a smol app: the runtime, HTTP and RPC suites' smol harnesses, and `fw-listener-smol`'s and `fw-server-hyper`'s test helpers, are each a line over it (below), and `block_on`'s own documentation carries a compiled example spawning on `Smol::current()`.

**Conformance.** `fw-runtime-conformance` holds the semantics every runtime must meet, as a scenario list stamped per runtime: a crate implements `Harness { type Runtime: Runtime; fn runtime() -> Self::Runtime; fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output; }` in its `tests/` and calls `runtime_suite!(HarnessType)`, which stamps one `#[test]` per scenario, each calling `block_on(case(runtime()))` with `runtime()` called inside the future `block_on` runs, so a runtime that captures the executor it runs on finds it. Fifteen scenarios: a returned future is `Finished`; a dropped handle detaches; an abort answers `Aborted` only once the future's drop has run, held to it by a guard whose drop sleeps 20 ms before it counts; a panic answers `Panicked` carrying its message with the userinfo redacted, `postgres://[redacted]@db.invalid/app` and not the password, on a second poll too, and goes no further, the next task spawned finishing; an end is kept, and an `abort` after it changes nothing; a panic while an aborted future drops, a task holding a value that panics in its destructor, ends `Aborted` and is logged exactly once at `warn` with the panic's message; `spawn_with` answers the value, `Err(Finished)` once the value is taken, an abort, and a panic with the redacted message; `abort_all` aborts every task; `join_all` returns once every task has ended and not before; a dropped set aborts its tasks; the app binds the runtime as one object; and a task spawned through the app redacts its secrets: a task panicking with a registered secret and a URL carrying a password, spawned on the bare runtime, keeps the secret and loses the password, the same task spawned through `Dep<dyn Runtime>` and through `AppHandle::runtime()` of an app whose module registers the secret has both replaced, and one spawned through the app whose state panics with the secret while its aborted future drops ends `Aborted` with the one `warn` logged carrying the secret replaced. The two scenarios that read a `warn`, the drop-panic one and the redaction one, read it through a recording `tracing` subscriber the suite installs as the process's global default once per test binary, through a `OnceLock`, and fail with `cases::SUBSCRIBER_TAKEN`, "the test binary installed its own subscriber, so this scenario can't capture the warning", when another was installed first, the panic inside the `OnceLock`'s initialiser leaving it unset so every later call fails the same way, and never pass without having looked: a runtime drops an aborted future on a thread of its choosing, which a thread-local subscriber would miss, so a runtime crate's harness installs none; the read is deterministic, the handle answering only once `poll_ended` is `Ready`, after the drop and so after the event. Every wait races the runtime's own `Timer::sleep`, five seconds for what is expected and 100 ms for what is not, so a runtime that loses a task fails rather than hangs. The suite names no runtime and depends on `fw`, `fw-transport`, `futures` and `tracing` alone; it is `publish = false`, a dev-dependency of each runtime crate, and `fw-runtime-tokio` runs it beside its own tests: a test binary of its own that installs `tracing`'s `NoSubscriber` first and requires the `warn` scenario's panic to equal `SUBSCRIBER_TAKEN`; a module loaded after `connect` registering a secret that a task then spawned through `AppHandle::runtime()` has replaced in its panic; and the `.timer` and `.runtime` composition, a timer after a runtime replacing only its clock on `App::builder` and on `TestApp`, under a frozen clock a day ahead read alike by `Dep<dyn Timer>`, `Dep<dyn Runtime>` and both `AppHandle` accessors with an hour's sleep through `Dep<dyn Runtime>` ending at once, a runtime after a timer replacing both, the app's hook timeout and a server's `Mounted::timer()` and `runtime()` reading the later timer, and the two override refusals with their rendered hints, which are the core's behaviour rather than a runtime's, and of `Tokio::run`: an answer from a plain thread, a dropped answer aborting its task, a panic resuming where the answer is awaited, and a shut-down runtime answering `Stopped`. `fw-runtime-smol` runs it on an executor of its own per scenario through `Smol::new(Arc::new(Executor::new())).with_workers(3).block_on(fut)`, `runtime()` answering `Smol::current()`: the test's thread and three workers run the executor until the scenario returns, and the three further threads are what let a task be polled on another thread than the one aborting or awaiting it, the case the abort scenarios are written against; a single-threaded harness would never reach it (70). The HTTP and RPC suites' `OnSmol` are the same two lines (§3.8, §5.2), `fw-listener-smol`'s and `fw-server-hyper`'s test helpers the same with one worker, so one `block_on` serves every smol harness and `Smol::current()` answers on the workers as on the caller, where a harness setting its own thread-local on the test's thread alone had `runtime()` panic in a task on a worker. `fw-runtime-smol`'s `tests/block_on.rs` pins it: a task spawned inside runs while the future waits for it, tasks are polled on threads beside the caller, `current` answers on the caller and on every worker, a panicking future stops the workers and leaves no runtime current, and the workers stop when the future completes, each on a thread of its own under a five-second bound, so workers left running fail the test rather than hang the binary.

**Two levels of runtime independence.** The goal is a test an alternative implementation of any plug point, a runtime, a backend, an embedding, a link, a broadcast adapter, can be held to, read as `cargo tree -p <crate> <flags> -e normal,features -i tokio --target=all`, which CI runs over every workspace member (below), and it is stated as two levels, each exactly testable. *Runtime-free*: no `tokio` crate anywhere in the dependency tree. The core, `fw-transport`, `fw-net`, the hubs, `fw-http`, `fw-rpc`, `fw-ws`, `fw-graphql-ws` and `fw-graphql-http`, their plug-point traits and types, the macro crates, `fw-runtime-smol`, `fw-rpc-tcp-core`, `fw-rpc-tcp-smol`, and the runtime, WebSocket and RPC conformance suites at their default features are at this level, which is what lets anyone implement a plug point without tokio: if tokio sat in a hub's tree, even as `tokio` with `sync` alone, every alternative backend's tree would contain it, so the hubs follow the core's rule and `async-lock`, `event-listener`, `futures-channel` and `futures-util` cover what `tokio::sync`, `JoinSet` and `select!` did, and the design's own crates at this level use none of `tokio::sync`, `async-channel` and its kin always being a choice. *Runtime-neutral*: the server layer, `fw-server-hyper`, the hyper backend, `fw-ws-hyper`, `fw-listener-smol`, and the HTTP suite, whose client is hyper's. It runs entirely on whatever runtime the app is given and depends on tokio only for features that contain no runtime, and the check reads it as two sets. `runtime-neutral` allows `default`, which is empty, and `sync`, which hyper brings: `fw-server-hyper`, `fw-listener-smol` and `fw-ws-hyper` without its `tokio` feature, HTTP/1.1 alone. `runtime-neutral+http2` allows those plus `io-util` and `bytes`, which `h2` brings: `fw-http-hyper` without its `tokio` feature and the HTTP suite, at default features and with `smol`, which serve or speak HTTP/2. None of the four is a runtime. In both sets tokio arrives only through hyper, `h2` or `tokio-util`: any other package that depends on tokio directly fails the entry, a third-party crate included, and a workspace member that depends on `tokio-util` directly fails it unless a `direct-tokio-util` line in `runtime-levels.txt` names the member with the reason, so the design's own crates at this level name tokio no more than those at the first do. hyper's dependency is outside the design's control, compiles no reactor, executor or timer, and runs nothing on tokio, and moving hyper out of one crate would change nothing a user experiences, hyper still being the server. A plug point inherits the level of the layer it plugs into: the hubs' traits and types are runtime-free, and `fw-server-hyper`'s `Listener` and `Incoming` are runtime-neutral as the layer is. Implementing `Listener` is writing the socket side of a hyper-based server, and its stream speaks hyper's I/O traits, which hyper consumes, so a listener author builds on that layer and sits at its level, getting tokio's `sync` through hyper and nothing that runs; at either level a plug point is implemented without a tokio runtime (115). The documentation wording: "Hyper-based servers run on any runtime. hyper itself depends on tokio's synchronization types, which contain no runtime, so `tokio` appears in their dependency tree with its `sync` feature, and where HTTP/2 is served with `io-util` and `bytes` as well, through `h2`." *Tokio-bound*: `fw-runtime-tokio`, `fw-listener-tokio`, the two hyper servers at their default `tokio` feature, the seven tokio links, `fw-ws-redis`, `fw-grpc` and the five embedding adapters, each for the reason the table gives. Sockets stay out of `Runtime`: every runtime abstraction that took them on ended at the lowest common denominator and grew features to escape it, so `fw-net` works with `std::net` sockets, which belong to no runtime, and each runtime-specific crate adopts them into its own reactor, `fw-listener-tokio` and `fw-listener-smol` for the hyper servers (§3.7), `fw-rpc-tcp` and `fw-rpc-tcp-smol` for the TCP wire (§5.3). The trees as read: `cargo tree -p fw-server-hyper -e normal -i tokio` prints tokio through hyper and through nothing else, with tokio's features `default`, which is empty, and `sync`; `fw-listener-smol` prints the same through `fw-server-hyper`, and so does `fw-ws-hyper` without its `tokio` feature; the HTTP backend without that feature, and the HTTP suite at its default features, reach tokio through hyper, `h2` and `tokio-util` with `sync`, `io-util` and the `bytes` that brings; hyper 1.x depends on tokio with its `sync` feature unconditionally, for the `oneshot` inside its upgrade future, and hyper's `http2` brings `h2`, which depends on tokio's `io-util` and on `tokio-util`. A planted tokio dependency with `net` on `fw-listener-smol` reads differently, the crate a direct dependent and `net` among the features, as does one with `net` on `fw-rpc-tcp-smol` or a `tokio-util` on `fw-rpc-conformance` (F383). The alternative, a hyper-free `fw-server-hyper` whose listeners hand out streams on their runtime's own traits, with the conversion into hyper's traits and the executor and timer adapters in each hyper server or a crate of their own, is not built: it would empty those two trees and no server's, since every crate that serves HTTP carries tokio through hyper, and the tokio path would convert twice per read or the listener's stream would leave hyper's traits. Moving `Listener` alone out of the layer, its stream on `futures-io` and `fw-server-hyper` adapting it back to hyper's traits, is not built either: the tokio listener's connections would cross tokio's traits, a compat layer and hyper's, an adapter and a buffer initialization on every read of every tokio HTTP connection, the cost 51 refuses for TLS, here on the main data path, to spare a listener author a dependency that runs nothing. Where each crate stands:

| Standing | Crates | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| runtime-free | `fw`, `fw-transport`, `fw-net`, `fw-graphql`, `fw-graphql-http`, `fw-graphql-async`, `fw-graphql-juniper`, `fw-runtime-conformance`, `fw-ws-conformance`, `fw-rpc-conformance` at its default features and with `smol`, `fw-test-certs`, `fw-runtime-smol`, `fw-rpc-tcp-core`, `fw-rpc-tcp-smol`, `fw-macros`, `fw-transport-macros`, `fw-http-macros`, `fw-ws-macros`, `fw-rpc-macros`, `fw-handler-codegen`, `fw-grpc-macros`, `fw-build` | the core and the transport-neutral pieces, timing through `Timer` and spawning through `Spawn`; the two GraphQL engines depend on `fw-graphql` and their library, async-graphql bringing no runtime at the features it is used with and juniper none; the five macro crates and `fw-handler-codegen` are in the core's and the hubs' trees already, and listing them names the crate that would bring tokio; `fw-grpc-macros` and `fw-build` are used by gRPC alone, which is tokio-bound, and are held at the level they meet, where tokio-bound would leave them unchecked; `fw-runtime-smol` is the second runtime, on `async-executor` and `async-io`, and prints nothing at any feature set; `fw-net` ends its TLS at rustls's `ServerConfig` (§2.7); `fw-test-certs` generates its certificates with `rcgen` and names rustls alone, reached by `fw-net`, `fw-http-hyper`, the two listener crates and the two TCP links through dev-dependency edges only (§1); `fw-ws-conformance` runs its client over the host's `futures-io` stream on the host's runtime and takes its slot on a `std` condition variable (§4.1); `fw-graphql-http` depends on `fw-graphql-ws`, and so on `fw-ws`, whether or not an app mounts subscriptions, so GraphQL over HTTP alone carries the WebSocket transport and no tokio with it (F362's feature-gating candidate, unbuilt); `fw-rpc-conformance` names no runtime, its waits on the harness runtime's `Timer`, its tasks through `fw::spawn_with` on it, its slots a `std` condition variable and its relay threads over `std` sockets, tokio behind its `tokio` feature alone (§5.2); `fw-rpc-tcp-core` is the TCP wire over `futures-io` on the runtime a link hands it, and `fw-rpc-tcp-smol` adds `async-net`'s sockets and `futures-rustls` to it (§5.3) |
