CI's `smol` job runs them on every push, each as its own `cargo test -p <crate> --test <suite> --locked` step so the suite that failed is named: `fw-runtime-smol`'s runtime suite; the HTTP suite against the hyper backend on `fw-listener-smol`; the WebSocket suite against the standalone server on smol, and against the HTTP port on smol and the pipe host; and the RPC suite against the smol TCP link, plain, CBOR and TLS; on a failure it ends with the print and upload steps the other suite jobs have, its artifact `conformance-failures-smol`. The `test` job runs the same targets inside `cargo test --workspace`; the job names them so the smol proof is a result of its own. It passes, so HTTP, WebSocket and TCP RPC serve on smol, with smol's sockets and no tokio runtime, and pass their suites in CI. The check below holds each crate to its level in CI, so a change that pulls a reactor into the server layer fails while hyper's dependency does not (F383). F385, the WebSocket suite's `drain_closes_with_1001` failing once on the pipe host, is the scenario racing `/echo`'s connection phase and not the paired-hook rule failing: the phase runs after the 101 under `refuse = close`, a drain that begins first refuses the connection with 1001 and runs no hook, and the scenario exchanges a message before it closes the app (§4.1). F386 is answered by `Link::connect` taking the client's runtime (§5.3).

**The check.** `scripts/runtime_levels.py`, standard-library Python that runs on 3.9, holds every workspace member to the level `runtime-levels.txt` at the workspace root gives it, and CI's `runtime levels` job runs it with `--locked` on every push. The list is one entry per line, `<crate> <level> [flags]`, each headed by a comment stating why the crate is at its level; the levels are `runtime-free`, `runtime-neutral`, `runtime-neutral+http2` and `tokio-bound`, the flags are limited to `--features`, `-F`, `--all-features` and `--no-default-features`, so an entry chooses a crate's features and never what the tree reads, and a crate checked at two feature sets has two entries. The members come from `cargo metadata --no-deps`, and a member with no entry fails, so a new crate is classified before it merges; a tokio-bound entry is listed and not read. For every other entry the script runs `cargo tree -p <crate> <flags> -e normal,features -i tokio --target=all` and collects every `tokio feature "<name>"` node wherever it appears, so cargo's `(*)` de-duplication hides none; `--target=all` reads every platform's dependencies, so the verdict is the same on the Linux runner and on macOS, and a tokio that one platform's dependencies alone bring fails everywhere. cargo answers a tree without tokio in two ways, and both pass: "did not match any packages", exit 101, when tokio is not in the resolved graph, and "nothing to print", exit 0, when it is there by a dev- or build-dependency edge alone, as on the four hubs whose tests run on tokio. A runtime-free entry fails on a tokio root at all, features or none; a `runtime-neutral` entry fails on any feature outside `default` and `sync`, a `runtime-neutral+http2` entry on any outside `default`, `sync`, `io-util` and `bytes`, and tokio's implicit features count, a planted `net` reading as `net`, `libc`, `mio`, `socket2` and `windows-sys`, each outside both sets. When tokio is in the tree the script reads it a second time with `-e normal`, package nodes alone, each line's parent the package it depends on: the children of `tokio` are its direct dependents, printed as `through`, and the children of `tokio-util` are tokio-util's; cargo prints a repeated node's children at its first occurrence only and every edge as a line, so the `(*)` de-duplication hides no direct dependent. A runtime-neutral entry of either set then fails on each package other than hyper, `h2` or `tokio-util` that depends on tokio directly, named as a workspace member or as no workspace member, and on each workspace member that depends on `tokio-util` directly with no `direct-tokio-util` line, so the level's "which hyper brings" is checked as written; the allowance covers the path and not the features, a listed member enabling tokio-util's `rt` failing on tokio's `rt`. The line is `<crate> direct-tokio-util <reason>`, the reason the rest of the line and required, split on whitespace before `shlex` reads it so that an apostrophe in the reason is no quote; a line with no reason, naming no member, or repeated for a crate is an error before any tree is read, and a line no runtime-neutral tree uses fails, unless a cargo error left a tree unread. One line names `fw-http-conformance`: its GOAWAY scenario drives `h2`'s client over the host's `futures-io` stream through `tokio-util`'s `compat`, `h2` reading tokio's I/O traits and hyper's client not exposing the frame, and an adapter of the suite's own between the two would implement tokio's traits and name tokio directly. A runtime-neutral entry's line prints `through` and, where a listed member's direct `tokio-util` was read, `; tokio-util direct from <crate>, listed`. Anything else cargo answers is an error, never a verdict: any other non-zero exit, carrying cargo's stderr; a zero exit with empty output and no "nothing to print"; a tree whose root is not tokio; and, before any tree is read, an entry naming no member, since given `-i` cargo widens an unknown `-p` to the whole workspace and exits 0, and a misspelled crate would read every member's tokio rather than be refused. An unknown level, a flag outside the four, or the same crate and flags twice is an error in the list. Exit status is 0 when every entry holds, 1 on a failure or an unclassified member, 2 on a cargo error or a malformed list; each entry prints one line, `ok`, `FAIL`, `ERROR` or `skip` with its level, crate, flags and the features found, then the failures and errors, then a count. The list classifies 50 members in 54 entries, 33 of them read. A runtime-free crate is read with `--all-features` unless a feature of its own brings tokio: `fw-http`'s `tokio-io` does, for `Upgraded`'s tokio traits, and `fw-rpc-conformance`'s `tokio` does, for its tokio harness, so those two are read at default features, the suite a second time with `--features smol`; the HTTP suite is read at default features and with `--features smol`, what the `smol` job runs, its `tokio` and `rocket` features bringing their hosts' runtimes; `fw-http-hyper` and `fw-ws-hyper` have two entries each, runtime-neutral without `tokio` and tokio-bound at their default features, so the list records both standings. On the tree as it stands the 27 runtime-free entries print no tokio, the three `runtime-neutral` entries print `default` and `sync` through hyper, the three `runtime-neutral+http2` entries print `bytes`, `default`, `io-util` and `sync` through `h2`, hyper and `tokio-util`, the suite's two with `tokio-util` direct from `fw-http-conformance`, listed, and the 21 tokio-bound entries are not read. The job runs after `check`, as checkout, the stable toolchain, `Swatinem/rust-cache@v2` and `python3 scripts/runtime_levels.py --locked`; a job of its own rather than a step in `check`, so a crate leaving its level fails under the rule's name, where a failing step in `check` would skip the compile behind it or report under the compile's name. Its cost is a runner and the registry: `cargo tree` compiles nothing and downloads every crate in the lock to read its manifest, 92 s with an empty cargo home and a few seconds warm, the six runtime-neutral entries read twice, the cache holding the registry and the job having no target directory to cache. Planted breaks read as the rules say. `tokio` with `sync` in `fw-rpc`'s dependencies fails `fw-rpc`, `fw-rpc-tcp-core`, `fw-rpc-tcp-smol` and both `fw-rpc-conformance` entries, "runtime-free, but its tree contains tokio [sync] through fw-rpc"; each break above that plants tokio on a member directly fails on the path beside the feature. `tokio-stream` without default features on `fw-listener-smol`, a third-party crate naming tokio with `sync`, fails the same two entries, "tokio-stream, no workspace member, depends on tokio directly"; ## 9. Development command [39]

`fw dev`, in `fw-cli` beside `fw new` and `fw generate`, watches the source through `watchexec`, rebuilds (`cargo build`), and restarts. `fw dev --listen 0.0.0.0:8080` holds a listening socket across restarts: the command binds the address **itself** and passes the socket to each child using the socket-activation protocol, `LISTEN_FDS`, `LISTEN_FDNAMES` and `LISTEN_PID`, with the address text as the socket's name, `%` written `%25` and `:` written `%3A`, since `LISTEN_FDNAMES` separates names with `:` and every socket address contains one. `--listen` takes an IP socket address, optionally written `tcp://`; a bare port, a `udp://` address and a host name are each refused with their own message, since the held socket goes to the endpoint written as the same address. The application changes nothing for it. `main` is written `Server::new("0.0.0.0:8080")` in development and in production alike, and under `FW_DEV=1`, which the command sets in every child, `EndpointSpec::resolve` in `prepare` resolves an `Endpoint::Addr` equal to an inherited socket's name to that socket, the address compared as parsed so three spellings of one address match; without the variable, with no name matching, or with inherited sockets the process cannot adopt, a `LISTEN_PID` naming another process among them, logged at `debug` for that case and `warn` for any other, the address binds as written, and the `LISTEN_PID` check keeps a stale variable harmless (§2.7). `EndpointSpec::resolve_as_written` is the lookup-free form, for a client, which connects to the address, and for a socket the activation cannot carry: the TCP client uses it, so a client in a child whose address equals the held socket connects rather than adopts, and the UDP link uses it on both sides, so a UDP endpoint at the held TCP address stays an address. An `Endpoint::inherited(..)` the application writes itself is matched by name as in production. UDP is outside `--listen`: the activation vets every inherited descriptor as a listening TCP socket, so an RPC application on UDP restarts without holding its socket, and the documentation says so.

`LISTEN_PID` has to equal the child's process ID, and `pre_exec` runs between fork and exec where only async-signal-safe calls are allowed and `setenv` allocates. The command therefore re-executes its own binary as a trampoline, `fw __exec -- <child> <args>`, which runs after exec with an ordinary allocator, sets `LISTEN_PID` to `std::process::id()` and `exec`s the child; `exec` keeps the pid, so the variable equals the child's. The trampoline runs only when a socket is held. The job's spawn hook sets `FW_DEV=1` on every child and removes `LISTEN_PID`, `LISTEN_FDS` and `LISTEN_FDNAMES` from its environment; the two socket variables are set in one place, by the spawn that places the socket. No shell is involved, and nothing runs between fork and exec but `command-fds`'s placement of the held socket at descriptor 3, `dup2` from another descriptor, and `FD_CLOEXEC` cleared through `fcntl` where the descriptor already is 3, which `dup2` onto itself would leave set, so the socket survives both execs. Each child receives a `try_clone` of the held socket, the original outliving every restart, made where the command decides to start a child and before it stops anything, so that a duplicate that cannot be made, the process out of descriptors, fails that start and nothing else: the failure is reported in red, "cannot duplicate the held socket for `<binary>`, so it was not started; the running application keeps serving, and the next change tries again", the middle clause only when one is running, with the OS error after it, no job is touched, and the next successful build tries again. The duplicate waits in a slot per job, an `Option<TcpListener>` under a mutex, filled on each start, each fill closing a duplicate no spawn took, and taken once by the job's spawn function, `Job::set_spawn_fn`, which places it at descriptor 3, sets `LISTEN_FDS=1` and `LISTEN_FDNAMES` and spawns, the command owning the descriptor and closing it once the child has spawned; a spawn finding the slot empty answers an `io::Error`, which the job reports in red, and starts no child. The spawn function rather than the spawn hook, `Job::set_spawn_hook`, because the hook returns `()` and cannot refuse a start, while the function answers `io::Result<Child>` and can; so no child is ever told `LISTEN_FDS=1` without a descriptor behind it, descriptor 3 in a child being whatever it inherited there and not known empty. A restart is awaited until the job has processed it, up to the stop's grace and the spawn, so its spawn has taken the duplicate before the next restart fills the slot; unawaited, back-to-back restarts fill the slot several times before the first spawn reads it, and the later spawns find it empty (117, 123). `fw-cli` carries no `unsafe`; the placement is `command-fds`'s (117, §0). In the child, `fw-net` sets `FD_CLOEXEC` on each inherited socket and leaves the three variables set (§2.7), so a subprocess the app spawns inherits neither the sockets nor a `LISTEN_PID` that matches it.

The restart sequence is build, then swap:

1. Each change runs `cargo build --message-format=json-render-diagnostics` with the command's mirrored flags (`--release`, `-p`, `--bin` or `--example`, `-F`, `--all-features`, `--no-default-features`, `--cargo-arg`) while the old child keeps serving. A failed build leaves the running application in place. A change during a build builds again before swapping, so a binary behind the source never starts.
2. A build that succeeds makes the next child's duplicate of the held socket first, and a duplicate that cannot be made fails the start there, in red, with the old child still serving; then it stops the old child with SIGTERM and a two-second grace before SIGKILL, the same grace Ctrl-C gets: an application past it is killed mid-drain, which a development restart accepts in exchange for not waiting out the app's own drain window, ten seconds unset, on every save; an open WebSocket or SSE client holds a restart two seconds and is then cut. The grace has no flag.
3. The new child starts on the same sockets, its spawn taking the duplicate and placing it, and the restart returns once that spawn has run. The binary is the one cargo's artifact messages name, chosen as `cargo run` chooses: `--bin` or `--example`, else the only binary, else the package's `default-run`, else an error naming `--bin`. A child that exits on its own is not reported; the next successful build starts it again.

While no child is accepting, the kernel queues connections in the listen backlog, which `fw dev` keeps open. Clients see a delay, never a refused connection. Socket holding is Unix-only. Off Unix `--listen` is accepted with a warning and the application binds the address itself, so a client can see a refused connection during a restart, and the documentation says so; a Windows handoff (`WSADuplicateSocket` into the child) is the path to add once the Unix one is built.

## 10. Shutdown, per transport [8]

All transports follow DESIGN §9.5. Here's what each does at each step:

| Step                                   | HTTP                                                                              | HTTP, embedded (§3.8)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | WebSocket                                                                                                                                 | RPC                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | gRPC                                                            |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| before-shutdown                        | serving normally                                                                  | the host serves normally                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | serving normally                                                                                                                          | serving normally                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | health still SERVING                                            |
| `drain` (stop accepting)               | GOAWAY (h2); idle keep-alives closed (h1); busy ones get `Connection: close`      | `Embedded::drain` resolves the handle's `stopping()`, which `run` wired to the host's graceful stop, and returns at once; salvo's `Closing` acceptor drops its listener and reports it closed through the handle, on which `run` sends the stop                                      | idle connections closed with 1001; busy ones stop reading; through `GatewayTable::drain` (X32), from the upgrade handler's `drain` (X21) on the HTTP port and on an embedding, and beside the accept loop's drain on `fw_ws_hyper::Server` | `Link::drain`: TCP `goaway`, the listener closed, a connection registering late sending its own; NATS drain, unconfirmed; AMQP `basic.cancel`, each `cancel-ok` awaited; Redis `UNSUBSCRIBE`, its reply awaited; MQTT unsubscribe, each UNSUBACK awaited; Kafka pause, with nothing to confirm; TCP and UDP end the inbound stream once no call is held and refuse later requests themselves                                                                                                                                      | GOAWAY through `fw-server-hyper`; health switches to NOT_SERVING |
| drain window                           | requests finish; SSE ends on `draining()`                                         | executions finish under `drain_timeout`; the host drains its connections under the same window where it takes a bound                                                                                                                                                                | in-flight messages finish, then 1001; `on_disconnect` as a terminal execution; a `refuse = handshake` connection phase under way is a task the drain waits for | in-flight calls finish; streams end on `draining()`; the inbound stream's end and the refusals spawned during the drain are waited for under the same deadline, what `close` then leaves unanswered counted and logged at `warn`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | in-flight calls finish                                          |
| a call arriving once `open` is refused | 503, `Retry-After`, `Connection: close`, answered directly: no pre-dispatch stage | 503, `Retry-After`, `Connection: close`, carrying `Routing::Unrouted`; on actix the adapter sets the head's connection-type flag; a request whose head is still arriving gets a closed connection where the host declares `DrainPending::Closed`                                     | nothing: busy connections have stopped reading                                                                                            | `err` of kind `unavailable`, from the server, or from the link on TCP and UDP once the inbound stream has ended; a broker declaring `holds_unserved` keeps the request for the next instance, the caller seeing its own `Timeout`; a link declaring `confirms_drain(false)` can lose a request already on its way, the caller seeing its own `Timeout`                                                                                                                             | UNAVAILABLE                                                     |
| cancel at timeout                      | `Drain` reason; connections reset                                                 | `Drain` reason; the host's connections are its own                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | close 1001                                                                                                                                | `err` of kind `unavailable`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | CANCELLED/UNAVAILABLE per stream                                |
| `close`                                | listeners and connections closed                                                  | the host future's completion awaited under `close`'s bound; a host still stopping past it is recorded `TimedOut`, and a `Window` host, or a `Reset` host holding an HTTP/2 connection, takes the whole window; the handle is `Closed` after and answers 503 with `Connection: close` | `GatewayTable::close` aborts every connection left, waits for their tasks and stops broadcast delivery: same-port connections through the upgrade handler's `close`, the standalone server's beside its accept loop's `close`, which closes the sockets | `Link::close`: links closed, NATS after an echo round trip per connection, MQTT once its DISCONNECT is written, TCP's aborted connections' writers released, UDP's socket read before it is dropped and the requests it holds refused `unavailable`, Kafka's consumers dropped on their own threads and its offsets committed on one (F370); the client's link closed by `RpcClientModule`'s destroy hook, or by the last drop of a client built with `RpcClient::new`, on its runtime, ending its connections on every link, TCP's writers shut and awaited, UDP's socket released, Redis's publisher and Kafka's producer dropped, the waiting calls failing `Unavailable` | listeners closed                                                |

Every refusal of a call because the server is draining or closing carries one phrase, "the server is shutting down": HTTP's 503, the RPC dispatcher's and the TCP, UDP, Redis and MQTT links' `err`, gRPC's UNAVAILABLE, WebSocket's refused upgrade and refused message, the graphql-transport-ws subscription at the drain, and the `Unavailable` the core's `Closed` is recognised as at render. The core's `Closed` keeps its own `Display`, "the application is shutting down", a Rust error's text the transport replaces on the wire. WebSocket's 1001 close frame at the drain, and the close a connect refused once the app is closing carries, read the same phrase, though a close frame ends a connection rather than refusing a call: one wording for one condition serves log searches and clients alike, and it fits within the 123-byte reason limit. One text keeps its own: "the server is over its in-flight limit" names a different condition.

A call still running when the drain window ends is cancelled with `CancelReason::Drain` and rendered with the same phrase: gRPC answers UNAVAILABLE, a WebSocket message ends its connection with the 1001 close, an RPC call answers `unavailable`, each from the cancellation itself and not from the connection's abort. Each server's `close` polls its connections' and calls' tasks once in its first poll, the task serving a call before the connection that writes its answer, so each rendering that needs no wait is written there: gRPC's status, the 1001 frame, the RPC `unavailable`, and HTTP's 503 where nothing has been written (§2.6). An expired shutdown cap gives `close` that one poll, so a client reads its transport's rendering and not a reset. The gRPC and WebSocket servers' `close` then waits up to 500 ms, once the drain has begun, for their connections to finish what the cancellation left them before it aborts them; an expired cap cuts that wait, and the abort runs as the cut `close` drops. A handler that observes the cancellation and answers in the poll it wakes in is answered as it chose, on all four transports (§2.6).

---

X16, X17, X19, X20, X24, X25 and X26 are additive core changes, X26 giving `AppBuilder::timer` the composition rule beside it, the clock alone after a runtime (§8). X18 changes the `__handler` protocol alone. X21, X22 and X23 touch `fw-http` and `fw-transport` and no core signature; X27 and X28 change `fw-http`'s and `fw-net`'s SPIs, `Backend::bind`'s `tls` parameter among them, and no core signature; X29 touches `fw-rpc` and `fw-runtime-tokio`; X30 is `fw-transport`'s, read by every transport. X31 changes `listen()`'s first check and the error type `AppHandle::mounted` answers, and adds `Mounted::runtime`; X32 is `fw-ws`'s alone, and no server trait changes for it. X33 touches `fw-runtime-tokio`, the seven link crates and `fw-ws-redis`, and adds `fw-runtime-smol`; the `Link` and `BroadcastAdapter` SPIs and the core are unchanged by it, a link's futures already answering through `BoxFuture` and `BoxStream`. X34 adds one defaulted method to each of those two SPIs, so a link or an adapter outside the workspace changes nothing and keeps the default, and changes `RpcClient::new`'s return type. X35 adds `runtime()` to `AppService` and changes no SPI trait: `Backend::bind` keeps its four parameters, `Listener` is new, the two hyper servers' types gain a parameter their tokio aliases hide, and the HTTP suite's `Host` gains `type Harness`, one line per host. X36 changes no SPI trait either: `Link` is unchanged by it, `fw-rpc-tcp-core` is for link authors by its description, and the RPC suite's `Broker` gains `type Harness`, one line per broker. X37 changes one `Link` method's signature, `connect` gaining the runtime parameter, which a link outside the workspace adds and uses or ignores, and adds three methods to `fw-runtime-smol`; the core is unchanged by it. X38 is `fw-rpc`'s alone, two builder methods on `StreamCall`, one removed from it and `RpcError`'s `source`; `Call`'s, `Emit`'s and `RpcClient`'s signatures, the `Link` SPI and the core are unchanged by it. X39 is `fw-rpc`'s alone too, one builder method on `RpcClient` and one on `RpcClientModule`; `StreamCall`, `Call`, `Emit`, the `Link` SPI and the core are unchanged by it.

| Over a load-shedding limit                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | runtime                                   | 503 with `Retry-After`, `REFUSED_STREAM`, close 1013, `unavailable` with `RetryAfter`, or UNAVAILABLE; every `max_inflight` bounds at 1,024 unset (§2.8), and on RabbitMQ and Kafka the request waits in the broker instead (§5.2)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Oversized frame or payload                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | runtime                                   | 413, close 1009, or `bad_request` with `payload_too_large`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| A reply frame the link's codec cannot encode, or one over its `max_frame`; a request frame the client's own link cannot encode                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | runtime                                   | `err` of kind `internal` under the call's `id`, written at once, the encoding failure logged at `error`; a reply stream's item ends the stream `internal` after the items before it (§5.3); the client's `RpcError` of kind `Internal`, before any I/O (§5.2)                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Connect guard refusal                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | runtime                                   | close code by kind or explicit `ConnectRefused::code`; a 401 or 403 before the upgrade under `refuse = handshake`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Passed deadline, caller gone                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | runtime                                   | cancellation with a `CancelReason`; `Timeout` rendering where a reply can still be sent, on HTTP, RPC and gRPC after the error handlers have run under `timeout_grace`; a stream they answer ended with that rendering and logged at `warn`, told by `Reply::Many`, a second length-prefixed message, a body still open at the grace's end, or a body the server waited on past the 1 MiB buffered for it, one ended on its first poll being delivered whatever its size (§2.4, §3.6) |
| `ConnectRefused::code(code, reason)` with a reason over 123 bytes, a code never sent in a frame (1004, 1005, 1006, 1015) or one outside 1000–4999                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | runtime, where built                      | `Err(CloseCodeError)` (§4.2)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| A client offering none of a gateway's `subprotocols`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | runtime                                   | a 101 without `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`; the gateway decides what follows (§4.1)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| A Pong that misses `pong_timeout`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 | runtime                                   | the connection ends as `Lost` (§4.1)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| UDP under `fw dev --listen`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | the command                               | refused: the activation vets every inherited descriptor as a listening TCP socket (§9)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| A duplicate of the held socket `fw dev` cannot make                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | the command, where it decides to start a child | the start fails in red naming the OS error, no job is touched and the running application keeps serving, the next change trying again; a spawn whose slot holds no duplicate fails and starts no child, so `LISTEN_FDS=1` is never set without a descriptor behind it (§9)                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| An `application/grpc` request on the HTTP server's port or an embedding host                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | runtime                                   | not routed to the gRPC server: the HTTP app answers it as any request, a 404 off its routes (§6.2)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

---

## 13. Decisions taken with defaults

1. **There is no per-module middleware.** One pre-dispatch stage in two sub-steps covers app-wide work scoped by path, and controller interceptors cover local work, both inside the error chain (§3.3). "Every controller in this module" takes the form of a module tier in the enhancer stack if a case needs it; until then `.at(prefix)` with a pattern-scoped entry covers it.
2. **`Conflict` maps to gRPC ABORTED.** Google's API guidance pairs HTTP 409 with both ABORTED and ALREADY_EXISTS. `CallError::with_grpc_code(..)` overrides it per error, and a `tonic::Status` returned as the error names any code as it stands (§6.2).
3. **`Timeout` renders as HTTP 504.** The server ran out of time, usually waiting on something downstream. 408 means the server gave up waiting for the _client's request_, which is a different situation.
4. **Connect guards run after the 101 handshake** and refuse with a close code, as [23] asks, since a close code is the only refusal a browser can read. `refuse = handshake` on a gateway refuses before the upgrade with an HTTP 401 or 403 instead, as RFC 6455 allows, for non-browser clients and proxy logs (§4.1).
5. **The WebSocket and RPC envelopes are this design's own**, JSON on every gateway and link by default, with MessagePack through `rmp-serde` (`codec = msgpack`, §4.2) and CBOR through `ciborium` (`codec = cbor`, §5.2) opted into per gateway or link. Nothing here aims at wire compatibility with NestJS or socket.io.
6. **A slow WebSocket consumer is disconnected** with 1008 by default, with drop-oldest as an option.
7. **gRPC reflection is on in debug builds and opt-in in release builds.** The GraphQL playground follows the same rule.
8. **`fw dev` socket holding is Unix-only, and holds TCP sockets alone** (§9). UDP is outside `--listen` until the activation vets a datagram socket.
9. **`fw-http-hyper` is the one backend, and actix-http owns no sockets.** An application wanting actix's per-core runtime model embeds in an actix-web host, where the model is kept (§3.8). A second socket-owning path would be a second reference for the conformance suite to keep in agreement, and nothing above it changes if one is added.
10. **The actix embedding declares `upgrades: false`.** actix's upgrade is a payload/body pair bridged across a `!Send` boundary rather than a per-request future, and a gateway on an actix host is refused in `prepare` (§3.8). The limit is the adapter's declaration, so lifting it changes the table and nothing else.
11. **One settings vocabulary.** A byte size is `*_limit: u64`; a count is `max_*: Count`; a time that may be off is a `Bound`, `*_timeout` or named for what it bounds; a time that is a value, never off, is a `Duration`. §3.6, §4.2, §5.3 and §6.2 read it: `message_limit`, `max_connections`, `max_inflight`, `max_outbound`, `ping_interval`, `pong_timeout`, `max_frame`, `max_per_connection`, `connection_init_timeout`. A `Count::Max(0)` or a `Bound::After(Duration::ZERO)` is refused in `prepare` with one hint on every transport (X22).
12. **Brokers carry the payload, not the envelope**, with the correlation in the broker's own mechanism; TCP, UDP and Redis carry the whole frame (§5.2). The request lane stays readable by a broker's own tools.
13. **The competing-consumer group defaults to the root module's full type path** on NATS, MQTT and Kafka, sanitised per broker and overridden with `.group(..)` (§5.2). A fixed name would let two applications on one broker compete for each other's requests with no error anywhere.
14. **A miss is `Timeout` where the link cannot signal it**, Kafka under auto-create, MQTT at QoS 0, and RabbitMQ for a pattern served once, whose queue outlives the server, declared through `Capabilities::miss_signal` for the first two and `Capabilities::holds_unserved` for the third, which Kafka declares too (§5.2). The Kafka link creates its handler topics at `bind` and anchors the group's offsets at their end while the group is empty, so a stopped server's topic exists, a request produced while no instance consumes waits for the next owner, and that case is a `Timeout` on every broker.
15. **`credit` is reserved and unsent** (§5.2). `max_inflight` bounds every link, 1,024 unset, and where the broker holds work the bound reaches it through `Link::max_inflight`, which `Server::prepare` calls beside `Link::prepare`, AMQP's prefetch and Kafka's pause; the rest refuse (54), and no link carries a prefetch setting of its own.
16. **WebSocket keep-alive is on by default**, 30 seconds for `ping_interval` and for `pong_timeout`, `Unbounded` turning it off (§4.1).
17. **A connection a connect guard refused never reaches `on_disconnect`, and every connection whose `OnConnect` ran does** (§4.1). The hooks come in pairs, in both directions (73).
18. **The gRPC build step uses a vendored `protoc`** (§6.1). It meets "no system protoc", and a pure-Rust compiler is a later swap behind the same API.
19. **gRPC serves on its own port alone.** gRPC on the HTTP server's port or on an embedding host is outside this design, and §6.2 names the extension point.
20. **Client-certificate verification is not built.** `fw_net::Tls` verifies no client certificate on any transport, and the gRPC example reads a token (§6.1). When built it lands in `fw-net`, once for every transport.
21. **One `GraphqlModule` serves one engine**; a second engine is reached through the DI's qualifier (§7).
22. **A metadata type may name its transport**, and is then refused on every other at compile time (X24, §2.5). A type naming none is valid everywhere.
23. **The gateway on the HTTP server's port is module-driven.** `WsModule` registers the hand-off, and the upgrade handler carries the server's lifecycle (X21), rather than a second socketless server the user binds in `main` (§3.5).
24. **One deadline rule.** A passed deadline on HTTP, RPC and gRPC runs the error handlers with a `Timeout` `CallError` under the server's `timeout_grace`, one second at `Default`, and renders canonically only when the grace passes first (§2.4). The argument that a caller past its deadline has stopped waiting applies to all three alike, and was weighed against the application's need to log, count or reshape its timeouts consistently. The handlers' answer is delivered when it is a single reply produced within the grace; a streamed answer is ended with the canonical timeout and logged at `warn`, since the grace bounds the handlers and not a stream they return, and a caller at its deadline reads nothing. Each transport defines a single reply by its own protocol, RPC a `Reply::One` or `Reply::None`, gRPC one length-prefixed message, HTTP a body that completes within the grace, HTTP having no message boundaries; a single payload written through `Body::stream` is delivered, and an `Sse`, which never ends, is not. The 1 MiB cap bounds only a body the server waits on: it exists so an error handler cannot make the server accumulate an unbounded body while it waits for the end, and a body whose end is reached on its first poll is already in memory, built by the handler, so delivering it costs nothing and refusing it would turn a valid single reply into a 504. `Full` and any body produced at once fall under that without a type being named. A body judged by its `size_hint` instead would cut a single reply sent through `Body::stream`, a false positive its author cannot see coming.
25. **A gateway is served on one port.** `port = http | own` on the gateway attribute selects the hand-off or `fw_ws_hyper::Server`, `http` unset, and no gateway is served on both (§4.1). A `port = own` gateway in an application binding no `fw_ws_hyper::Server` is served by nothing and reported by nothing, since no module sees whether the server exists.
26. **A prefix nothing reads is refused.** `Transport::READS_PREFIX` says whether a transport reads `.at(prefix)`, `false` unless declared, and the freeze refuses the prefix on a controller none of whose handlers' transports do, or that mounts no handler (X25, §2.5). `Ws` answers `true` beside `Http` and `WsConnect`, since a controller with message handlers mounts its gateway's connect handler too. A controller mixing HTTP routes with gRPC methods keeps its prefix for the routes.
27. **The RPC call shape is read from types, never from spelling.** An `Inbound<T>` parameter and a stream reply are each found by an autoref probe, the reply's over the generated call closure's future output, so an alias or an opaque type counts and no attribute overrides the read (§5.1).
28. **Broadcasts travel as JSON** between processes and are re-encoded per gateway on delivery, so one publish serves gateways of both codecs; a byte string reaches a MessagePack gateway as an array of numbers (§4.3).
29. **Connect guards are graphql-transport-ws's only authorization point.** No `Ws` guard, interceptor or error handler runs per operation on that gateway, and the documentation of gateways states it (§7).
30. **A broker link connects once at `bind`.** An unreachable broker is one `StartupError::Bind` at startup, not a retry loop; a retry window is a `Bound` to add when a deployment needs one (§5.3). Kafka's committed-offsets read is the one retry inside `bind`, on three coordinator codes within its own timeout (37): there the broker is reachable and the error is one librdkafka classes retriable, so the retry hides no configuration error.
31. **A module-level setting is refused at `wire()`.** `RpcClientModule::timeout` and `RpcClientModule::idle_timeout`, `GraphqlConfig::connection_init_timeout` and a `GrpcEndpoint` URI live on modules, which have no `prepare`; each is recorded through `try_value` and reported with the wiring errors, which precede any socket as `prepare` does (§5.4, §6.3, §7).
32. **A host's drain behavior is declared and asserted, never noted.** `drain_pending`, `drain_abandoned` and `drain_http2` on `EmbedLimits` (§3.8) record what each host was observed to do, and a scenario checks each in both directions; a note asserts nothing, and a host's next version changes the behavior unseen. actix declares `DrainPending::Closed` rather than its `run` delaying `stop(true)` past `stopping()`, which would add a second signal to work around one host, or actix-web being pinned below 4.15, which trades a declared limit for a version trap; and it declares `DrainHttp2::Reset` in every build, since Cargo unifies features and the adapter cannot read whether another crate turned actix-web's `http2` on.
33. **No conformance scenario passes on silence**, in any of the three suites (§3.8, §4.1, §5.2). A request the client's timeout ends fails its scenario unless the scenario is about a timeout, and a scenario that cannot apply to a host or link is declared in the stamping macro and reported ignored, never passed. salvo's listener held open through the drain was the first thing the rule caught. A scenario that fails while its environment starts names the underlying error: each suite's `report` joins every cause under `source()`, and every startup path panics with it, so a broker container, a bind or a connect that fails is reported with its chain rather than as a timeout downstream.
34. **A broker's hold is declared, and the declaration is asserted.** `holds_unserved` lets the drain scenario accept the caller's `Timeout` on RabbitMQ and Kafka, and the scenario then shows the hold by delivering an event emitted during the drain to the next instance; `durable_replies` lets the recovery scenario require the held call's answer on Kafka, and the environment shows the cut and the outage, observed by the relay rather than arranged by a sleep, the handler's answer moment standing for the publish with a second to spare (§5.2, §5.3); `confirms_drain(false)` lets the drain-window scenario accept the caller's `Timeout` for a call sent during the drain on NATS and UDP, and the scenario then requires the call sent once the server has closed refused `Unavailable`, so the declaration is shown to be a window and not a server that never stopped, while a link declaring nothing is held to the confirmed drain. Declaring any of the scenarios not applicable would hide a stronger property than the one it skips.
35. **A client link ends its reply lane on a lost connection** rather than carrying calls across a reconnect (§5.3). A reconnect that lets in-flight calls vanish reports nothing; the RabbitMQ client drops lapin's auto-recovery for the same reason, and the next call connects again anyway. Kafka's reply topic loses nothing, so its client keeps the reconnect and declares it.
36. **The salvo server stays the caller's.** `run` takes `salvo::Server<Closing<A>>`, the public `Closing<A>` acceptor closing the listener when the drain begins, rather than building the server itself over a private wrapper, which would lose `with_http_builder`, `http1_mut`, `http2_mut` and `fuse_factory`; the type requires the wrapper, `Closing::new` registers the acceptor with the handle both sides share, and `run` sends the stop once `listeners_closed()` resolves, which pairs the two through the handle with no extra parameter and no dependence on salvo's poll order; a `Closing` from another handle is refused before serving, a warning there leaving `run` nothing to wait on (§3.8).
37. **A Kafka group anchors its offsets at `bind` while it is empty** (§5.2), the one moment Kafka accepts the commit; a topic added while the group runs starts at its end on each assignment until a handler settles a record there, and the documentation says so. The committed-offsets read the anchor asks the coordinator for is retried on `NotCoordinator`, `CoordinatorLoadInProgress` and `CoordinatorNotAvailable` alone, within the read's 10 s timeout, 100 ms doubling to 1 s between attempts (§5.3): a coordinator loading or moving is the broker's own transient, librdkafka classes the three retriable, and asking every deployment to wait for Kafka's coordinator before the server binds would push a broker detail onto every operator. Any other error fails `bind` at once, as decision 30 has it. Each attempt runs on a thread of its own and the wait between attempts is the app's `Timer`, which the link reads from the `AppHandle` in `prepare` (57).
38. **`RpcClientModule` closes its link on the app's destroy hook** (§5.4), as the server's `close` closes its links, so a client link's connections do not outlive the app on any link: TCP's writers are owned by the link and awaited, UDP's reply lane owns its socket, and Redis's publisher and Kafka's producer are taken out of the slot the `RpcClient` keeps until its next call. The suite's client-close scenario holds every link to it and requires the close's report clean, since a hook the core drops at its bound ends the link's tasks itself and would pass a `close` that did nothing.
39. **A heavy environment bounds its own suite, and a host bounds what its memory allows.** `Broker::PARALLEL`, `None` unless declared, holds each stamped scenario to a slot from before `start` until its environment is dropped, and `FW_CONFORMANCE_PARALLEL`, read by every suite, lowers that to what one host can run, the smaller of the two applying (§5.2). Kafka declares four: a container per scenario keeps offsets, topics and the relay cut apart with no namespace, and a container exiting before its ready line fails its scenario rather than retrying, the exit being a symptom of a host running short. What a host's memory allows is not the broker's to declare: a bound written into a suite for one machine would slow every host, and CI runs each suite at the broker's bound with the variable unset.
40. **Generated code is lint-clean in the user's crate** under clippy's default set with `-D warnings` (§1), stated as a rule over all generated code that compiles there rather than as a list of generators, so a generator added later is covered without being named. `fw-macro-lints` expands every attribute and derive macro over a proto `fw-build` compiles, and CI's `generated code lints` job lints that crate alone on a pinned stable clippy: on `stable`, a lint a new clippy adds would turn the job red on a change unrelated to the macros, so the pin is bumped deliberately, in a commit of its own that fixes whatever the new release trips, where the new lints are the change under review. The existing test crates carry hand-written code with warnings of their own, which `-D warnings` would fail on code no user inherits. An `allow` goes into the generated code where the lint is one the user cannot act on: the reply-shape probe's diverging closure (§5.1) and the marker module named as its wrapper (§6.1). The same statement-over-all-generators holds for names: every probe or helper a macro emits into a user's crate carries the `__ulo_` prefix, and an inherent call it makes goes by path, never by method syntax, so a user's blanket trait whose methods every type has meets neither (core DESIGN §3.4). A probe sharing a user's method name is ambiguous where its arm applies and the user's method where it does not, which turns a check returning `()` into a refusal that never fires. `ulo-codegen-tests` pins it: `blanket_traits.rs` compiles every attribute and derive beside blanket traits naming every method the generated code calls, `construct`, `check` and `matches` among them, and `ui/refusals_beside_a_blanket_trait.rs` holds that four refusals still fire with a blanket trait of those three in scope.
41. **A container's published port is probed for a shadowing listener before the suite connects to it** (§5.2). A VM-backed engine picks the port without seeing the host's sockets, and a host listener on `127.0.0.1` at that port receives the suite's connections in the broker's place, which reads as a broker that would not bind or answered bytes that were not its protocol. `relay::unshadowed` starts the container again, at most five times, each restart logged; a registry of the suite's own relay ports would miss a listener another program opened, the container's bridge address is not routed by Docker Desktop on macOS, and `[::1]` depends on the engine publishing on IPv6. The probe runs on macOS alone, since Linux refuses the bind that forms the shadow and would refuse the probe beside the engine's own listener.
42. **A conformance startup failure is written to a file, which CI prints and uploads** (§3.8, §4.1, §5.2). `startup_failed!` panics as `panic!` would, after writing the message under `failures_dir()`, so the cause survives a runner that keeps part of the test output; the `test` and broker jobs print the directory into the job log and upload it as an artifact when they fail. `--nocapture` is not used: it interleaves every scenario's output and adds nothing a failing test's own capture carries. A scenario's own assertions write no file; the files are for an environment that did not start.
43. **A drain is confirmed, and a link that cannot confirm it declares so.** A server has stopped accepting only once the broker has stopped routing to it, so a broker link's `drain` returns on the broker's own statement of that, MQTT's UNSUBACK, AMQP's `basic.cancel-ok` and Redis's `UNSUBSCRIBE` reply, Kafka's pause needing none since no broker routes to a group member, and the wait runs under the drain deadline alone, since a bound of its own would be a second knob for the same window; a broker slow to confirm shows in the logs rather than as unexplained timeouts, a drain dropped at the deadline logging the filters MQTT had not confirmed. `Server::drain` waits under that deadline for the inbound stream to end and for every refusal spawned during the drain to be sent, since a call arriving during the drain would otherwise see `Timeout` where the design promises `Unavailable`, and `close` counts and logs what the deadline left unanswered (§5.3). TCP and UDP end their inbound stream once the draining server holds no call and answer later requests themselves: a drain waiting out its deadline with nothing pending is a defect, not a link's declared behaviour. NATS and UDP declare `Capabilities::confirms_drain(false)`, asserted in both directions by the drain-window scenario (§5.2): async-nats 0.46 has no public path that confirms an unsubscribe, its `flush` resolving on the client's own write with no `PING` sent and its `unsubscribe` removing the subscription at once, so unsubscribe-then-flush loses every request in the window where the drain loses some; and UDP tells no caller to stop sending, so a datagram arriving after the socket closes reaches no one, `close` having answered `unavailable` every request the socket already held, and the ICMP port unreachable a connected client socket may receive being often filtered and not relied on. The capability is positive, `confirms_drain`, stating what a link does as `miss_signal`, `holds_unserved` and `durable_replies` do, where a name for what it lacks reads backwards beside them; and it is `true` from `Capabilities::new`, so a link that declares nothing gets the strict assertion and forgetting to declare fails a test rather than loosening one. Its doc names what a caller sees.
44. **`on_stream_end` reports the reply actually written.** A stream discarded before the response is sent was never the reply and reports nothing: the first report an execution receives is the one kept, and a discarded stream's `CutOff` would hide the real reply's outcome. Every transport tracks where it writes. HTTP's service and the RPC and WebSocket dispatchers wrap the stream in `Tracked` as they hand it to what writes it, `fw_rpc::Reply::Many` and `fw_ws::Reply::Many` carrying the bare stream (§2.6, §4.1, §5.1); gRPC's dispatcher sees an encoded body, so `encode_stream` marks the reply and the dispatcher's outermost body reports at the trailers, the protocol's own end marker deciding, `grpc-status: 0` as `Completed` and any other status, an `Err` item's included, as `CutOff`, which is where §2.6 places gRPC's clean end and where a report before the transport has finished writing would contradict it (§6.2). One exception holds on HTTP, RPC and gRPC: a stream the error handlers answer after a passed deadline is the reply, dropped unwritten, and reports `CutOff(Deadline)`; a WebSocket message has no deadline. On RPC the wrap follows the link's capability check, so a stream on a link that cannot carry it is never the reply, the `err internal` the link writes is, and the stream reports nothing. The core's doc on `on_stream_end` states the rule with no exception.
45. **MQTT's flow-control window is narrowed and documented, not declared.** MQTT 5 §3.10.4 lets a broker deliver after the UNSUBACK a publish it held back for the client's flow control, and one delivered after `close` has queued the DISCONNECT gets no answer (F355). A boolean cannot express a drain confirmed unless more than Receive Maximum requests are outstanding, and declaring `confirms_drain(false)` would loosen every drain scenario on MQTT to cover one corner, which hides more than it reveals. Both sides of the link announce a Receive Maximum of 65,535 instead, MQTT 5's largest, so the broker has less reason to hold a publish back: MQTT 5 reads an absent value as 65,535, but Mosquitto 2.0.18 then applies its own `max_inflight_messages`, 20 unset, and holds the rest back, which the link's suite pins through a server that acknowledges nothing and must still receive every request published. The remaining condition is stated precisely in the MQTT row and the crate's documentation, a request lost at shutdown only when more are outstanding to the instance than the broker's flow control allows, the announced 65,535 or a smaller cap the broker applies itself, and the drain scenarios keep their strict assertion at a load below it (§5.3). The announcement bounds nothing the server takes in: rumqttc acknowledges a publish as its event loop reads it, so the excess is refused `unavailable` by `Server::max_inflight`, 1,024 unset. F355's full cause is that publishes the broker queued for the instance behind a full window are dropped with its session, which is also why the link refuses over the bound rather than holding work there (55).
46. **A runtime is given, never found, and the core and the hubs depend on none.** `Runtime` is `Timer + Spawn`; `.runtime(r)` binds it as one object with the clock, `AppHandle::runtime()` hands it to a link or a backend, `RpcClientModule` reads `Dep<dyn Runtime>`, and `RpcClient::new(link, runtime)` takes it as an argument (§8, §5.4). A `Handle::try_current` in a drop was the hidden coupling the rule exists to remove. The test is one sentence, an alternative implementation of any plug point has no tokio in its tree, and a hub carrying `tokio` for `sync` alone fails it by definition, so `fw-rpc` runs on `async-lock`, `event-listener`, `futures-channel` and `futures-util` where it ran on `tokio::sync`, `JoinSet` and `select!`, and `fw-ws` on `async-tungstenite`, `event-listener`, `async-broadcast` and `futures-channel` where it ran on `tokio-tungstenite` and the same three (60). Sockets stay out of `Runtime`: every runtime abstraction that took them on ended at the lowest common denominator and grew features to escape it, so the links stay tokio-based behind the runtime-neutral `Link`, each on a tokio runtime of its own so that an app on another runtime calls them (64), a link on another runtime is its own crate, and `fw-net` hands out `std::net` sockets for each runtime crate to adopt. `fw_runtime_tokio::Tokio` holds the `Handle` it spawns and sleeps on, and no unit form exists beside it (F360): the unit form spawned on whatever runtime was current at the call, which is a panic in a drop off a worker thread, and keeping both would keep that.
47. **A `TaskHandle` detaches on drop, a `TaskSet` aborts on drop, and `poll_ended` waits for the future's drop** (§8). Cancel-on-drop for the handle would end every fire-and-forget spawn in the hubs the moment its handle went out of scope and make a drain depend on where a handle happened to be dropped; the set aborts because the `JoinSet` it replaces did, the hubs' serve futures rely on it when the core drops them, and the set's owner going away is the signal its tasks have no one left to serve. A task its spawner detached outlives the spawner's drop with whatever it holds, so each RPC link holds every loop it spawns that holds a socket or a connection through a handle that aborts on drop, kept by the link and not by the state the loop holds: TCP's and UDP's an `Owned` in `Core` and `Udp`, the broker links' a `Drop` on their `State`, and NATS's an `AbortOnDrop` in its state, so a link dropped without `close`, as the `App` value's drop leaves one (149), releases its listener, socket or connections (F428, 151, 152). `poll_ended` is `Ready` only once the future is dropped, since a server's close does `abort_all` then `join_all` and relies on no part of any task running afterwards; the weaker rule, `Ready` once the runtime accepted the abort, would leave a drain unable to say so. `TaskEnd::Panicked(Arc<Redacted>)` carries the panic's message, converted by `redact_panic` as `PanicRecovered`'s and `FailureReason::Panicked`'s are, with the app's registry for a task spawned through the app's runtime and the userinfo strip alone for one spawned on a bare runtime outside any app (89); a panic in an aborted future's drop reads `Aborted`, the abort being the intended outcome, and is caught by the core's wrapper and logged at `warn` rather than left to the runtime (76). `spawn_with` leaves its value in a slot the handle reads once the task ends, which keeps a channel out of the core, and answers `Result<T, TaskEnd>`, whose `Err` can only be `Aborted` or `Panicked` and whose poll after the value was taken is `Err(Finished)`, stated in its doc so that nobody reads it as the task's failure.
48. **`.runtime(..)` and `.timer(..)` compose, each overriding only what it sets, and `override_value::<dyn Runtime>` is refused** (§8). `.runtime(r)` sets the spawning and the clock, `.timer(t)` the clock alone, applied in order: `.timer(t).runtime(r)` is `r` for both, and `.runtime(r).timer(t)` is `r`'s spawning with `t`'s clock, bound as `dyn Runtime` through a private composite whose `Timer` half is `t`, so the clock services read, the one the core's waits read and the one a transport sleeps on through `Mounted::runtime()` are one, and a real executor under a test's clock is written as those two calls. A later call that cleared the runtime would make `.runtime(r).timer(t)` lose the ability to spawn, failing far from the line that caused it, while a composite keeping `r`'s clock would have the transports' timeouts on another clock than the hooks'. The cost is identity: after both calls `Dep<dyn Timer>` is `t` and `Dep<dyn Runtime>` the composite, two objects that agree on the clock, where `.runtime(r)` alone binds one. The override is refused as the timer's is, as `WiringError::RuntimeOverride` with the hint `TestApp::runtime(..)`, since an override would split the one object.
49. **`listen()` refuses an app that binds any transport with no runtime, as the core's `RuntimeMissing`** (§8, X31). A runtime is a core concept as the timer is, and the timer was already required at `listen()`; `Runtime` includes `Timer`, so the check generalises the old one in place of a flag on `Server`. Every transport spawns through the runtime or hands its upgrades to code that does, HTTP's hand-off and `fw-ws`'s driver among them, so there is no server for which the flag would be false, and a server's own refusal in its `prepare` would repeat the core's for each transport. The refusal comes before any `prepare`, so it is reported before any socket and before a transport's own failures, as `StartupError::Bind` with the error in its `source`, naming the first queued server's transport and `.runtime(..)`, which sets the timer too, for the app given `.timer(..)` alone; `.timer(..)` alone stays valid for an app that binds nothing, a job or a CLI command that needs a clock.

A module's client leaves its link to the module's destroy hook (38).
53. **The hubs' watch is `event-listener` over a `std` mutex, written once in `fw-transport`'s `__private`** (§5.3, §4.2). 54. **`Count::Default` on `max_inflight` is 1,024 on every transport, and a broker that holds work holds it there** (§2.8, §5.2). `Default` means the framework's default, and a default of no bound turns a load spike into a memory spike with nothing pushing back; on a broker it is worse, the broker being the buffer an unbounded consumer drains into one process's memory. HTTP takes the bound too, so the vocabulary means one thing everywhere, and a default changed before release costs nothing. The bound is read in one place, `Count::max_inflight()`. WebSocket has two bounds by one mechanism: `max_inflight`, 64 per connection, the messages one connection may have in flight before its read loop stops, which holds one chatty client, and `server_max_inflight`, 1,024 across the server's connections, which holds memory, each connection reading only while a place is free and a message read as the last place went waiting unhandled on its connection, so the pressure lands in the clients' TCP buffers rather than as refusals (§4.2, 85); the alternatives were 1,024 per connection with no server-wide bound, under which a server of c connections may run 1,024 × c handlers, or 64 alone. Links that cannot hold work, TCP, UDP, NATS, Redis and MQTT, refuse `unavailable` with `RetryAfter`. The conformance scenario holds every link to its declaration, six calls against a bound of two.
55. **MQTT refuses rather than holds work** (§5.3). Holding it, the acknowledgement sent once the handler completes and a Receive Maximum equal to the bound, would make the requests in the window the broker's to pass on when the session ends, which MQTT 5 §4.8.2 recommends and does not require; Mosquitto 2.0.18, the suite's image, never did, in 60 runs over a clean DISCONNECT, an UNSUBSCRIBE then DISCONNECT, an aborted event loop, a killed process and a keep-alive timeout, at Receive Maximum 65,535 and 4, a persistent-session control showing the messages held in the member's session and leaving with it. Holding work at a broker that strands it with the departing instance would turn a narrow drain edge case into routine loss, so the link refuses with `RetryAfter`, keeps its Receive Maximum at 65,535 and keeps F355 documented with its full cause. The behaviour is the broker's, not the protocol's: EMQX or HiveMQ may redeliver, and the shape for one is an opt-in on the link, verified by running the drain scenario against that broker and never assumed from the specification's "should" (F365). The probe, not the specification, decided it, and the row cites it so the decision is not reopened from the "should" alone.

58. **A client call registers under the lane's lock, and a late TCP connection sends its own `goaway`** (§5.3, §5.4). 65. **`Tokio::run` is one public helper in `fw-runtime-tokio`, and the result comes back through the task's `JoinHandle`** (§8). 66. **What runs through `run` is what needs tokio's context, a command handoff stays inline, and every frame goes through one writer per link side** (§5.3). 71. **`fw-ws-redis` with no runtime is refused by `BroadcastAdapter::prepare`, from `WsModule`'s init hook at `connect` and from each hub serving gateways at `listen()`, and a publish without one still fails** (§4.3). 153. **A `close` claims the servers at its call, and a `close` holding its claim when the `App` value drops keeps them: the claims are a count kept beside the drop's flag under one `std::sync::Mutex`, the drop releases only when the count is zero, and once the app has dropped the last claim to end or drop releases; a `close` whose claim finds the servers already released by a drop runs no step and answers `ShutdownFailure::Dropped`** (§10, core §9.5, 146, 149, F426). `AppHandle::close` is `fn close(&self, signal: Signal) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shutdown, ShutdownError>> + Send + use<>`, an inherent method, so every `handle.close(sig).await` compiles unchanged; `shutdown::close` takes `Closing::claim` before it builds the `async move` block, and the block's first poll triggers the shutdown and runs the sequence. `Closing` owns an `Arc<AppShared>`, so the future holds what the shutdown needs whatever happens to the handle or the `App` value, and `+ use<>` states that it borrows nothing from the handle: in edition 2024 an `impl Future` return captures the borrow of `self`, and `tokio::spawn(handle.close(sig))` would not compile, leaving a caller to clone the handle into a task whose first poll took the claim and reopened the window the call closes. `serve` and `App<Connected>::close` go through the same function and own the `App` value's hold themselves; in `serve` the claim is declared after the moved hold and drops first, the count falling before the hold's drop reads it. `ShutdownCell` holds `release: Mutex<Release>`, `Release` holding `app_dropped`, `closing`, `released` and `servers_closed`. `Closing::claim` increments `closing` and records, at the call, whether the servers were already released by a drop: `released` set and `servers_closed` not. `Owner::drop` calls `app_dropped`, which under the lock sets `app_dropped` and reads whether `closing` is zero, and only then, outside the lock, calls `release_servers`; `Closing`'s drop decrements the count and, the app dropped and the count at zero, sets `released` and releases outside the lock. The close step sets `servers_closed` under the same lock before its own release (146), so a release by a drop is told from the close step's, and the later releases, by a claim and by a drop after it, take an empty `Vec`. `released` is what a claim reads rather than the count: a claim answering `Dropped` still counts, so a second `close` made beside it after the drop found a count of one, ran the hooks over an empty list and answered `Ok` until the claim read the flag. The drop reads no phase: a runner dropped inside the before-shutdown hook leaves the phase at `Stopping`, and a drop that returned without releasing from `Stopping` on, probed, kept an abandoned shutdown's servers for the life of the last handle and failed 149's abandoned-shutdown test. Every `close` counts, the ones waiting on another's sequence among them: a waiter takes over the `OnceCell`'s initializer when the runner's future drops and resumes the sequence where it stood, and with the count taken inside `sequence` instead, probed, a runner's abandonment counted down to zero while a waiter was still to resume, released the servers, and the waiter's close step closed none. A `close` made before the drop runs the whole shutdown, its hooks and every server's `close` included, whether its future was polled before the drop or first polled after it: `Owner`'s drop frees nothing but the servers, and with a claim held it frees nothing, the singleton store, the graph and the phase living in `AppShared`. One dropped unpolled releases the servers as its claim drops, if it is the last. A `Dropped` answer runs no step: no trigger is recorded, the phase is the one the drop's release left, `Closed`, and the outcome is not stored in the shutdown's cell, so each later `close` answers `Dropped` again; its report's signal is the winning one when a shutdown had been triggered and the call's own otherwise, and it counts no execution. Its `Display` reads "the app was dropped before its shutdown closed its servers: they were released without their `close`, and no shutdown hook runs after the drop", which holds also for an abandoned shutdown whose before-shutdown hooks ran before the drop. A `close` after the drop of an app whose close step ended answers that shutdown's outcome. The claim and the drop's check take the same lock, so of a claim on one thread and the drop on another one runs entirely before the other. Nothing holds the release lock across an await or runs user code under it, it and the list's lock are read through when poisoned, and no path poisons it. A server's drop is user code and runs on the thread dropping the app, or on the thread ending or dropping the last claim, an aborted task's worker or a runtime shutting down and dropping its tasks among them; the shipped servers' drops abort tasks (47, 151, 152) and, on NATS, give up a hold on the roots' load (147). The docs on `App`, `AppHandle`, `AppHandle::close`, `AppShared::servers`, `release_servers`, the `release` field and the shutdown module's step 6 say so. The tests are in `fw-runtime-tokio`'s app tests, over `Recording`, a server keeping the `AppHandle` its `prepare` is handed, whose `drain` and `close` log that they ran and wait at a gate and whose drop is logged, `Gated`, a root module whose singleton logs its drop and whose before-shutdown hook logs and waits at its gate, and `paired`, two servers bound `a` then `b`. `an_app_dropped_before_a_running_close_s_close_step_leaves_it_every_server`, `an_app_dropped_during_a_running_close_s_drain_leaves_it_every_server` and `a_close_abandoned_after_the_app_s_drop_releases_the_servers` hold the claim of a running `close`. `a_close_called_before_the_app_s_drop_and_polled_after_it_closes_every_server` reads nothing touched at the drop, then the hook, `Phase::Closed`, `close b`, `close a`, both drops and the store last; Pending sign-off: that the mark is a count of claims and not the phase the sixty-sixth response named, a departure from its mechanism and not its behaviour; that the first two running-close tests do not tell the close step's release from `Closing`'s, the close step's being held by 146's `a_closed_app_lists_no_addresses` and `a_close_on_an_unserved_app_drops_its_server` and 149's fourth; and that a server's drop can run where a `close` future drops. A `close` that holds its claim and is neither polled to its end nor dropped holds the servers for as long as it is kept, and since the claim is taken at the call this now covers a `close` made and never polled as well as one polled once; such a future stored in something the app owns, a singleton among them, holds `Arc<AppShared>` from inside the app's own state, a cycle no drop reaches.
